en: Volume III, Part 2 [279]:
Now, the rule for the second section, called "Depositing," is stated.
Regarding that, Nārada states the nature of deposit:
"When one deposits one's own property with another out of trust and without hesitation,
that is called 'deposit' (nikṣepa) by the wise as a head of legal dispute."
*Upanidhi* and *nyāsa* are sub-varieties of deposits (*nikṣepa*). Bṛhaspati states their specific nature:
"That which is given unannounced, concealed, without a specified number, without being shown, and marked with a seal, is known as *aupanidhika*."
"That which is deposited in another's house out of fear of kings, thieves, or enemies, or due to deception regarding gambling debts— that is proclaimed as *nyāsa* (a deposit).
Thus says Nārada as well.
That which is deposited in the unfathomable and unknown ocean, one should know as an *upanidhi*; the wise understand a *nikṣepa* to be that which is counted.

[280] Thus says Yājñavalkya as well: "When an object kept in a container is delivered to another person without being described, and it is subsequently lost, that object is considered a *upanidhi* (sealed deposit); it must be restored in exactly the same condition. (YDh 2.65)

A casket, chest, or similar container, and the goods contained within it—without specifying their particular form, number, or other attributes—are deposited in another's hand for the purpose of safekeeping; such property is termed *aupanidhika*. Regarding the procedure for depositing a *nikṣepa*, Manu says:
"A wise man should entrust a deposit to one who is of noble birth, endowed with good conduct, knowledgeable in dharma, truthful, possessed of a large following, wealthy, and trustworthy" (MDh 8.179).
Bṛhaspati also says: "Having examined the location, the house, the site itself, as well as that debt, its various merits, truthfulness, purity, and the kinsmen, one should deposit the treasure."
Nārada further states that this deposit is of two kinds:
"That [deposit] is declared to be of two types: one with witnesses and likewise the other.
In the case of its denial, there should be proof in the same manner."
[281] Thus says Bṛhaspati as well: "That which is given either in the presence of witnesses or in secret is declared to be of two kinds;
it must be protected like a son, for it perishes through neglect."

"By whatever procedure it was deposited, by whom, and for what purpose it was manifested—exactly in that manner it must be returned; otherwise, it is not to be given, and [the one who withholds it] is an adversary.
Here, the term "adversary" (*pratyantara*) refers to anyone other than the depositor who holds ownership over the property deposited. Manu also says:
"In whatever manner a person deposits any object in the hand of another, it must be received back in that very same manner; as the delivery, so the recovery. (MDh 8.180).
Here, *dāya* means giving, placing, or depositing; *graha* means taking back. Bṛhaspati states the reward for the one who protects [the deposit]:
"The merit that would accrue from giving gold, silver, garments, and so forth,
that same merit belongs to one who protects a deposit as well as one who has come for refuge.
Thus, the fault of the consumer [of the deposit] was shown by that very same [author].
"As there is guilt for a woman in betraying her husband, or for a man in killing his son or friend,
so is there guilt for men in consuming or neglecting a deposit.
Bṛhaspati states that there is no fault, however, when the loss occurs due to divine intervention or other such calamities.
If it should meet with destruction due to an injury caused by two kings,
there is no fault in that case regarding the property along with the person who received it.

[282] Thus; the word "of the one who reproaches" (*garhītuḥ*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. By the word "king" (*rāja*), a cause for which there is no remedy is indicated. For this very reason, Kātyāyana states:

"Even in the case of what is not due to the king or fate, where a deposit has been destroyed, that loss is said to belong to the depositor along with his goods, provided it was not lost by the receiver. Thus it is said.
Nārada also says: "If [the object] is lost along with the debtor due to an act of fate (daiva) or the king, that loss falls upon the creditor; provided it was not caused by his own deceit."
The mention of "fate" (*daiva*) is intended to include thieves by implication; for this very reason, Yājñavalkya states:
"But he shall not be made to pay for what has been stolen by the king, by fate, or by thieves" (YDh 2.66). Manu also says:

"If it has been stolen by thieves, carried away by water, or consumed by fire, he need not pay [the fine] provided that he does not take anything from that [property]. (MDh 8.189) The meaning is that if he takes even a small portion of that wealth, then he must pay. And so says that same [author]:
"One would obtain nothing from the ocean if one did not draw anything from it. (MDh 8.188).

Regarding this, Kātyāyana states that in certain cases, even if something is lost due to some cause or another, the person who received it shall not be made to pay for it by way of its original source:
"But where the depositor, having learned of the loss of the property, deposits it elsewhere..."
"Even if it is destroyed despite all efforts, the borrower is not at all liable for payment.
Regarding destruction through negligence and the like, Bṛhaspati says:
"If, having taken a deposit, one should destroy it by means of separation or negligence..."
"Or, if he refuses when asked, he shall be compelled to pay it back with interest.
Kātyāyana also says:
"A deposit or other property belonging to another, which has been placed [with him] and neglected..."
"And he by whom [the loss] was caused through ignorance must indeed pay that [amount].
Regarding this, Vyāsa states a specific rule:
"If [the goods] were consumed, he should be made to pay with interest; if they were neglected, he should be made to pay the equivalent amount."
"One should cause [the borrower] to pay back whatever portion of the property was lost through negligence, even if it is slightly less.
Following a request for repayment, if the object has not been returned and subsequently perishes due to divine or royal intervention, only the value must be paid to the depositary. Thus says Vyāsa:
"If there is destruction after the request, even if caused by divine or royal [force], he [the depositary] [is liable only for the value]."
The receiver shall be made to restore it; otherwise, he deserves punishment.

[284] Thus; the word "merely the principal" (*mūlamātram*) is understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. For it is improper to demand payment with interest when the offense consists merely in the delay of returning [the deposit]. Regarding the penalty for failing to give it back after being asked, Nārada says:
"But he who, being asked by the depositor, does not return the deposit, shall be punished by the king and, if [the property] has been lost, shall be made to pay an equivalent amount. Thus.
Furthermore, regarding one who uses a deposit without the permission of the depositor, that same [author] states the punishment:
"If he should recover property there without the permission of the depositor, he shall be punished for that as well and shall restore it along with its interest. Thus.
Yājñavalkya also says:
"One who lives according to his own will shall be fined, and he must pay that [debt] along with interest" (YDh 2.67).
In this context, the fine should also be understood as being equal [to the debt]. To this effect, Manu says:

"The king shall cause the one who misappropriates a deposit to pay a fine equal to its value; likewise for the one who misappropriates an open deposit, without distinction. Thus [says Manu, MDh 8.192].
Bṛhaspati also says:
"Where the borrower denies [the debt] by means of witnesses or by oath,
the king, having established the truth, shall cause him to pay the deposit along with an equal fine as a penalty.
Thus Manu states the punishment for the depositor's false testimony.
"Whatever deposit was made by someone with certain people in the presence of a family, it should be understood to be exactly that much; one who speaks falsely deserves punishment. (MDh 8.194).
One who speaks in contradiction to the testimony of witnesses regarding a deposit made in their presence is liable to punishment. However, regarding a deposit made without witnesses, Bṛhaspati says:
"Where a dispute arises concerning a secret deposit, an ordeal is ordained as the means of discernment for both parties.
Thus [it is said]. Manu states the punishment for the depositor and the receiver when they speak falsely:
One should seek out the thief of a deposit and the person who did not actually make the deposit by all possible means and even by Vedic oaths.

"He who does not return a deposit, and he who demands what was never deposited—both of these should be punished like thieves, or made to pay a fine equal to the value of that [property]. (MDh 8.190–91).
For one who returns a deposited object at an improper time, the fine is double. Regarding this, Kātyāyana says:
"But the deposit should be accepted at the proper time; one should avoid accepting it when the time has passed.
One who returns it after the time has lapsed shall be fined and made to pay double [the value]. Thus it is said.

When a deposit has been placed in another's hand out of fear, it should be reclaimed once that fear has passed. Even when that fear has passed, one should not offer it back of one’s own accord; for Bṛhaspati records: "One should return it only when requested. If it is given of one's own accord while that fear still persists, that gift is deficient in timing and is due solely to wickedness; therefore, it is proper to punish even the one giving it. As for him who does not return the deposit by force, Manu says that the king should seize him and compel him to give it back.
If, however, he does not give that gold to them according to the rule, he should be seized and compelled to pay; such is the established principle of Dharma.

"Regarding property that has been deposited, as well as that which has been entrusted out of friendship, the king shall reach a decision without harming the holder of the deposit. (MDh 8.196) "Without harming" means without striking. Nārada states that there is no fault if the depositor dies and the wealth passes to the next of kin.
"But he who would give [the deposit] himself to the next-of-kin of the deceased—
neither the king nor the relatives shall compel him to restore it.
When, however, he does not give it himself, then [the author] says regarding the next-of-kin:
"One should seek that object with affection, using only gentle means;
or, having investigated his conduct, one should settle the matter through conciliation alone.
Thus Nārada extends the legal principles stated regarding deposits (*nikṣepa*) by analogy to borrowed items (*yācita*) and the like.
"This same rule is seen to apply in cases of borrowed items, pledges, and so forth; as well as in the case of artisans, deposits, bailments, and counter-deposits. Thus says Yājñavalkya.
[288] "This rule applies to borrowed items, those held in trust, deposits, and the like" (YDh 2.67).

A "borrowed item" (*yācita*) is an ornament or similar object belonging to another that has been requested for occasions such as festivals and brought into one's own presence. An "item held in trust" (*anvāhita*) is wealth belonging to another that is kept with oneself having been designated as belonging to a different creditor. "Deposits" (*nyāsa-nikṣepa*) have already been explained previously. Bṛhaspati also says: "In the case of an item held in trust, a borrowed item, an artisan’s deposit, and a pledge..."
"This same rule applies when [an object] has been entrusted for the purpose of seeking refuge.

Regarding this, "entrustment to an artisan" (*śilpinyāsa*) refers to gold or similar materials placed into the hands of a goldsmith or other craftsman for the purpose of making a ring or other articles. By this, it is stated that if an item entrusted to an artisan's hand is destroyed—provided it was not due to an act of God (*daiva*) or the king (*rāja*)—the goldsmith and others shall not be made to pay for it. On this point, Kātyāyana states an exception:
"If the deposit is being processed by those [artisans] within a fixed number of days..."
"A craftsman should restore it to its former state; even if it was destroyed by fate, he must be made to pay for it.
Regarding items such as cloth placed in the hands of washermen and others for the purpose of making ritual offerings (*nairmālya*) and so forth, the same author says:
"If destruction occurs due to a fault of the deposit, the craftsman shall not be made to pay for it."
If [the work] was entrusted for the purpose of restoration, he should cause it to be paid back due to defects in craftsmanship.

[289] Thus it is said. Regarding a case where yarn and such materials have been placed with a weaver or similar artisan for the purpose of making cloth, and are lost while in the state of being a fragmentary cloth or the like, or are lost because they were not accepted by the owner when offered by the weaver or others upon completion—concerning that too, he (Yājñavalkya) says: "And whatever work has been lost through craftmanship, that belongs to the laborer; if he wishes to give it back in full, it shall be lost to him if he does not accept it. Thus it is stated.

If a workman’s craft—such as weaving and the like—is impaired or destroyed, that loss belongs to the workman alone; the meaning is that he should perform the work of weaving again even without receiving further wages. If the owner does not provide the thread and other materials again, then even in the absence of further weaving and so forth, the wages already paid to the workman shall not be recovered by the giver. If the owner, having provided sufficient or complete cloth and the like, refuses to accept it from the workman who desires to deliver it, that sufficient quantity shall be lost to him. Regarding the matter of borrowed goods, a specific rule has been stated by that same author: *na dadāti pratiśrutya daṇḍyo māṣakaviṃśatim | dāpyas tv adadat taṃ tu daṇḍyaś ca dviguṇaṃ damam ||* "If one does not give after having promised, he should be fined twenty māṣakas; but if he does not give the thing [borrowed] at all, he should be made to pay it back and be fined double the amount. *Yājñavalkya Smṛti*, Vyavahārādhyāya 2.184–185.
If, after having assigned that work or fixed a time limit,
one who has been requested does not pay when the work is half-finished or when the time has arrived, he shall not be compelled to pay.

[290] Thus: if one has requested something for the purpose of a task that is to be accomplished over a long period of time, or if one should request it by fixing a specific duration, saying, "Let it be given for as long as a year," and then, while that task is still underway or within the fixed period, the borrower does not return the loaned item when asked, he is not to be made to pay interest. He need only return the loaned item itself once the task is completed or when the fixed period has expired. If even then he does not return it, then in the event of its destruction due to fate or other causes, he must pay its value; so says that same author.
"If a task has been performed when the time for it had arrived, one should not pay even if requested;
however, if that [task] is lost or [the performer] dies, the borrower shall pay its value. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, he [Yājñavalkya] states that in some cases, even if the time has not arrived, the borrowed item must be returned upon request.
"Furthermore, if there is a failure of the task, that loss shall belong to the owner himself;
however, if the time for delivery has not yet arrived, he must be made to pay even for work that is only half-done.
Thus ends the section on deposits (*nikṣepaprakaraṇam*).
Now, regarding sale without ownership, Nārada states its essential nature:
"Having found, or having recovered by force, property belonging to another that had been deposited, lost, or stolen..."
"That which is sold in the absence of the owner is to be known as *asvāmivikraya* (sale by one who is not the owner). Bṛhaspati also says:
"A deposit, an object sent for delivery, a pledge, what is borrowed, and a security..."
"One who sells to a person in secret is called a non-owner. Thus stating that a transaction entered into by a non-owner is nullified, Kātyāyana says:
"One should annul a sale by a non-owner, as well as a gift or a pledge."
Nārada also says: "But that purchase or sale which is made by one who is not the owner is always to be known as invalid in legal proceedings."
Therefore, the owner shall take back property sold by one who is not its owner. And so says Nārada:

"Having recovered property sold by one who is not its owner, the owner shall obtain it. Furthermore, the recovery of that property must be done only after reporting it to the king, because otherwise a penalty is prescribed. And so says Yājñavalkya:
"He who recovers property that has been stolen or lost from the hand of another, without having reported it to the king, shall be fined ninety-six *paṇas*. (YDh 2.172).
Furthermore, when the owner is unable to recover it from the hand of another, he says the same:
"Having recovered property that was lost or stolen, one should cause the thief to be apprehended;
or, if there is a lapse of time or place, one should seize him oneself and hand him over. (YDh 2.169)

Having seen one's own lost or stolen property in the possession of either a finder or a thief, one should have that finder or thief apprehended by royal officers and others. The meaning is that if there is a lapse of time or distance in order to bring the royal officers and others, then one should seize the person oneself and hand them over to the king. Furthermore, when one sees one's own property in the hand of a purchaser only after the sale has already taken place, he says the same:
"One may recover one's own property if it was sold by another; the fault lies with the purchaser if the transaction was not publicly announced."
"A thief [is one who] steals from a low person in secret, for a low price, or at an improper time. (YDh 2.268)

If the owner sees his own property sold by another, he may then recover it and take possession of it; for a sale by one who is not the owner lacks the capacity to transfer ownership to another. However, the buyer incurs fault if the purchase was made secretly or in concealment. He becomes a thief—meaning he is to be punished like a thief—if the purchase is made from a "low" person (one lacking a legitimate means of acquiring goods), in secret (in a private place), for a "low price" (at a significantly lower value than the item's worth), or at an "improper time" (such as at night). As stated by Manu: *Yad āhitam nyāsayogair yac ca śilpair apāśritam | kanyābhṛtiḥ śiṣyādhyāpanam auṣadhyākarakarma ca || kusīdaṃ caiva saptaitān vāṇijyopāyān pracakṣate |* *Yas tv etāny upāyāni hy asatām āśrayed dvijaḥ | sa vai vāntāśanaḥ prokto muniśāstreṣu sarvadā ||* *Vāṇijyopāyān iti vacanād anyatrāpi vāṇijye 'satām āśrayaṇe doṣaḥ |* *Asambhave tu kretāraṃ paripṛcchet sabhāsadaḥ | apahnave tasya dravyasya naṣṭaṃ dāpyo damaṃ tathā ||* *Anāgataṃ tu yaḥ kaścid gṛhītvā bandham icchati | na tatra prāpnuyāt kiṃcid anyatra kṛtasaṃvidā ||* *Gṛhītvā yo hi bandhaṃ tu krayārthaṃ na prayacchati | sa nigṛhya tathā bandhaṃ māsaṃ rakṣet sabhāsadaḥ ||* *Māse 'tikrānte vikretur dravyasya rūpakaṃ bhavet | dvitīye 'rdhatṛtīye tu kretur eva tad iṣyate ||* *Yadi kretā svakīyaṃ dravyaṃ na darśayati tadā kretur doṣaḥ |* *Hīnād dravyāgamopāyahīnāt, raha ekānte, hīnamūlye alpatareṇa dravyeṇa adhikamūlyakraye ca, velāhīne rātryādau kṛte kraye ca sa coro bhavati | taskaravad daṇḍyo bhavatīty arthaḥ |* As has been said by Manu: *Yena krītaṃ tu tat kṣetraṃ krayeṇa dharmataḥ sthitam | na sa śaknoti taṃ bhoktuṃ kretāraṃ naiva cāhvayet ||* *Yadi kretā svakīyaṃ dravyaṃ na darśayati tadā kretur doṣaḥ |* *Hīnād dravyāgamopāyahīnāt, raha ekānte, hīnamūlye alpatareṇa dravyeṇa adhikamūlyakraye ca, velāhīne rātryādau kṛte kraye ca sa coro bhavati | taskaravad daṇḍyo bhavatīty arthaḥ |* As stated by Manu: *Yena krītaṃ tu tat kṣetraṃ krayeṇa dharmataḥ sthitam | na sa śaknoti taṃ bhoktuṃ kretāraṃ naiva cāhvayet ||* *Yadi kretā svakīyaṃ dravyaṃ na darśayati tadā kretur doṣaḥ |* *Hīnād dravyāgamopāyahīnāt, raha ekānte, hīnamūlye alpatareṇa dravyeṇa adhikamūlyakraye ca, velāhīne rātryādau kṛte kraye ca sa coro bhavati | taskaravad daṇḍyo bhavatīty arthaḥ |* As stated by Manu: *Yena krītaṃ tu tat kṣetraṃ krayeṇa dharmataḥ sthitam | na sa śaknoti taṃ bhoktuṃ kretāraṃ naiva cāhvayet ||* *Yadi kretā svakīyaṃ dravyaṃ na darśayati tadā kretur doṣaḥ |* *Hīnād dravyāgamopāyahīnāt, raha ekānte, hīnamūlye alpatareṇa dravyeṇa adhikamūlyakraye ca, velāhīne rātryādau kṛte kraye ca sa coro bhavati | taskaravad daṇḍyo bhavatīty arthaḥ |* As stated by Manu: *Yena krītaṃ tu tat kṣetraṃ krayeṇa dharmataḥ sthitam | na sa śaknoti taṃ bhoktuṃ kretāraṃ naiva cāhvayet ||* *Yadi kretā svakīyaṃ dravyaṃ na darśayati tadā kretur doṣaḥ |* *Hīnād dravyāgamopāyahīnāt, raha ekānte, hīnamūlye alpatareṇa dravyeṇa adhikamūlyakraye ca, velāhīne rātryādau kṛte kraye ca sa coro bhavati | taskaravad daṇḍyo bhavatīty arthaḥ |* As stated by Manu: *Yena krītaṃ tu tat kṣetraṃ krayeṇa dharmataḥ sthitam | na sa śaknoti taṃ bhoktuṃ kretāraṃ naiva cāhvayet ||* *Yadi kretā svakīyaṃ dravyaṃ na darśayati tadā kretur doṣaḥ |* *Hīnād dravyāgamopāyahīnāt, raha ekānte, hīnamūlye alpatareṇa dravyeṇa adhikamūlyakraye ca, velāhīne rātryādau kṛte kraye ca sa coro bhavati | taskaravad daṇḍyo bhavatīty arthaḥ |* As stated by Manu: *Yena krītaṃ tu tat kṣetraṃ krayeṇa dharmataḥ sthitam | na sa śaknoti taṃ bhoktuṃ kretāraṃ naiva cāhvayet ||* *Yadi kretā svakīyaṃ dravyaṃ na darśayati tadā kretur doṣaḥ |* *Hīnād dravyāgamopāyahīnāt, raha ekānte, hīnamūlye alpatareṇa dravyeṇa adhikamūlyakraye ca, velāhīne rātryādau kṛte kraye ca sa coro bhavati | taskaravad daṇḍyo bhavatīty arthaḥ |* As stated by Manu: *Yena krītaṃ tu tat kṣetraṃ krayeṇa dharmataḥ sthit

[293] "Having acquired property sold by one who is not its owner, the true owner shall recover it; the purchaser's title is established if the purchase was made openly, whereas there is theft if the purchase was made in secret. Thus Bṛhaspati also has shown that the purchaser is either blameless or culpable, depending on whether the purchase was made unknowingly or knowingly.

"But where it has been purchased for a price and previously reported to the king, no fault exists therein; one becomes a thief only through secret sale. Thus, when the purchaser has reported [the transaction] to the king even before the purchase for a low price, there is no fault. The meaning of the term "secret sale" (*upavikraya*) has been shown by that very same [author].

"Buying within a house, outside a village, at night, from an unreliable person, or for a low price—this should be known as *upavikraya* (fraudulent sale). Here, "from an unreliable person" means from a *caṇḍāla* or similar individual. The mention of an "unreliable person" is intended to include by implication those such as slaves who have not been authorized by their owner. For this very reason, Nārada says:

"By purchasing from a slave who lacks his master's consent, from an invalid person, in secret, for a low price, or at an improper time, one becomes a partaker of that fault. The phrase "partaker of that fault" means a partaker of the fault of a thief. Kātyāyana states how the owner may establish proof by means of evidence when there is a dispute regarding the sold property: [295] *Krayeṇa sa kretā mūlyaṃ labheta nānyathā* | *Vināśe vyayakṛd dravyaṃ pramādyec caiva naśyati* || iti | "By means of the sale, the purchaser shall recover the price, and not otherwise. In the event of loss, he who caused the expenditure shall bear the cost, and if he was negligent, he shall perish [lose the claim]. Thus it is said.

"But the owner of the lost property shall establish that wealth as his own through witnesses and other means. Here, "the owner of the lost property" (*nāṣṭika*) refers to one whose wealth has been lost. "That wealth" (*taddhana*) refers to the lost wealth. "Through witnesses and other means" (*jñātṛbhiḥ*) refers to witnesses and so forth. "Shall establish as his own" (*svakam prakurvīta*) means he shall prove it to be his; this is the meaning. When it is asked how he should prove it, Yājñavalkya says:
"The lost [property] must be proven by title and possession; otherwise, it is not so."
"His self-restraint is bound fivefold; it has not been revealed to the king. (YDh 2.171).
As for the source [of this], it should be understood as stated in another Smṛti:
"What is acquired, what is obtained through gift or purchase, that which is gained by valor, and likewise that which is received through marriage..."

[295] "The acquisition of wealth is sixfold, including that which comes from a kinsman or from one who has no offspring. Regarding this, Kātyāyana states that even the non-loss of ownership over one's own wealth must be secured through the power of giving: "Having made it ungiven, relinquished, or sold, one recovers one's own wealth."

The meaning is that, having established by means of proofs that "this has neither been given nor sold," the original owner (nāṣṭika) recovers his own wealth from the seller and others. Regarding this matter, Bṛhaspati states a specific rule: "But if the former owner comes and investigates that property, the source [of acquisition] must be shown there; from that, the buyer's innocence shall be established."

The seller is the root [of the matter]. Regarding this, Vyāsa states immediately after the appearance of the seller: "Once the original source has been recovered, the buyer is by no means to be prosecuted;
rather, at that time, the dispute shall be between the owner seeking restitution and the seller."
But when the seller, having been produced as the root of the matter, offers no further defense, then Bṛhaspati says:
"Where the seller, once produced, fails in the legal proceeding,
he shall pay the purchase price and a fine to the king, and the value of the property to the owner."
[296] Thus says Nārada as well: "The seller shall give to the owner what was his own, and to the buyer the price that was paid;
likewise, he shall pay a fine to the king—such is the rule regarding sale without ownership."
But when the original seller has gone to another country, Kātyāyana says:
"A period for the recovery of the original [seller] must be granted according to the number of *yojanas* [of distance];
and one should effect a public purchase in the presence of witnesses and one's own kinsmen."
"In that case, no other action—neither divine nor human—is prescribed;

once the purchase has been validated by the king, he (the seller) should not be made to say anything. This is the meaning: if a purchaser, even after a lapse of time, is unable to produce the original source but does provide proof of the purchase, he is the lowest of men; yet he is not to be punished by the king, and consequently, the owner who lost the property shall not recover it. Thus it was stated by Manu:
"Now, if the root source is untraceable, but the purchase was proven by witnesses, the seller is released by the king without punishment, and the original owner recovers his property" (MDh 8.202).
The recovery of the wealth from the purchaser occurs only after he has paid half the value. And so says Kātyāyana:

Where a merchant has sold goods situated in a marketplace that were known to be such by royal officers, yet purchased from an unknown source, or where the seller has died; [in such cases, the purchaser may be held liable].
"The owner, having paid half the price, may recover his own property;

in that case, by legal proceeding, half of what was stolen shall belong to the two [parties]. This means "from one whose source is unknown" and "from one whose place of origin is unknown. Between the two options—publicizing the purchase or producing the original source—it is the option of producing the source that should be adopted, provided it is possible. Thus it has been stated by Kātyāyana:
When the defendant has presented the original source, if the plaintiff should speak again of a purchase, he is merely bringing forward the source itself;
there is no need for a proof of purchase.
"But one whose root [of ownership] cannot be brought forward must clear up the purchase itself.
He [Yājñavalkya] himself states that when one neither produces the root [document] nor demonstrates the purchase, then he is to be punished:
"Not producing the root, or failing to clear up the purchase..."
"According to the claim, he shall be made to pay the wealth to the creditor and a fine as well.
He [Yājñavalkya] himself states the loss of the owner:
"If the owner does not recover his own wealth through his kinsmen..."
And for the sake of preventing such a contingency, he deserves punishment like that of a thief.

[298] Thus, "prasaṅga" means an excessive consequence. Yājñavalkya states the measure of the fine: "A lost item must be recovered through [the owner's] title or possession; otherwise, if it is not proven by him, the fine to the king shall be five times its value. (YDh 2.171)

The *pañcabandha* (fivefold fine) is that in which a fifth part of the disputed wealth is attached as a penalty; this refers to cases of minor offense. However, regarding major offenses, Vyāsa states: "If the plaintiff fails to prove through witnesses that the property was used for an illicit purpose, he shall be made to pay double the fine, and the purchaser shall forfeit that property."
As for the statement of Marīci, which establishes the buyer's ownership when the sale has been publicly announced: "That which was displayed in the marketplace, known by the king’s officers,
and purchased by the buyer during the day— he, being pure, recovers the wealth."

Thus, this refers to a case where the lost owner has not proven his ownership of the property; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the counter-example in the Anuvacana which states, "Now, if the original price cannot be recovered. When the purchaser does not establish the purchase through witnesses and other means, and the lost owner likewise does not prove his own ownership, Bṛhaspati declares the decision:

"But in a lawsuit lacking evidence, the king himself shall make the determination based on the status of the individuals, according to whether they are equal, inferior, or superior [in their claims]."

The king shall reach a decision by dividing the wealth that is the subject of dispute between the two men—the man who denies ownership (*nāṣṭika*) and the buying man—into equal, lesser, or greater portions, declaring, "This is yours.

If it is objected: "Even in the absence of human means of proof (*mānuṣapramāṇa*), since divine means (*divya*) exist, a lawsuit devoid of proof is simply not possible," it is replied: Because in this very case of a sale without ownership (*asvāmivikraya*), the absence of divine means is stated. And so says Kātyāyana:
"One should not perform a public sale with virtuous kinsmen or one's own relatives;
no other rite is prescribed there, whether divine or human.
Furthermore:
The claimant should first establish his own wealth through his kinsmen;
afterwards, for the sake of his own purification, the purchaser should establish the purchase through his own relatives.

By this statement, the absence of evidence other than witnesses is understood. As for that which was stated by Kātyāyana—“In a legal proceeding where there is no document and no witnesses, one should prescribe divine [ordeals]”—that should be understood as referring to cases where there is no traditional law (smṛti) prohibiting divine ordeals. Furthermore, Kātyāyana speaks of the loss of wealth for both the buyer and the owner even in a lawsuit where such evidence exists:
In that case, half of the two [penalties] shall be removed according to legal procedure;
otherwise, there is the fault of an unknown purchase, or likewise the failure to provide protection.

"These two have been declared by the wise to cause the loss of property for both the buyer and the owner: purchase from one whose location is unknown, and purchase made without [the owner's] knowledge.

Purchase from one whose location is unknown is "purchase from an unknown source" (*avijñātasthānakāt krayaḥ*). Alternatively, "purchase from an unknown source" refers to a purchase made because it was not known that this person was the actual owner. Marīci also says:

[301] "Because it was acquired without knowledge, where no fault exists on the part of the seller, an equal loss should be assigned to both the buyer and the owner. Thus Nārada states that even for one who uses what has been given by the owner without his consent— just like the seller— the owner may impose a fine.
One should eat only what has been specifically designated, whether it be a woman, an animal, or even the earth;
however, he who eats what has not been offered must cause the enjoyment [of that food] to be given away.
But one who enjoys by his own power any property not specifically assigned— be it clothing, a field, a house, or the like— deserves punishment like a thief.
Likewise, one who eats the meat of an ox, a cow, or even a new slave without it being specifically permitted,
shall pay a fine of four paṇas.
A female slave, a boat, or a draft animal used as a pledge is not subject to [the creditor's] enjoyment;
however, the user shall clear that debt by means of the sale price of the goods.
On the day [of sale], a female slave was two paṇas, a milch cow eight paṇas,
a bull thirteen [paṇas], and a horse and land sixteen [paṇas].
He who forcibly enjoys a boat, a horse, a bow, a plough, or the tools of a craftsman, shall be made to pay eight paṇas for each day.
[302] "For a mortar, half a *paṇa*; for a pestle, two *paṇas*;
and for a winnowing basket, half a *paṇa*—the Sage has declared these to be two *paṇas*.
Thus ends the section known as "Sale by One Who Is Not the Owner."
Now, the legal category known as *saṃbhūyasamutthāna* (joint enterprise) is discussed;
its nature was stated by Nārada:
"Where merchants and others perform an undertaking collectively..."
"That is known as the legal title of 'partnership' (saṃbhūyasamutthāna).
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati points out those who are qualified [to engage in it]:
"By those who are of noble birth, capable, untiring, wise, and knowledgeable in coinage..."
"One should perform joint activities with those who are pure, brave, and knowledgeable regarding income and expenditure.

Thus [it is said]. "Activity" refers to agriculture, trade, crafts, sacrifices, music, and military affairs. Expertise in coinage is useful for commercial activity; mere knowledge of income and expenditure is useful for agricultural activity; wisdom is useful for artistic activities such as music; for sacrificial activity, however, nobility of birth, wisdom, and purity are required; and for military activity, bravery alone is required. Dexterity and diligence, however, are useful in all cases. For this very reason, that same author prohibits those who lack dexterity and so forth.
[303] "Those who are unattached, not indolent, free from disease, not afflicted, fortunate, and without dependence—wise men should perform activities such as trade together with these.
As for those who engage in activities such as trade collectively, they shall share in the profit according to their respective contributions to the capital. And so says Bṛhaspati:

"But for those who carry out the transaction with gold, grain, liquids, and so forth, their profit shall be of that same kind, according to whether the shares are equal, deficient, or excessive. Thus it is said.
He [the author] states that just like the profit, the loss and so forth are likewise the same: "The same applies to loss and so forth."
"Whatever portion—whether equal, less, or more—has been contributed by someone, he shall incur expenses accordingly, perform the work, and likewise receive the profit. Thus [it is said].
Yājñavalkya states an exception to the rule that "profit is according to the capital."

"For merchants performing work for the sake of profit in partnership, the gain and loss shall be according to the capital, or as determined by agreement" (YDh 2.259). "By agreement" means by convention (*samaya*). The meaning is that the gain and loss are to be understood as determined or apportioned according to the specific status of the individuals, and not merely according to the capital. Vyāsa states what must be done by those acting in partnership:
Whether face-to-face or out of sight, those who deceive one another may conduct buying and selling according to the nature of various commodities.
"Those who do not protect their goods shall pay the toll on the road;
otherwise, those standing outside the toll station shall be made to pay double.
Thus says Nārada as well.
"They shall, remaining steadfast in their own agreement, examine the goods, the collective fund, expenditures, receipts, the load, the quality, and so forth, without deviation.
Thus Bṛhaspati states the method of decision when those acting in partnership have a dispute among themselves.
Those very same persons are declared to be both examiners and witnesses for one another in a doubtful matter, provided they are not subject to deception and are not possessed by divine affliction.
"Whosoever among them is known to be a cheat in buying or selling must be cleared by means of oaths; this rule applies to all disputes.
Regarding the loss of property caused by fate or the king, he says the same:
"When there is loss or destruction therein caused by fate or the king, that [loss] is declared to belong to all [the partners]; it should be apportioned according to their respective shares.

Here, "loss" (*hāni*) refers specifically to diminution (*kṣaya*), whereas "expenditure" (*vyaya*) is for the purpose of increase. Regarding the destruction of property due to an individual's fault, he himself says:

"Or, if one who has not been appointed should, out of negligence, cause [the property] to be lost while it is being guarded, he alone must provide that [compensation]; it shall be given by him to all the partners. Here, "one who has not been appointed" means one who has not been authorized by the partners. Regarding the fact that there is a greater share of profit for the protector against thieves and the like, Kātyāyana says:

"But whoever recovers property from a thief, from water, or from fire, a tenth part of that shall be given to him; this rule applies to all types of property. The meaning of "shall recover" is that he should protect [the property] according to his ability. Bṛhaspati also says:
"But that person who, out of fear of the king or fate, protects [the property] according to his own ability—after giving him a tenth part, they may take [the remainder] from then on.
As for one who does not recover, through means such as legal proceedings, money lent by partners along with those partners, he suffers the loss of profit. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
"But that which is given by those acting in concert must likewise be requested [from them] as a whole;

and whoever does not request it is deprived of his share. Thus he says the same regarding the fact that one person alone, with the consent of all, shall perform the business for everyone: "Whatever has been given by those assembled together must be requested from them in the same manner. And whoever does not ask for it is deprived of his profit. Thus he says the very same thing concerning the fact that a single person, approved by all, shall carry out the business for all.
"But when a single man, approved by many, gives wealth or causes a legal document (*karaṇa*) to be executed, it shall be considered as having been done by all.
Here, *karaṇa* refers to a written document and so forth. Manu states what must be performed by officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who act in concert:

"But the officiating priests, having assembled as invited at a *sattra* sacrifice, should perform their duties according to their respective fitness and likewise receive the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
The meaning of "likewise" is that they should receive the fee in accordance with the work performed. And so says that same [author]:
“By men acting together here in the performance of their respective duties, the apportionment of shares must be made according to this rule of procedure” (MDh 8.211).

And this apportionment of shares applies specifically to the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) prescribed merely as being connected to the sacrifice in such terms as “its sacrificial fee is one hundred and twelve,” and not to that which is prescribed by specifying particular officiants. For this very reason, it was stated by that same author:
"Or the Adhvaryu may take the chariot at the establishment of the fires, and the Brahman the horse;
the Hotṛ may take the horse, and the Udgātṛ the cart at the purchase [of the Soma]. (MDh 8.209).
He (the same author) states the apportionment of the shares of the sacrificial fee:

"Of all [the heirs], the principal ones are entitled to half; others are entitled to half of that [half]; those entitled to a third receive a third part; and those entitled to a fourth receive a fourth part. (MDh 8.210)

Among all sixteen officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the four principal ones—the Hotṛ, Adhvaryu, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, and Udgātṛ—are entitled to half of the hundred cows. By virtue of the necessity of completing the shares for all, they receive half through a portion consisting of forty-eight forms. The others—the Maitrāvaruṇa, Pratiprasthātṛ, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, and Prastotṛ—are entitled to half of that; they receive half through a portion of twenty-four forms, which is half of the principal share. Furthermore, those who receive a third—the Acchāvāka, Neṣṭṛ, Agnīdhra, and Pratihartṛ—receive a third through a portion consisting of sixteen parts, which is one-third of the principal share. Those who receive a quarter—the Grāvastotṛ, Netṛ, Potṛ, and Subrahmaṇyā—receive a quarter through a portion of twelve cows, which is one-fourth of the principal share. The internal distribution among the four principal priests is equal. In the same way, the internal distribution among those following them is also equal. Thus says the *Kātyāyana-sūtra*: "Twelve each for the first group, six each for the second group, four each for the third group, and three each for the others. Manu states that the share to be given should be according to the degree of participation in the performance of their respective sets of duties.

"If a priest chosen for a sacrifice should abandon his own duty, a share corresponding to that work must be given to him by the co-performers" (MDh 8.206). "By the co-performers" means by those acting in concert; it has been stated that one should give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to the portion of work performed. He states an exception to this in a certain case: [the same author says]:
"When the sacrificial fees have been distributed, one who abandons his own work shall receive his entire share, provided he has it performed by another. (MDh 8.207).
"By another" means by someone among those belonging to his own group who is nearby. Regarding the death of an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) during the course of the ritual, Nārada says:

"Even in the event of a calamity befalling the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), another shall perform that ritual; he shall receive from that [performer] the portion of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) as it was originally assigned. Thus Bṛhaspati states what must be done by those who work together, such as farmers.
"A wise person should engage in agriculture together with those who are equal in terms of the draft animals, the drivers, the seeds, and so forth, as well as the equipment for the fields.
Here, "draft animals" refers to ploughs and the like; "drivers" refers to oxen and the like. He states what should be avoided regarding the fields: he himself says:
"One should carefully avoid a field that is saline or infested with mice, especially one located on a mountain, near a city, or by a royal highway. Thus he speaks.
He [the same author] states those things to be avoided among external factors:
"A wise farmer should not employ as a draught animal one that is emaciated, too old, small, diseased, fleeing, one-eyed, or lame.
Regarding the specific reduction in yield resulting from individual defects, the same author says:

"He who suffers a loss of the field due to the failure of the external seed must restore that very [loss] to all those who live by agriculture. In this passage, the mention of "external seed" is intended as an illustration for all the implements of cultivation. He [Yājñavalkya] himself states the distribution of profits among artisans working in association:

"Where goldsmiths and others perform their craft collectively, they shall receive wages according to their respective shares in accordance with the work performed. Here, *nirveśa* means wages. Kātyāyana also says:
"Those skilled in the knowledge of the crafts and the master artisan shall be the craftsmen;
they shall take one, two, three, or four shares according to their respective portions.
Thus Bṛhaspati states that among those who construct palaces and the like, the principal share belongs to the chief.
"Whether it be a palace, a temple, or even a city, for those who build them together according to dharma, the leader deserves two shares. Thus he [Yājñavalkya] states.
He [the same author] also describes the nature of the artisans:
"An artisan (*śilpī*) is defined by the wise as one skilled in the arts who fabricates gold, base metals (*kupya*), thread, wood, stone, and leather.
Here, "base metal" (*kupya*) refers to tin, lead, and so forth, distinct from gold and silver. He [Yājñavalkya] himself speaks of thieves:
But whatever has been recovered from a foreign land by thieves at the command of their master,
they shall give a sixth part to the king and divide the remainder among themselves according to their respective shares.

"The principal [shareholder] shall receive four parts; the hero shall obtain three parts; the capable one shall take two parts; but the others shall have equal shares. This refers to wealth brought from a foreign land, meaning from the territory of an enemy. This rule concerns property recovered from the territory of a powerful enemy. However, regarding property recovered from the territory of a weak enemy, Kātyāyana says:
If wealth has been seized from a foreign kingdom by thieves at his command,
they shall set aside one-tenth for the king and divide the remainder according to the prescribed rule.
"But the one who is the leader among the thieves shall take four shares;
the brave man three shares; the capable man two; and the rest, each only one.
He says that the same applies to the loss as well: "The loss is exactly like this."
"If among them, whoever should incur a seizure [of property] that has been extended [to others], they shall bear the responsibility for its release according to their respective shares. Thus,
he [Yājñavalkya] himself stated the method for calculating the shares of dancers.
[312] This very rule has been declared by the virtuous as the law for dancers:
for one who knows the rhythm receives half, while the singers receive equal shares.
"The leader deserves two shares; this is the rule for those working in partnership.

Thus, the chief among artisans has been described. This law, consisting of two shares, is cited for the leader among dancers and others who work in partnership. This same division should be understood to apply to those partners who have not previously formed an association. And likewise, that same [text] states:
"Of merchants, farmers, thieves, and artisans..."
"The decision regarding all those who act as partners in an undivided enterprise [is final].

Thus ends the section titled "Partnership" (*saṃbhūyasamutthāna*). Now follows the section titled "Non-delivery of what has been given" (*dattāpradānika*), preceded by the conclusion of the section on partnership.
Regarding this legal subject,
Bṛhaspati says:
"Thus has been declared in its entirety the remedy for those who act in concert."

"The nature of what is not to be given (*adeya*), what is to be given (*deya*), what has been given (*datta*), and what has not been given (*adatta*) is now described. This means that the essential character of these four types—beginning with what is not to be given—is being explained. For this very reason, Nārada says:
"He who, having improperly given away property, desires to take it back..."
That legal dispute is known in tradition as "non-delivery of what has been given."

[313] "That which is not to be given, that which is to be given, that which has been given, and that which has not been given—this fourfold path of giving is to be understood in legal proceedings. Thus [it is said]. Bṛhaspati states the various types of things that are not to be given:

"Common property, sons, wives, and so forth, one's entire estate, a deposit, that which has been requested, and what has been promised to another—these eight types are traditionally held to be not to be given. Here, "common property" refers to items such as chariots that have multiple independent owners. Nārada also states:

That which has been deposited with another, that which has been borrowed, a pledge, that which is held in common, a trust, one's wife and sons, and one's entire property when there is offspring; [these must not be divided].
"For even when a person is beset by the most grievous calamities, the teachers declare that certain things must not be given away, namely that which has already been promised to another.
Just like a loan for use (*anvāhita*) and other such items, a woman's property (*strīdhana*) is also not to be given away. For this very reason, Dakṣa says:

Common property, what has been requested, a deposit, a pledge, one's wife, that wealth [already mentioned], what has been entrusted for delivery, a sealed deposit, and one's entire estate— these cannot be divided when there is a male descendant.
"Even in times of distress, nine things must not be given away by the wise;
he who gives them is a foolish soul and that man becomes liable to penance. Thus, Manu has declared a punishment for accepting those things which ought not to be accepted.
"He who takes what should not be taken, and he who gives what should not be given—both of these are to be punished like thieves and fined the highest amercement.
Here, the mention of "what should not be taken" (*adeya*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for "what has not been given" (*adatta*) as well; for this very reason, Nārada says:
"He who takes what is not given out of greed, and he who bestows what should not be given—
both of these are to be punished by a king who knows the Dharma.
When it is asked, "What then should be given?", he himself says:

"Whatever wealth remains in excess after supporting one's family must be given away; by withholding it, one incurs sin. The meaning is that one should give while still maintaining the family. Kātyāyana also says:

"Except for the house, whatever property remains after providing for the maintenance of the family—that is one's own wealth which may be given; otherwise, it should not be given. Thus says Yājñavalkya as well.

"One's own property may be given away without detriment to one's family, with the exception of one's wife and son" (YDh 2.175). In this regard, the prohibition against giving away a son applies specifically to an only son; for if even he were given away, it would result in the extinction of the lineage. For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha prohibits the gift of an only son: "But one should neither give nor accept an only son; for he is for the sake of the continuity of the ancestors" (VaDh 15.3–4). Kātyāyana says the same. And thus, the authority over a son and a wife consists only in their instruction.
"And in sale as well as in gift, there is no power over a son belonging to the father.

From such statements as these, it is understood that the words of the *Sūtra* establishing the non-transferability [of a son] refer to the case of an only son. Even among those with multiple sons, only one who is capable of enduring separation from his parents may be given away; "in sale as well as in gift, they should not be led [into such acts] against their will."
One should, however, unite one's wife, sons, and all possessions with oneself alone.

Thus, because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) of Kātyāyana: "Those who are unwilling should not be led [into marriage]," this refers to a situation where there is no distress; however, even in times of distress, giving away or indeed selling [the child] must be performed.
Otherwise, one would not proceed [with the rite]; such is the settled conclusion of the scriptures.

For it has been stated by that very author with reference to those [other sons] alone. A specific method for the adoption of a son (*putrapratigraha*) has been shown by Vasiṣṭha: [316] “One intending to adopt a son shall summon his kinsmen, inform the king, and having offered oblations with the *vyāhṛti* mantras in the middle of the house, he should adopt one who is not a distant relative (*adūrabāndhava*), provided he is not too closely related. (*VaDh* 15.6). “Not a distant relative” means one whose relatives, such as maternal uncles and so forth, are nearby; that is, one distinct from both those who are not closely related and those who are too closely related, such as a brother’s son and the like. Regarding immovable property (*sthāvara*), Prajāpati states the wealth that must be given:

"Whatever field is acquired from among the seven sources of income—whether it be ancestral or acquired by oneself—that is intended to be given. This means that whatever is acquired or exceeds [the usual] from these seven sources of income is intended to be given as a gift. However, property acquired by oneself that has not been authorized by brothers whose wealth is undivided must not be given; for Bṛhaspati states: "That which is acquired by oneself may be given at one's own will. As for what was stated by that same author:
Whether partitioned or unpartitioned, heirs have equal rights to immovable property;
even a single heir is not empowered in any case to give, mortgage, or sell it.

[317] Thus, this refers to immovable property that is undivided, or immovable property exceeding seven [in number], since it is specifically stated that only what exceeds seven may be given. Some things must be given only with the wife's consent; some must be given even by the head of the family only with the consent of his brothers and others; and some, even if acquired by a slave through his own efforts, must be given only with the master's consent. And so says that same author: "That which is a gift from a wife (saudāyika), inherited in due order, or obtained through valor—such a gift attains validity when authorized by the wife, the kinsmen, or the owner."

*Saundāyika* is that which is obtained at marriage. *Kramāyāta* is that which has come down through the lineage of the grandfather and so forth. That which is approved by the wife and her kinsmen and remains with a surplus should be given;

however, regarding property obtained at marriage or inherited through lineage, there is no obligation to give away the whole, because it has been stated by that same [author]: "In the case of what is obtained at marriage or inherited through lineage, there is no such thing as giving away the entirety."
Thus the nature of what may be given and what may not be given has been described;
now, however, the nature of what is properly given and what is improperly given is described.
In this regard, that which is given is of seven kinds, while that which is not given consists of sixteen forms. And so says Nārada:
Giving is said to be of seven kinds, while taking what is not given consists of sixteen forms.

Those who know the rules of giving recognize that what is given for the price of merchandise, as wages, out of satisfaction, out of affection, as a return for a favor, or for the sake of favoring a wife or a parrot, constitutes a gift.
But what is taken without it being given may be so through being afflicted by exhaustion, anger, grief, agitation, or pain;
likewise, through bribery, jesting, exchange, or the employment of deception.

[318] That which is performed by one who is a child, deluded, lacking independence, afflicted, intoxicated, or insane; and that which is done with the expectation of gaining a reward, thinking, "This person is my agent."
"If one says 'this is a worthy recipient' regarding an unworthy recipient, or if an act is joined with unrighteousness,
that which is given through ignorance is declared in the Smṛti to be as if not given at all."

The price of merchandise refers to the value of goods purchased. Wages refer to that which is given for work performed. A gift out of satisfaction refers to what is given to bards, minstrels, and the like. A gift out of affection refers to what is given to one's daughter and others. A gift by way of recompense refers to what is given as a return favor to one who has rendered assistance. The bride-price refers to what is given to the kinsmen of a maiden for the purpose of her marriage. A gift for the sake of favor refers to what is given for the sake of spiritual merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*). These seven kinds of gifts, beginning with the price of merchandise, once given, are not to be reclaimed. And so says Yājñavalkya:
"What has been promised as a gift must indeed be given; once it has been given, one must not take it back again. (YDh 2.176)

That which is given out of fear, such as from being taken captive; that which is given out of anger to another in order to vent one's wrath toward a son or others; that which is given under the influence of grief caused by separation from a son or similar misfortune; that which is given by those afflicted with disease, meaning those tormented by incurable illnesses; that which is given as a bribe (*utkoca*) to officials for the sake of removing obstacles to a task; that which is given in jest or as a joke (*parihāra*); that which is given through the exchange of goods—where one person gives his own property to another, and the other likewise gives his to him, thus given through an exchange of gifts (*dānavyatyāsa*); that which is given to one person when it was intended for another; that which is given through fraudulent means, such as intending to give a hundred but giving a thousand after having so resolved; that which is given by a child (*bāla*), meaning one who has not reached sixteen years of age; that which is given by a fool (*mūḍha*), meaning one ignorant of worldly affairs and the Vedas; that which is given by one who is not independent (*asvatantra*), such as a son or a slave; that which is bestowed by one who is insane (*unmatta*), meaning seized by madness such as epilepsy; that which is given to one who does not provide a return-favor out of a desire for a reciprocal gain, thinking, "This man will perform this work for me"; that which is given to an unworthy person merely because of a claim of worthiness, such as when one says, "I am a knower of the four Vedas," to one who knows none; and that which is given after obtaining wealth with the thought, "I shall perform a sacrifice," but then employs it for gambling and the like—this gift, though of sixteen kinds, is called "not given" (*adatta*) because it is subject to being reclaimed. And so says Kātyāyana:

That which is given by those who are not masters of themselves due to lust or anger, by the distressed, the weak, the insane, or the deluded, as well as what is given through error or in jest, may be taken back.
However, a bribe that may have been promised for the sake of accomplishing a task must not be given under any circumstances, even once that purpose has been achieved.
"But if she had already been given [in marriage] previously, he must be made to give her back by force;
and Gārgya and Mānava state that the fine shall be eleven times [the value].
He [the same author] states the nature of the bribe as follows:

[320] From associating with thieves, violent criminals, and those who have gone astray as adulterers; likewise, from the appearance of those who have strayed and perished, and from the practice of untruth.
"Whatever has been obtained by these [mediators] is called a bribe (*utkoca*);

in that case, the giver shall not be punished, but the mediator alone shall share in the guilt. Here, "mediator" (*madhyastha*) refers to one who repeats what has been said. By the word "and" (*ca*), the receiver (*grāhaka*) is included. The meaning is that both of them share in the guilt and are subject to punishment. The status of being "given" regarding what is given out of distress (*ārtadatta*) applies to matters other than religious duties (*dharmakārya*). And so says that same [author]:

"Whether given by one who is healthy or by one who is afflicted, provided it was given for the sake of dharma; if he dies without having [formally] bestowed it, his son must be made to give it—of this there is no doubt.
Thus Manu also states that a gift or the like made under a condition is subject to revocation.
"What has been pledged, sold, or gifted through fraud, or received as a gift through fraud—whenever one detects such deception, all that shall be annulled. (MDh 8.165).
Here, *yoga* means *upadhi* (fraud). Nārada has stated the punishment for giving what should not be given and for accepting such a gift.
"He who, out of greed, takes what is not given, and he who gives what should not be given—
the giver of what is not to be given shall be punished, as shall the receiver of what was not given. Thus ends the section on the non-delivery of what has been given.
Now, the title of dispute known as "Non-payment of Wages" is discussed;
Nārada states its nature:
"The procedure for the giving and receiving of wages for servants has been declared."
"Non-payment of wages is recorded as a title of dispute.

Here, *vetana* means the price for work. Its *anapākarma* refers either to the non-delivery of wages to a servant or the returning of what has already been delivered. Regarding the delivery thereof, Nārada states the specific rule:
"The master of the work shall pay wages to the servant in the proper order."
"That which is determined at the beginning, middle, and end of the work.
He [Yājñavalkya] states a specific rule regarding the absence of such a verbal agreement as "I shall give this much for your performance of the work":
"But when wages are not fixed, they shall receive a tenth part."
Merchants and farmers shall obtain profit from cattle, heroism, and grain.

[322] Thus: "The strength of cattle" refers to milk and other products derived from the cows and so forth being tended. Yājñavalkya states that if the master of the work does not give a tenth part to the servant, then he must be made to pay it by the king: "But he who causes work to be done without having fixed the wages shall be made by the ruler to pay a tenth part of the profits from trade, cattle, and grain. (YDh 2.194)

As for that which was stated by Bṛhaspati—"The plowman shall take a third or a fifth part"—that refers to one who cultivates a field that requires great effort to till. Even in that case, it should be understood that the third and fifth parts are presented as optional alternatives according to the specific circumstances. And so says that very same author:
"One who is hired for food and clothing shall take a fifth part from the crop grown on the ploughed field;
likewise, one who is hired by that same means [food and clothing] shall take a third part when the crop has been harvested.

This means that a farmer hired for food and clothing shall take a fifth part of the crop produced from the field; one not hired for those two shall take a third part. Even when there is an agreement stating "I will give this much," in some cases a wage determined by the master's discretion may be given that is less than that, and in other cases even more than that may be given. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
"If one should transgress the place or the time, or should effect a gain otherwise, then the master's will shall prevail; if there has been excess, more than that excess should be given. (YDh 2.195)

If one exceeds the prescribed place and time for the means of acquiring profit, such as trade, without the master’s permission, and makes the profit small by incurring excessive expenditure, the master may give him something according to his own will. However, to him who produces great profit through his own initiative, more than the stipulated price should be given; this is the meaning. He (Yājñavalkya) himself states the method of distributing wages when a task is performed by several servants:
"To each person, however much work he performs, that much shall be his wage."
"If it is incurable for both [the patient and the physician], then one should perform the treatment as prescribed when it is curable. (YDh 2.196)

Furthermore, when a single task with a fixed wage is undertaken by two or more people, and it is impossible for either one of them alone to complete it, such that the work remains unfinished by both, then whatever portion of the work each person performs, they shall be paid a wage determined by an arbitrator according to the extent of that work; however, it shall not be equal. But when the work is accomplished and completed by both, then exactly what was agreed upon and stipulated as the total amount shall be paid to both; neither shall the full wage be paid to each individually, nor shall it be paid by calculating a proportion based on the specific share of work performed. Nārada describes the status of servants as follows: [The text continues with Nārada’s verses regarding the master-servant relationship.]

[324] "Their tools for work, as assigned for the performance of their tasks, must be protected by him with a sense of trustworthiness and never with deceit. This means that the tools for work—such as ploughs and the like—belonging to those who are the masters of the labor, and which have been entrusted to a servant for the sake of a specific task, must at all times be guarded by him without guile. Bṛhaspati also says:

"A laborer, moreover, should not practice deceit toward his master; he incurs a loss of wages, and then a legal dispute ensues. Regarding him who accepts the wage but does not perform the work, the same author says:
"When one who has received wages does not perform the work because he is dead,
if he was capable [of working], he shall be made to pay a fine and twice that amount as wages.
Regarding the case of one who has not received wages, Yājñavalkya says:

"If he has not taken [the goods], he should be made to pay the value equally; the implements must be protected by the servants" (YDh 2.193). The meaning is that he should pay the master exactly the amount of wages for which the service was undertaken, but not a fine to the king. Alternatively, having paid the agreed-upon wages here, he should be compelled to perform the work by force. Regarding this, Nārada says:
"Having promised to perform the work but failing to do so, he should be made to do it by force after paying the wages."
"Having received wages, one who does not perform the work shall receive double the wages.
The phrase "having promised" is intended to include the commencement [of the work] as well. Thus Kātyāyana says:
"But he who, having undertaken the commencement of a task, does not complete it at all..."
"He must be compelled by force; if he does not act, he deserves punishment.
Regarding the measure of that punishment, Vriddha-Manu says:
"He who, having made a promise, does not fulfill it, should be compelled to do so even by force."
"If he should not perform that work, he shall incur a fine of two hundred.
This means two hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*. As for the statement of Manu:
"A servant who, being unafflicted, does not perform the work as prescribed out of pride..."

"He shall be fined eight *kṛṣṇalas*, and his wages shall not be paid" (MDh 8.215); this refers to cases where half [of the work] remains unfinished. However, when only a small portion remains, one should withhold the wages while exempting him from punishment. Regarding this, the same author says:
"Whether afflicted by illness or in good health, he who does not cause the work to be done..."
"No wages shall be paid to him, even for work that is only slightly incomplete" (MDh 8.17).
Regarding one who, having undertaken work for a specified period, abandons the work before the time has elapsed, Nārada says:
"Abandoning the work before the time is complete, he shall suffer the loss of his wages."

"In the case of non-performance due to the fault of the master, he shall receive his wages. This means: "due to the fault of the master," such as the master's infliction of violence and so forth. Nārada says:
"[327] If the goods should be lost through the fault of the carrier..."
"He shall be made to pay for whatever has been lost therein, except for loss caused by fate or the king.

[This refers to] loss due to the fault of the driver or the fault of the hired laborer. Vṛddha-Manu says: "He shall be made to pay for what is destroyed through negligence; he shall pay twice as much for what is destroyed through malice."

"But he shall not be made to pay for what has been stolen by thieves, or burnt, or carried away by water. "Destroyed by malice" means destroyed through injury such as a severe blow. "Twice liable to pay" means he shall be made to pay double. Regarding a servant who causes an obstruction to the departure, Katyayana says: "A carrier who obstructs the departure shall be made to pay double the wages."
Vṛddha-Manu states: "If, when the time for work has arrived, one should not perform it but instead creates an obstacle, another person should be employed; he shall be made to pay double the wages."
Yājñavalkya [328]:
A carrier shall be made to pay for goods lost through no fault of the king or by an act of God;
likewise, one who causes an obstruction to the journey shall be made to pay double the wages.

"If he abandons [the work] when it has commenced, he shall be made to pay a seventh part of the wages; if on the way, a fourth part; and if he abandons it while the employer is still on the road, he shall be made to pay the entire wage, as shall the deserter. (YDh 2.197–98)

If a commodity is not damaged by the king or by fate—that is, if it is lost by the carrier through negligence (*prajñāhīnatā*), then he must be made to pay the value of that commodity according to its price. However, if one who has accepted the work abandons it at the very time of departure and causes an obstruction to the journey, he must be made to pay double the wages. If, however, when there is an opportunity to hire another servant, one abandons the work he had undertaken, that servant shall be made to pay a seventh part of the wages. Furthermore, if one abandons the work while the journey has already commenced on the road, he shall be made to pay a fourth part of the wages; if he abandons it halfway, he must be made to pay the full wages. If the master himself causes the servant to abandon the work at the aforementioned places, he too shall be made to pay the aforementioned seventh part and so forth. This applies to cases where the servant is not ill and so forth, for there is no fault in the case of one who is ill. But when one who was ill completes the work upon recovery by counting the intervening days, then he shall indeed receive the full wages.
