"But one who was distressed, once he has become healthy, shall perform [the work] as stated from the beginning;

even after a very long time, he shall certainly receive that wage. (MDh 8.216) The requirement for the abandoning master to pay a fourth part or more of the wages refers to cases where the goods have not been sold. However, regarding the case where the goods have been sold, a specific rule has been stated by Vṛddhamanu:

"If a merchant, having sold that merchandise on the road, should abandon his servant, then [the wage] for him must also be given; he shall receive half of the wages. Regarding the case where merchandise is obstructed by an injunction and the case where merchandise has been seized by the king or others, Kātyāyana says:

And as it is said: "If that merchandise should be lost or stolen on the road, the carrier shall receive wages only for the portion of the journey he has completed. Thus Nārada speaks to the carrier of goods regarding a vehicle or other means hired for hire.

Having hired carriers for goods by means of vehicles or draft animals, if one abandons them before reaching the destination, he shall be made to pay a fourth part of the hire; if he abandons them halfway, he shall pay the full amount.
"Even a carrier who does not bring [the goods] shall suffer such a loss of wages.
Regarding one who, having hired a cart or similar vehicle, takes it away without providing any service and departs for another region without paying the hire, Vṛddhamanu says:
"He who, having hired a cart, takes it and goes elsewhere..."
"He shall not return the vehicle; he too must be made to pay the hire. Thus [it is said].

Kātyāyana states that the hire is the price for the temporary use of the object; even for one who has mounted [the vehicle], even if no service has been rendered, and even if the elephant, horse, or other [animal] has not yet been returned after the task for which it was intended is finished, the hire does not cease until the return of the animal. He says: "He who, having taken elephants, horses, cows, donkeys, camels, and so forth, by means of hire..."
Having completed his business, he should depart; otherwise, he must pay the hire just like a woman.
"He who, having taken a house, water, and so forth on lease, does not return them to the owner, must be made to pay that lease [fee] for as long as he has not returned them.

By the word "water" (*vāri*), its receptacle is indicated; by the word "benefit" (*upakāra*), its receptacle is indicated. Regarding one who provides a lease for the construction of a house on another's land, Nārada says:
"Whoever, having built a house on another's land, should dwell there after paying the *stoma*, he should depart taking with him that [house], as well as the grass, wood, and bricks.
Likewise, *stoma* means rent. He himself states this regarding the non-payment of *stoma*:
Having stayed on another's land without a formal agreement and without a designated boundary,
one should by no means take grass, wood, or other such items while departing.
Whatever grass or wood has been placed upon the bricks, all of that, as it emerges, shall be reported to the owner of the land.

[332] Thus; the meaning is: "in the case of an unstipulated agreement regarding the taking of grass, wood, and so forth. But when it has been stipulated, it is according to that stipulation. "He should inform" means "he should announce. Regarding the breaking of jars and other vessels taken for the purpose of returning a ladle or similar items after paying a fee, the same author says: "One should bring back the containers used for carrying the offerings (stoma) once the time [of the festival] is full. One should deliver to the borrower what is broken or lost, except in the case of an accident (saṃplava). Thus it is said.

*Saṃplavaḥ* means mutual friction or conflict. If, due to such [conflict], whether slightly or completely, the object is damaged, one must restore it to its former state and return the vessel or its value to the owner. However, if the damage occurs other than through *saṃplava*, the meaning is that the renter alone is liable for it. Regarding one who does not pay wages to a servant who has performed his work, Bṛhaspati says: "If an employer does not pay wages to a servant after the work has been completed, he should be compelled by the king to pay them, along with a proportionate fine."
Kātyāyana states the punishment for one who abandons a sick servant on the road:

"He who abandons on the road a companion who is exhausted or afflicted by disease shall incur the first *sāhasa* fine; likewise, he who fails to provide protection for three days in a village [shall do so]. Thus it is said.
Regarding prostitutes and their clients, Nārada says:
"Having received the fee, a prostitute who does not wish to comply shall pay double; likewise, a client who does not wish to comply shall suffer the loss of his fee. [333]

This refers to cases where [the woman] is not ill and so forth; however, regarding the case of illness, there is another Smṛti text: "One who is ill, distracted, busy, or devoted to royal duties—if she does not come when invited, she is declared to be like a barren mare."

She who has become agitated regarding extremely urgent matters is described by the term *saṃbhrāntā*. In that same context, she who is distracted or preoccupied is called *vyagrā*. A *vaḍavā* is a female slave; here, the mention of "slave" is intended to indicate a courtesan (*paṇyastrī*). Regarding the enjoyer [of such a woman], Nārada says:
"If a man, having enjoyed a woman, does not pay the fee (*śulka*) accordingly, or if he has intercourse with her out of order, or strikes her with his nails and so forth..."
"He who approaches [a woman] in an improper place, or causes her to be driven away by many [men],
shall be made to pay eightfold the bride-price (śulka) and an equal amount as a fine.
Regarding the punishment and other matters for the offense of a courtesan, it is stated in the *Matsya Purāṇa*:

"Having received her fee, if a courtesan goes elsewhere out of greed, he should cause her to pay a fine; he should also pay the fee to the other man. Thus [it is said]. Regarding this, Nārada states the final decision: [334]
"Those libertines who reside in the houses of courtesans there are known to provide a decision regarding doubts concerning matters arising from them.

Thus, having approached [the topic], the legal dispute (vivādapada) known as "Non-payment of Wages" (*vetanasyānapākarma*), which is included within the legal dispute called "Service" (*aśuśrūṣā*), has been explained according to the order of enumeration stated by Manu.
Thus has been described the head of dispute known as non-payment of wages;
now, the head of dispute known as failure to serve when summoned is being addressed.
Regarding its nature, Nārada says:
"And having undertaken service, he who does not perform it;
this is called the title of dispute regarding the undertaking of non-service.
Service consists of carrying out orders. And the servant is of five kinds. Thus, that same [author] says:
[335] The wise have observed in the treatises that there are five types of attendants;
four types of laborers; and the remaining fifteen types of slaves.
Pupils, resident students, and hired servants—the fourth being the laborer on extra work—these are to be known as laborers; slaves, however, are those born in the house and so forth.
The wise have declared that their lack of independence is their common characteristic;
however, the distinction between them is said to lie in their birth-rites and their livelihoods.
Action, too, should be known to be of two kinds: indeed, the unwholesome and the wholesome.
The unwholesome is said to be the work of a slave, while the wholesome is recorded as the work of a laborer.
Cleaning the house door, impure places, streets, and refuse heaps; touching private parts, limbs, or food remnants; and the taking up and discarding of feces and urine.

"Furthermore, serving a master with one's limbs at his command is to be known as inauspicious action; other than that, it is auspicious. In this context, a *śiṣya* is one who seeks the knowledge of the Vedas; an *antevāsī* is one who seeks training in a craft (*śilpa*); a *bhṛtaka* is one who performs work for wages; an *adhikarmakṛt* is a supervisor over those performing work. An "impure place" (*aśucisthāna*) is a pit or similar location for the disposal of leftovers; an "avaskara" is a place for discarding heaps of dust and so forth swept from a house. And the *bhṛtaka* is of three kinds. As it has been said by that same author:
"The best laborer is one who performs the work; the middling is a cultivator; and the lowest is a carrier of burdens—thus is the hired servant of three kinds.
The nature of the slave has also been shown by that same author:
One born in the house, one purchased, one obtained, one received as an heir,
one supported during a time of food-scarcity, and likewise one who has been placed there by the master.
Rescued from great bondage, won in battle as a prize,
and having approached you saying "I am yours," he was made to enter the life of a wandering mendicant.
"One who is a slave by inheritance, one brought as a prize for a mare,
and one who has sold himself— these are declared in the legal treatises to be the fifteen kinds of slaves."

One born in the house (*gṛhajāta*) is one born in one’s own home from a female slave. One who is bought (*krīta*) is one acquired for a price. One who is received (*labdha*) is one obtained through acceptance or similar means. One who has come by inheritance (*dāyāgata*) is one acquired as an heir to property. One supported during a famine (*annākālabhṛta*) is one nourished for the sake of slavery during a time of scarcity. One pledged (*āhita*) is one brought into subjection by a master through the receipt of wealth. One released from debt (*ṛṇamokṣita*) is one who has accepted servitude as a reciprocal act for being freed from debt. One captured in war (*yuddhaprāpta*) is one seized after being defeated in battle. One won at a stake (*paṇe vijita*) is one defeated in gambling or other such games where servitude was the wager. One who has submitted saying "I am yours" (*tavāham ity upagata*) is one who has come of his own accord, saying, "I am your slave. One who has fallen from the religious life (*pravrajyāvasita*) is one who has lapsed from the state of renunciation. One made for a fixed term (*kṛta*) is one who has agreed, "For this much time you shall be my slave. A slave for food (*bhaktadāsa*) is one who has accepted servitude solely for the purpose of receiving sustenance at all times. One brought by a mare (*vaḍavāhṛta*) is one who, out of desire for her, enters into servitude after marrying that female slave of the household. One who sells himself (*ātmavikretā*) is one who sells his own person. Thus there are fifteen types. As for that which was stated by Manu:

"Those captured under a banner, those who are slaves by virtue of food provided, those born in the house, those purchased, those given as gifts, those inherited from a father, and those enslaved by way of punishment—these seven are the sources of slavery" (MDh 8.415).

This statement is intended to establish their status as slaves, not to serve as an exhaustive enumeration. Regarding this matter, a specific rule concerning the performance of work by students has been stated by Nārada:
"Until the acquisition of knowledge, the student should serve his guru with self-restraint;
he should behave toward the guru’s wife and likewise toward the guru’s son in the same manner.
Here, "knowledge" refers to the triple Veda (*trayī*). This has been stated by Bṛhaspati:

[338] "The triple Vidyā is declared to be characterized by the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman; for its sake, one should perform the service of the teacher as enjoined. A specific rule regarding the performance of work by students has also been stated by that same author:
"Craftsmanship is said to be the fashioning of gold, silver, and so forth, as well as dancing and the like; having acquired that, one should perform work in the house of the guru.
Thus [says] Nārada as well.
"Or, desiring to acquire his own craft, he may dwell with a teacher for a well-determined period of time with the permission of his relatives.
Regarding what must also be done by the teacher, that same [author] says:
"The teacher should instruct him in his own home, providing him with food;
he should not make him perform other work, and should treat him like a son. Regarding a teacher who makes [the student] perform other work, Kātyāyana says:
"But he who does not cause [the pupil] to master the craft, yet causes him to perform other tasks, shall incur the first *sāhasa* fine; from that, the pupil withdraws.
Thus Nārada says that one should remain for that duration even if the knowledge has been acquired before the stipulated time.
"Even if he has been trained, the apprentice shall complete the work at the appointed time;
whatever labor he performs therein, its fruit belongs to the teacher alone.
Thus says Yājñavalkya as well.
"Even one who has mastered the craft shall dwell in the teacher's house for the prescribed period;
as a resident pupil (*antevāsī*), he provides the fruit [of his labor] in exchange for the food obtained from the teacher. (YDh 2.184). Regarding the wicked [pupil], Nārada says:

"He who abandons an unoffending teacher while he is instructing him should be compelled to stay by force; he deserves corporal punishment and imprisonment. Here, "corporal punishment" refers to flogging and the like. Nārada states what must be done upon the completion of the stipulated period:
"Having mastered the craft, the apprentice, having circumambulated the teacher at the appointed time and honored him according to his ability, departs.
Bṛhaspati has also shown the distinction between those who work for wages based on the nature of the labor and those based on the duration of time.
He who enjoys another's female slave should be known as a *vaḍavābhṛta*;
he should perform that work for her master, just as a man who is supported by food [performs labor].
One is described as bearing many objects, while another is said to bear a portion;
furthermore, the states of inferior, middling, and superior have been declared for all of them.
"One who has been supported for a day, half a month, six months, three months, or a year shall perform the work promised and receive what was agreed upon.

In this regard, the multiplicity of support for wealth should be understood through its smallness or greatness according to the capacity of the capable person. Furthermore, that smallness or greatness should be understood in accordance with one's ability. And so says Nārada:
"Servants are to be known as threefold: superior, middling, and inferior;
their wages depend upon their work and are determined according to their ability and devotion.
Thus [it is said]. Bṛhaspati states that there are two types of sharecroppers (*bhāgabhṛta*).

"The share-crop farmer is known to be of two kinds: one who lives by the crop and one who lives by the milk; he receives from the grain that has grown and likewise from the milk—of this there is no doubt.
Thus [it is said]. Nārada states the nature of the *adhikarmakṛt* (the laborer for extra work):
"One who is authorized over the affairs of a family is to be known as an *adhikarmakṛt*; he is not considered a *kauṭumbika*.

Having thus defined the disciples (*śiṣya*) and students (*antevāsin*), as well as the laborers such as hired servants (*bhṛtaka*), Kātyāyana explains the distinction of slaves (*dāsa*) from these by means of demonstrating the etymological derivation of the word "slave" (*dāsa*).
Bhṛgu says that by giving away one's own independent self, one becomes a slave, just like a wife.

[341] Thus. This is the meaning: just as one becomes a wife (*dāra*) by giving one’s own body for the sake of the husband’s enjoyment, so too does one become a slave (*dāsa*) by giving oneself to an independent master—this is what the teacher Bhṛgu maintains. By this, it is meant that those who serve having attained a state of absolute subservience to another are slaves (*dāsas*), whereas those who serve having attained merely a state of being for the sake of another are laborers (*karmakaras*). Furthermore, slavery is to be understood as applying only to the three castes other than the Brāhmaṇa, because he himself stated: "A Brāhmaṇa never enters into servitude. Even among those [three], he says that servitude occurs only in the direct order of castes (*ānulomyena*).
"Slavery is [permitted] for the castes in the direct order of succession, not in the inverse order;
for Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who abandon their own specific duties.
This prohibition of slavery in the inverse order should be understood to apply to those other than those who have fallen from their status by abandoning their own *dharma*. And so says Nārada:
Slavery is not ordained by way of the inverse order of castes;
elsewhere, slavery is considered to be like marriage, except for those who have abandoned their own duty.

[342] Thus, because of the statement that "the status of a slave is considered like that of a wife," Kātyāyana declares that a Brāhmaṇa may enter into slavery with respect to someone of his own caste (*savarṇa*). However, he states:
"But one must never cause a Brāhmaṇa to perform servitude toward someone of a different caste.
Furthermore, he says that if a Brāhmaṇa voluntarily accepts the state of servitude, he shall not perform any inauspicious work.

"Even if he is accomplished in learning and study, the best of the twice-born should not perform that deficient work out of desire; even in that case, he should not do anything unwholesome. "Deficient" (*ūna*) means inferior; "even out of desire" means for his own sake, without receiving wages, having been sent for the purpose by his own will. Manu states what must be done by the master regarding the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya:
"A Brāhmaṇa shall support with compassion a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who are distressed for lack of livelihood, making them perform their own respective duties" (MDh 8.411).
Regarding one who forcibly compels a twice-born man to perform servile labor, the same author states the following punishment:

"But if a Brāhmaṇa, out of delusion, should cause initiated twice-born men to perform servitude against their will because of his power, he shall be fined six hundred [paṇas] by the king. (MDh 8.412). "Power" (*prabhava*) means the state of being powerful (*prābhavatva*); it is because of that [power] [that he acts]. He [the same author, Manu], moreover, states that one may cause a Śūdra to perform servitude in any manner whatsoever: The same [author] says: "But a Śūdra may be made to perform servitude in any way at all. (MDh 8.413).
"But one may compel a Śūdra to perform service, whether he has been purchased or not;

for he was created by the Self-existent One himself solely for servitude" (MDh 9.413). Regarding this, Nārada states that among the fifteen types of slaves, those four who are born in the house, purchased, acquired [as booty], or inherited, are released from slavery only through the favor of the master, and not otherwise.
"In that regard, the first four categories are not released from slavery except through the favor of the master; their servitude is hereditary.
Thus Nārada states that even for one who has sold himself into slavery, the state of servitude does not depart except through the favor of the master.
"That lowest of men who, being devoid of self-mastery, sells himself—

he is the most base among them, and even he is not released from servitude. Thus, that same author states that even for one who has fallen from the state of renunciation, there is no liberation from servitude.
"For a man who has fallen from the religious life shall indeed become a slave to the king;
for him there is no release, nor is there purification by any means whatsoever.
Thus [says] Yājñavalkya as well.

"One who has fallen from renunciation becomes a slave to the king for as long as life lasts. (YDh 2.183) This slavery of one who has fallen from renunciation applies to those other than Brāhmaṇas. Regarding the Brāhmaṇa, however, Kātyāyana says he is to be banished:
"Those twice-born men of the three castes who have fallen from renunciation..."

"One should cause a Brāhmaṇa to be banished, and a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya to enter into slavery. Regarding the manner of banishment, Nārada says: "But he who, having taken up the life of a wandering mendicant, does not abide by his own duty..."
"Having branded him with the mark of a dog's foot, the king shall quickly banish him.

Thus [it is said]. He (Yājñavalkya) himself states the method for removing the servitude of those such as the *annabhṛta* and *kālabhṛta*, excluding those who have fallen from their religious vows (*pravrajyāvasita*) and those who sold themselves:
"One who has been maintained by food or during a time of famine is released from servitude by giving two cows."
That which was consumed during a famine cannot be purified by ritual action.
A slave for food is released simply by being lifted out of his status as food;
likewise, even one who was pledged [as a slave] is freed if the master releases him after receiving the money.
Having paid a debt sufficient for himself, he is released from that debt;
likewise one who has submitted saying "I am yours," or one captured in battle, or one won at a stake.
By the giving of a head-for-head ransom, they may be released through an equivalent act;
even one who has committed a crime is liberated once the appointed time has passed.
"By the capture of the mare, however, one who was taken as a slave by a mare is released.
Thus Nārada states that even through saving the life of their master, all types of slaves—those born in the house and so forth—are released from slavery:
"And whoever among these should rescue their master from a life-threatening danger..."
"From slavery he shall be released and receive a share of the inheritance.
Thus [it is said]. Yājñavalkya states the emancipation of those who are like slaves: "One who has been forcibly enslaved by thieves, as well as one who has been sold, is released. (YDh 2.182)
By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), those who have been pledged and those who have been given are also included. Nārada also states:
"Those who have been stolen by thieves, those who have been sold, and those who have been forcibly made slaves—these must be liberated by the king; servitude is forbidden with respect to them."

But regarding one who, having previously accepted servitude to one person, accepts servitude to another as well—that person may be released by the latter; so he himself said: "He who, being not his own master, offers himself saying 'I am yours'—he shall not obtain that desired object; the former owner shall receive him."
He himself states the procedure for the liberation of a slave:
"If one, with a joyful mind, should wish to make his own slave free,
he should take [the slave] by the shoulder and break a water-pot full of water over him."
One should sprinkle water containing rice grains and flowers upon his head,
and having said three times, "He is no slave," one should release him while facing the east.
"From that time forward, he should be declared protected by the favor of his master;
his food may be eaten and he may receive gifts, becoming esteemed by the virtuous. Thus ends the section on legal disputes known as "Service after Undertaking."

[348] Now, the legal procedure concerning the title of dispute known as the breach of agreement is stated; its definition has been shown by Nārada through the method of negative differentiation (*vyatireka*).

"The established rule of heretics, guilds, and so forth is called *samaya* (convention). The non-abandonment of that convention is recorded as a ground for litigation (*vivādapada*). This means that the non-abandonment of a convention—its non-transgression and its observance—is what constitutes a subject of dispute when it is being violated. Bṛhaspati states the matter relevant to this:
"Having summoned Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas, well-versed in the scriptures (*śrotriya*), and maintainers of the sacred fire (*agnihotrī*),
he should establish them there and provide for their livelihood.
Thus says Yājñavalkya as well.

"Having established a residence in the city and appointed there the Brāhmaṇas who are masters of the three Vedas (*traividya*), the king should provide them with a livelihood and say: 'Let your own duty (*svadharma*) be observed. (YDh 2.185) He should say to those Brāhmaṇas who are *traividya*—that is, endowed with the knowledge of the three Vedas—"Let your own duty, as ordained by the Śruti and Smṛti for the various castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*), be performed by you, O venerable ones. And the perfection of their livelihood has been shown by Bṛhaspati:

[349] "The king should grant them house-sites with non-confiscable taxes (*anācchedyakara*), having recorded in his own edict that they are to be enjoyed and shall remain so. This means that those lands which have non-confiscable taxes— that is, no taxes to be collected— and which are to be enjoyed such that no taxes are known to be levied, he should grant them to them after recording in his own edict that they are to remain with non-confiscable taxes for future kings as well.
Bṛhaspati states what they must do:
"They shall perform the daily rites, the occasional rites, the rites for specific desires, as well as those for pacification and prosperity;
and they shall provide a decision on matters in doubt. Thus it is said.

Yājñavalkya also says: "But that which is conventional and does not conflict with one's own dharma, as well as that which is established by the king—that too must be protected with effort. (YDh 2.186)

That dharma which arises from convention (*samaya*)—consisting of the maintenance of lineage customs, temples, and so forth, without violating the *śrauta* and *smārta* duties—must also be protected with effort. Likewise, a king must provide food for travelers without contradicting his own duty; and that which arises from convention, such as "Horses and the like must not be sent into our enemy territory," must also be observed. Thus, the specific duties of particular groups appointed by the king have been stated. Bṛhaspati, however, speaks of the common duties of all groups, such as villages and the like: [Text follows...]
The convention and the formal agreement of villages, guilds, and assemblies must be observed during times of distress, as well as in matters of dharma.
"The burden of the world is known to be common to all;
therefore, its alleviation must be performed by each and every person. Thus it is said.

By the word "ca" (and), heretics (*pāṣaṇḍa*), guilds (*naigama*), and so forth are included. Consequently, when there is a time of distress for villages, guilds, corporations (*gaṇa*), heretics, guilds, and the like, or during a religious duty (*dharmakārya*), whatever conventional agreement (*samayakriyā*) is necessary—without which the distress would be difficult to avert and the religious duty difficult to accomplish—that conventional agreement must be made by all joining together. "Vāṭa" means a wolf. The meaning is that when fear arises from thieves lurking in the vicinity (*vāṭacora*), then the suppression of those thieves must be carried out by everyone acting in concert. As for the religious duty, however, a specific rule has been stated by that same author: [The text continues with the verse: "When a village is besieged by enemies, or when a fire breaks out, or when a thief is present, they shall act together; otherwise, they incur a fine of one *māṣaka*. In the case of a siege by enemies, they must collectively fight the enemy; in the case of a fire, they must extinguish it; and in the case of a thief, they must suppress him. If they do not do so, each incurs a fine of one *māṣaka*. Regarding the phrase "or when a fire breaks out," the word "or" (*vā*) implies other calamities such as floods. Regarding "when a thief is present," this refers to the apprehension of a thief who has entered the village. "Together" means collectively. "Otherwise" means if they do not act thus. "They incur a fine of one *māṣaka*" means that each individual shall be fined one *māṣaka*. This is the meaning. Furthermore, in the case of a religious duty, the following has been stated: "When a village is afflicted by disease, or when a famine occurs, or when a great danger arises, they shall provide assistance according to their ability. When a village is afflicted by disease, they shall provide medicine, food, and drink to the sick according to their capacity. When a famine occurs, they shall distribute grain and so forth. When a great danger arises, such as an attack by a king or a forest-dweller, they shall collectively provide protection. "According to their ability" means that they shall act in proportion to their respective wealth and power. If they do not do so, they incur a fine of one *māṣaka*. This is the meaning. Furthermore, regarding the distribution of water and the like, it is said: "In times of distress, they shall distribute water, fodder, and fuel; and they shall maintain the boundaries and the paths. In times of distress, such as a drought, they shall distribute water for drinking and bathing. They shall also distribute fodder for cattle and fuel for cooking. And they shall maintain the boundaries between fields and the public paths. If they do not do so, they incur a fine of one *māṣaka*. This is the meaning. Furthermore, regarding the settlement of disputes, it is said: "When a dispute arises among them, they shall settle it themselves; if they fail to do so, the king shall impose a fine. When a dispute arises among the villagers concerning land, water, or other matters, they themselves shall investigate and settle it. If they do not do so, the king shall impose a fine of one *māṣaka* on each of them. This is the meaning. Furthermore, regarding the maintenance of the village, it is said: "They shall maintain the watchtowers, the boundary markers, the wells, and the temples. They shall repair the watchtowers for defense, the boundary markers to prevent encroachment, the wells for the sake of water, and the temples for the sake of merit. If they do not do so, they incur a fine of one *māṣaka*. This is the meaning. Furthermore, regarding the collection of taxes, it is said: "The village headman (*grāmika*) shall collect the tax from the inhabitants; he shall deliver it to the king, and he shall protect the village. The village headman shall collect the prescribed tax from the villagers and deliver it to the king. He shall also protect the village from external threats. If he does not do so, he incurs a fine of one *māṣaka*. This is the meaning. Thus, these rules for villages have been explained. Now, the rules for cities are being stated: "In a city, the king himself shall appoint a magistrate (*adhipati*); he shall supervise the city and shall punish the wicked. In a city, the king himself shall appoint a magistrate. That magistrate shall supervise the city and shall punish those who commit crimes. If he does not do so, he incurs a fine of one *māṣaka*. This is the meaning. Furthermore, regarding the protection of the city, it is said: "He shall maintain the walls, the moats, the gates, and the towers; and he shall station guards at the crossroads. He shall maintain the city walls for defense, the moats for protection, the gates for entry and exit, and the towers for observation. And he shall station guards at the crossroads to prevent crime. If he does not do so, he incurs a fine of one *māṣaka*. This is the meaning. Furthermore, regarding the distribution of goods, it is said: "He shall distribute grain, salt, oil, and honey; and he shall maintain the markets and the weights. He shall distribute grain for the poor, salt for seasoning, oil for lamps and anointing, and honey for medicinal purposes. And he shall maintain the markets and ensure the accuracy of the weights and measures. If he does not do so, he incurs a fine of one *māṣaka*. This is the meaning. Furthermore, regarding the prevention of theft, it is said: "When a thief is caught, he shall be punished; if he is released, the magistrate shall pay the value of the stolen goods. When a thief is caught red-handed, he shall be punished according to the law. If he is released without punishment, the magistrate shall pay the value of the stolen goods to the owner. If he does not do so, he incurs a fine of one *māṣaka*. This is the meaning. Thus, the rules for cities have been explained. Now, the rules for corporations (*gaṇa*) are being stated: "In a corporation, the leader (*gaṇin*) shall act for the common good; he shall punish those who violate the rules. In a corporation, the leader shall act for the welfare of the members. He shall punish those who violate the established rules of the corporation. If he does not do so, he incurs a fine of one *māṣaka*. This is the meaning. Furthermore, regarding the distribution of property, it is said: "He shall divide the common property equally; he shall protect the weak and shall support the aged. He shall divide the common property of the corporation equally among the members. He shall protect those who are weak and shall support the elderly and infirm. If he does not do so, he incurs a fine of one *māṣaka*. This is the meaning. Thus, the rules for corporations have been explained. Now, the rules for heretics (*pāṣaṇḍa*) are being stated: "In a community of heretics, the teacher (*ācārya*) shall teach the doctrine; he shall maintain the monastery and shall punish the transgressors. In a community of heretics, the teacher shall teach the doctrine to the disciples. He shall maintain the monastery and shall punish those who transgress the rules of the order. If he does not do so, he incurs a fine of one *māṣaka*. This is the meaning. Furthermore, regarding the distribution of alms, it is said: "He shall distribute alms, clothing, and medicine; and he shall maintain the sacred texts and the rituals. He shall distribute alms to the needy, clothing to those in need, and medicine to the sick. And he shall maintain the sacred texts and perform the prescribed rituals. If he does not do so, he incurs a fine of one *māṣaka*. This is the meaning. Thus, the rules for heretics have been explained. Now, the rules for guilds (*naigama*) are being stated: "In a guild, the elder (*sthavira*) shall oversee the business; he shall settle disputes and shall protect the merchants. In a guild, the elder shall oversee the commercial affairs. He shall settle disputes among the members and shall protect the merchants from external dangers. If he does not do so, he incurs a fine of one *māṣaka*. This is the meaning. Furthermore, regarding the distribution of profits, it is said: "He shall divide the profits fairly; he shall provide loans and shall maintain the workshops. He shall divide the profits of the guild fairly among the members. He shall provide loans to those in need and shall maintain the workshops for production. If he does not do so, he incurs a fine of one *māṣaka*. This is the meaning. Thus, the rules for guild
The construction of assembly halls, water-stations, temples, tanks, and gardens;
likewise, the performance of sacraments for the destitute and the poor, and the act of sacrificing.
"The building of dwellings and their cessation must be carried out by us according to our respective shares;
that this document has been written in such a manner constitutes a righteous formal agreement."
"But it must be observed by all; however, for one who is capable and yet violates it, the punishment shall be the confiscation of all property and banishment from the city. [351]

Sacrificial rites refer to the giving of gifts to those who perform Soma sacrifices and the like. Kulāyana refers to the wandering of those afflicted by famine and such calamities. When that has occurred, whatever arrangement is to be made is expressed by the word "tat" (that). Nirodha means maintaining [the community] until the end of the famine and other such hardships. "Aṃśataḥ" (by shares) means that it should be carried out using the wealth collected through houses, fields, men, and so forth, or by one who remains wealthy. Thus, once the formal agreement (*samayakriyā*) has been made, it is not only to be observed by the members of the community, but also by the king; so says Nārada.
"The king shall likewise protect the established conventions among heretics, guilds, corporations, associations, bands, and assemblies, both in the fort and in the countryside. Thus it is said.

Heretics (*pāṣaṇḍas*) are those outside the Veda who wear the sectarian marks (*liṅga*) prescribed in the Vedas, or all others who possess such marks. Among them, there exist conventions (*samayas*) such as those regarding malevolent magic (*abhicāra*). Merchants (*naigama*) include traders, merchants, and the like; among them, there exist many conventions, such as the rule that "those who insult a man carrying a sealed message must be punished. Alternatively, "merchants" refers to those such as the Pāśupatas and others who accept the authority of the Veda because it was composed by a trustworthy person (*āpta*); while "artisans" refers to weavers and others who subsist through trade and crafts, among whom there are conventions such as "this must be sold only through this specific guild"; and "yugas" refers to elephant-riders, horsemen, and so forth. The meaning of the words *vrāta* and *gaṇa* has been shown by Kātyāyana.
"Multitudes bearing various weapons are declared to be 'assembled' (vrāta);
that which is a collection of families is proclaimed to be a 'gaṇa'. Thus [it is said].

There are conventions such as: "In a *pūga* or a *vrāta*, one must not depart from the battle after abandoning one another," and so forth. Regarding a *gaṇa*, there are conventions such as: "The piercing of the ears (*karṇavedha*) must be performed on the fifth day or in the fifth year. Regarding a fortress (*durga*), there exists a convention that one who has taken grain or other goods intending to go elsewhere must not sell them. In a district (*janapada*), however, there are many kinds of conventions, such as the collection of tolls (*śulka*) either from the hand of the seller or from the hand of the buyer. The meaning is that the king should act in such a way that this collection of conventions does not fall into ruin nor is it transgressed. Bṛhaspati states a specific rule regarding groups (*samudāya*) of persons: [The text continues with Bṛhaspati’s verse: "Those who have entered into an agreement among themselves should fulfill it; otherwise, they shall incur the sin of killing a Brahmin. The meaning is that those who have entered into an agreement among themselves must carry out that very agreement; otherwise, they incur the sin of killing a Brahmin. This is because the agreement itself is the cause of their protection. Thus ends the section on conventions. Now, the author describes the means of punishment (*daṇḍa*). [The text continues: Punishment is of four kinds: corporal (*śārīra*), monetary (*ārthika*), both, and social exclusion (*nirvāsana*). Among these, corporal punishment consists of branding with the mark of a dog's foot, the mark of a headless corpse, or the mark of a monkey, or the cutting off of the nose, the ears, the hands, or the feet, or banishment from the kingdom. Monetary punishment consists of fines ranging from one *paṇa* up to the confiscation of all property. Both [corporal and monetary] punishment consists of the aforementioned branding and so forth, along with the confiscation of all property. Social exclusion consists of expulsion from the city or the kingdom. Among these, corporal punishment is for the lowest class of offenders, monetary punishment for the middle class, and both for the highest class. "Having first established mutual trust through a sealed deposit, a written document, or neutral mediators, they should subsequently carry out their affairs. Here, "neutral mediators" refers to sureties; "affairs" refers to the business of the corporation. Kātyāyana also says:
"Established in their own duties, they should always perform all their tasks according to that dharma which belongs to the corporations.
Thus Bṛhaspati distinguishes between what is to be rejected and what is to be adopted among those who carry out the business of the corporation.
Those who are hostile, addicted to vices, modest, lazy, or timid;
those who are aged, greedy, or childish—these should not be appointed as counselors for state affairs.
"Pure, knowers of the Vedic dharma, skillful, self-controlled, of noble birth,
and proficient in all tasks— such persons of the highest caliber should be appointed.
When it is asked how many such persons are to be appointed, he himself says:
"Two, three, or five persons who speak for the welfare of the community should be appointed; their word must be obeyed by the village, guilds, assemblies, and so forth.
Regarding one who transgresses the word of those speaking for the welfare of the community, Yājñavalkya states the following punishment:
"The words of those who speak for the welfare of the assembly must be carried out by all;
he who acts contrary to that shall be made to pay the first fine. Thus [says Yājñavalkya, 2.188]. Kātyāyana also says:
"He who destroys what is consistent with reason, he who provides no opportunity for the performance of a task,
and he who speaks what is unreasonable— such a person shall be made to pay the first amercement. Thus says Bṛhaspati as well.
"But he who would harm what is common property, or revile one learned in the three Vedas, or obstruct a formal agreement or a ritual act— he shall be banished from that city.
Thus [Manu] stated the punishment even for members of a corporation (*samūha*) for performing an act contrary to dharma out of hatred or other such motives.

"When those possessed by hatred should cause harm to one person, all of them shall have their property confiscated by the king and be punished according to the consequences (*anubandha*). "According to the consequences" means according to the extent of the aftermath, so that they do not abandon the agreement. He states that the king should prevent the primary offenders from being subjected to punishment: [355] "If, through anger, they should commit violence against one another, the king should punish them all equally, even if they are his own kin. He says this because the king must protect the subjects from the wicked. Furthermore, he says: "In cases where there is no witness, nor a document, nor a clear sign, the king should investigate the truth by means of oaths (*śapatha*) and ordeals (*divya*).
