"When a disagreement arises among the leaders of the assemblies,
the king shall then investigate the matter and establish them upon their own path.
Regarding the punishment for one who, being a leader, misappropriates the property or assets of the assembly, Yājñavalkya says:

"Whoever misappropriates the property of the community (*gaṇadravya*) or whoever violates an agreement (*saṃvid*), having confiscated all his possessions, the king shall banish him from the realm. (YDh 2.187).
Bṛhaspati states that for those who expose secrets and the like, banishment from the city is indeed the punishment.
One who inflicts wounds, a slanderer, a creator of dissension, as well as one who commits violence,
and one who hates guilds, corporations, or the king, shall then be swiftly banished.
The guilds, the leaders of the assemblies, and those residing in the city fortresses shall impose verbal censure and social exclusion upon evildoers.

"Whatever punishment or favor toward men is carried out by them according to their own duty, that must also be approved by the king; for they are traditionally considered to have been delegated with full authority.

The meaning of "delegated with full authority" (*nisṛṣṭārthāḥ*) is that their actions have been authorized. Nārada states how the king should conduct himself toward all assemblies, such as those of heretics (*pāṣaṇḍin*) and others:
Whatever the duty, whatever the ritual for their attendance,
and whatever the means of their livelihood may be— one should approve of them accordingly.

"Whatever is contrary to the king's interest, whatever is inherently contemptible, whatever action is faulty, and whatever is not ordained by the sacred tradition— even if such a thing has already been set in motion— a king who desires his own welfare should cause it to be desisted. Thus [it is said].

Dharma consists of such things as wearing matted hair (*jaṭā*) and so forth. Ritual action (*karma*) includes wandering for alms at dawn when they have become stale, and so forth. The rule for attendance (*upasthānavidhi*) is the gathering in a pavilion or similar place upon hearing the sound of a drum or other signal for the sake of communal business. The adoption of a livelihood (*vṛttyupādāna*) is the taking up of the garb of an ascetic for the purpose of subsistence. [357] It is contrary to the king when a *śūdra* acting as an official performs the adjudication of dharma in a dispute involving members of the three higher castes. Its contrariness has been stated in another *smṛti*: "That king with whom a *śūdra* performs the adjudication of dharma..."
"His kingdom becomes agitated, and his army and treasury perish. Thus it is said.

That which is naturally despised (*prakṛtyavamata*) is that which is inherently disapproved among heretics and others, such as the consumption of betel and other things that obstruct [proper conduct], including alchemy and the like. Mutual association (*mithaḥ saṅghātakaraṇam*) refers to performing intermediate *stomas* separately before the formal assembly (*upasthāna-vidhi*), or the placing of ritual jars and so forth. Mutual affliction (*parasparopatāpa*) refers to the seizing of each other's property and the like by resorting to royal officials. Faulty performance (*doṣavat karaṇam*) refers to that which contradicts the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, such as the practice of prostitution and the like among widows and others, as devised by heretics and others. Manu states the punishment for violating an agreement:
A man who, having made a formal agreement with truth regarding villages, districts, or assemblies,
should later break that agreement out of greed— him the king shall banish from the realm.
Having brought him to trial, the king should compel that violator of agreements to pay four suvarṇas, six niṣkas, and one silver śatamāna.
[358] "In this manner, a righteous lord of the earth shall administer the rule of punishment against those who violate their agreements within villages, castes, and assemblies. (MDh 8.219–21).

Regarding the oath by truth, the determination of these penalties—consisting of banishment, four *suvarṇas*, six *niṣkas*, or one hundred *mānas*—must be established in accordance with the caste, learning, virtues, and other qualities of the individuals involved. Yājñavalkya speaks concerning one who does not give to the assembly the property entrusted to them by the king for the purpose of honoring the group:
The lord of the earth, having honored those who have come for the business of the assembly with gifts, respect, and hospitality, should dismiss them once their business is accomplished.
"Whatever one sent on behalf of the collective business may obtain, that he shall hand over; if he does not hand it over himself, he should be made to pay eleven times [the amount]. (YDh 2.189–90).
And the wealth handed over by one sent on behalf of the collective business, all the members of the collective shall divide and take. Thus says Bṛhaspati:

"Then whatever may be obtained, that shall be equal for all. This rule regarding taking after distribution refers to the subject of atomic substances (*aṇudravya*). Regarding that same subject, he himself says:
"It should be divided according to shares, whether every six months or every year."
One should give to the deaf, the elderly, the blind, women, children, the afflicted, and the sick.
“Such is this eternal law regarding those who live in common and others.
He [Yājñavalkya] states that even a share obtained through the favor of a king is equal for all:
“Whatever has been acquired or protected by them, or whatever debt has been incurred for the sake of the community...”
"And whatever was obtained through the king's favor, all that shall be shared equally.
This refers to cases where the property has not been consumed. However, regarding consumption, Kātyāyana says:
"Whatever debt may have been incurred for the sake of a group, if it has been consumed [by an individual], [he must pay it]."
"Or, if it has been set aside for one's own sake, it should be given by those very [members]; that would be the rule.
Regarding those who have propitiated the corporation (*samudāya*) but, due to disturbances within the corporation or other reasons, have become excluded from it, he says the same:
"Those who have entered into the midst of the guilds (*gaṇin*) or groups of artisans..."
All of them indeed share equal portions with the previous debtor.
"In the same way, one should behave toward meals and in the performance of acts of giving and merit;
while remaining in the group, one shares in the portion, but having departed, one shares in no portion.
This is the legal subject known as "Breach of Agreement" (*saṃvidvyatikrama*).
Now, the rescission of a purchase is discussed; its nature was stated by Nārada:
"When a purchaser, having bought a commodity for a price, does not regard it highly..."
"Repentance after purchase" is said to be this subject of dispute.
To prevent the arising of such repentance after having purchased, the buyer should examine the goods thoroughly even before the sale. And thus says that same [author]:
"The buyer should himself examine the merchandise beforehand for its qualities and defects."
"What has been purchased after being approved by examination shall not belong to the seller again.
Thus, that which is purchased after being approved by examination belongs to the buyer alone even if its defects are subsequently perceived, and not to the seller. And so says Bṛhaspati:
"Having accepted what has been examined and highly approved, one should not abandon it again."
[361] Thus, the non-return of an item examined at that time refers to cases with a fixed period, because immediate examination is prescribed therein. And so Vyāsa says:
"For skins, wood, bricks, thread, grain, liquor, and juice, as well as for cloth, silver, and gold, the examination must be performed immediately."
He [Yājñavalkya] himself states the time limit for examining purchased goods according to their specific nature:
"One should examine a milch animal within three days, but a draft animal within five;
the examination of gems, pearls, and corals shall take place within seven days."
For men, it should last for half a month; for women, it is double that.
"Within ten days for all seeds, and within one day for metals and clothes;
if a defect in the merchandise is discovered before that time, it must be returned by the seller, and the buyer shall recover the price. Thus [it is said].

However, Kātyāyana states that once the period for examination as previously described has elapsed, the item need not be returned: "But when something is purchased without being examined and is later found to be defective, that merchandise must be returned to the owner at the proper time; otherwise, it need not be returned."

[362] Thus: "That substance which is 'unrecognized'—meaning not fully understood in its true nature through examination—must be returned at the time previously specified for examination. Otherwise, even if it is recognized as defective after that time has passed, it need not be returned to its owner because it was purchased [at that price]. Nārada states that one must first ascertain the increase or decrease in value of commodities according to place and time:
"One should know the loss and the gain of commodities, as well as their market availability."

The meaning is that one should know that the price of goods such as horses will increase at this time and in this place; likewise, one should know the source of their arrival for the purpose of ascertaining lineage and so forth, as well as the birthplace of the producer and other such details. Having thus examined [the goods] thoroughly, Yājñavalkya states that no rescission of the sale should be made without considering the time and the observation of its merits and defects: "An ignorant merchant, having purchased goods without knowing their depreciation or appreciation, should not rescind the sale; if he does so, he shall be liable to a fine of one-sixth [of the value]. (YDh 2.258)

[363] Thus: after the time of purchase, for goods that have been examined, a buyer who did not perceive an increase in value resulting from the change in quantity shall not exercise the right of rescission (*anuśaya*); nor shall a seller who did not perceive a loss of value due to a high price fix the price. By implication, it is stated that a buyer or a seller may indeed exercise the right of rescission when they do possess knowledge of the timing of such loss or increase in value. If, however, in the absence of these three causes—the defect of the commodity, its increase in value, or its loss in value—one exercises the right of rescission even within the period for rescission, one shall be fined one-sixth of the value of the commodity. Likewise, even if the causes for rescission exist, one who exercises the right of rescission after the lapse of the period for rescission shall also be fined in this same manner.
This [rule] refers to objects that are not perishable through use. Regarding objects that *are* perishable through use, Nārada states the time limit for returning them:
"If a buyer, having purchased a commodity for its price, considers it a bad purchase, it must be returned to the seller on that very same day, provided it has not been damaged."
Regarding the return [of the object] on the second day or subsequent days, a specific rule has been stated by that same author:
"If the buyer returns it on the second day, he should pay a thirtieth part of the price;
on the third day, however, double that amount; and from then on, the loss falls upon the buyer alone."
The meaning is that one should not harbor resentment toward others. Furthermore, as stated by Manu:
"If, after having bought or sold anything here, one should have cause for regret, he may give back or take back that object within ten days."

Thus, this refers to houses, fields, vehicles, beds, and so forth, which do not perish through use, because the period of ten days and so on has been prescribed specifically for those. And so Kātyāyana says:
"In the case of land, the impurity lasts ten days for both the seller and the buyer;
for the *sapiṇḍas*, it lasts twelve days, and after that, even for a small amount."

The punishment declared by Manu should be understood to apply to one who, regarding items that are imperishable and of stable value, creates a debt by allowing the period for the payment of the interest to lapse:
"But after ten days have passed, one shall neither give nor cause to be given;
both he who takes and he who gives [the loan] should be fined six hundred [paṇas] by the king. (MDh 8.152)

Enjoyment [of goods] is distinct from the seeds and other such items. Regarding clothing as well, Nārada states: "If a garment has already been worn, is disfigured, or soiled, even if it was purchased with defects, it shall not belong to the seller again."
Thus ends the section on regret after purchase; now follows the non-delivery after sale.
Its nature was described by Nārada: "When, having sold a commodity for a price, it is not delivered to the buyer— that is called the legal head of dispute known as 'non-delivery after sale'."
The two-fold nature of merchandise has been stated by that same [author]:
"In this world, there are two kinds of property: immovable and movable;
all of that is called 'merchandise' (paṇya) in the context of the laws of purchase and sale."

"However, the wise have recorded its method of giving and taking as being sixfold: by counting, by weighing, by measuring, and by [specifying] action, form, and quality. (YDh 2.176) *Gaṇima* refers to that which is to be counted, such as pomegranates and the like. *Tulima* refers to that which is to be weighed on a scale, such as gold, sandalwood, and the like. *Meya* refers to rice and the like. That which is characterized by action—such as horses, buffaloes, and so forth—is indicated by actions like riding or milking. That which is [distinguished] by form refers to courtesans and the like. That which is [distinguished] by quality refers to rubies and the like. Regarding this merchandise of six kinds, Yājñavalkya states that one who sells it but does not deliver it must be made to pay it along with interest.

If one who has received the price does not deliver the merchandise to the buyer, he shall be made to pay that price together with interest; or, if the buyer has come from another region, he shall be made to pay the profit derived from that region. (YDh 2.254)

[366] Thus: If a seller does not deliver the goods for which the price has been paid to a buyer who is a local merchant and who requests them, and if those goods—which at the time of purchase were of high value—can subsequently be obtained for a much lower price, then the seller must be compelled to give them to the buyer along with their *udaya* (profit), that is, together with interest. However, when there is no profit resulting from a decrease in the value of the goods, but rather only as much as was agreed upon at the time of purchase—that is, "this is the goods for such a price"—then the seller must be compelled to give the goods along with the profit derived from selling them in that same place, combined with the profit in the form of interest stipulated as two-fold, three-fold, and so forth. As Nārada says:
"If the price should fall, he shall bring back the merchandise with interest;
this is the rule for stationary traders, while those who travel to various regions receive the profit of their respective directions.

When, however, due to a decrease in market value, the merchandise becomes less than its original worth, then the seller must be made to pay the value of that merchandise—such as clothing, houses, and so forth—along with the benefit derived from it, consisting of the use of the goods for clothing, food, shelter, and the like. As Nārada says:
"If, after selling a commodity for its price, one does not deliver it to the buyer, one shall be made to pay the profit of immovable property, or the fruit of the labor for movable property. [367]

By the word *kṣaya* (depreciation), the loss of value is meant. Although it is impossible to give that [loss] itself back, nevertheless, an article corresponding to it must be given. In the case of moving goods, however, he [the seller] should be made to pay the price based on the [current] state of those goods. But when the buyer has come from another country for the purpose of purchasing merchandise, then the seller must cause the buyer to receive the merchandise along with whatever profit was gained by selling it in that other country. Viṣṇu, moreover, prescribes a fine for the seller: "He who, having received the price, does not deliver the merchandise to the buyer, shall be made to pay that [merchandise] together with its profit, and shall also be fined one hundred *paṇas* by the king. Regarding him who, after selling, does not hand over [the goods] due to regret (*anuśaya*), and him who, after buying, does not take them due to regret, Kātyāyana says:
He who, having purchased and obtained something, does not accept it, or he who does not give back an undamaged item,
shall recover his own property by paying a tenth part of the price.
"One should never cause [the object] to be delivered if it has not been obtained, if the time for delivery was difficult, or if it was done after [the period];
such is the law. However, after ten days have passed, there can be no rescission."

The phrase "not spoiled by water, etc. is an ellipsis; [the meaning is] that [the goods] are not spoiled by water and so forth. Regarding "milkable, transportable, and other merchandise," the ellipsis is "by milking, etc. The "time for the purposeful action" (*arthakriyākāla*) is the time for milking and so forth regarding milkable, transportable, and other merchandise. If, when that time has arrived, one fails to take or fails to give [the goods], the king shall cause the offender to pay a tenth part [as a fine]. However, even without giving that [fine], he shall recover his own property. This rule is to be understood as applying prior to ten days; beyond that, no rescission (*anuśaya*) should be made. Yājñavalkya states that even in the case of one who sells but does not deliver, if the sold merchandise—which remains in the possession of the seller—is destroyed by fate or other causes, the loss falls upon the seller alone.
"When merchandise has been damaged due to an act of God or the king, the loss falls upon the seller himself if he does not deliver it when requested. (YDh 2.256).
By the qualification "when requested," it is understood by implication that there is no loss for the seller if [delivery] was not requested. Nārada also says:
If the merchandise should be damaged, burnt, or stolen,
that loss belongs solely to the seller who, having sold it, does not deliver it.

[369] Thus it is said. Just as there is a loss for a seller who does not deliver what has been requested, so too is there a loss for a buyer who does not accept the commodity being offered; regarding this, that same author states: "If a buyer does not accept the purchased commodity while it is being given, that same fault which belongs to a seller who does not deliver shall belong to him."

Yājñavalkya also states: "Even if it has been sold, the article may be reclaimed by the seller if the buyer has not yet taken possession; for if the loss occurs through the fault of the buyer, that loss shall belong to the buyer alone. (YDh 2.255)

Nārada states that the punishment for those two is equal: one who, having shown a faultless commodity, sells one that is defective, and one who, having sold it to one person, delivers it to another. "But he who, having shown a faultless item, delivers one that is defective, shall be made to pay double its value and an equal amount as a fine."
"And having sold it into the hand of one person, he likewise delivers it to another;
he too shall be made to pay double that amount as a fine, and an equal amount as a penalty.
This refers to a case where the act is intentional.
[370] If an unwise man, knowing that a commodity is defective, sells it,
he shall be made to pay double that amount, as well as an equal fine as a penalty.

This is because it was stated by Bṛhaspati: "But in the case of an unintentional [purchase], the buyer must simply return it. For this very reason, he (Bṛhaspati) himself stated regarding the rescission of such a purchase: "That which was sold by one who is intoxicated, insane, or out of fear, or by one who is not independent or deluded, must be relinquished; it shall belong to him again."

Therefore, such a rule is to be understood as applying to a purchase where the price has been paid. However, regarding merchandise for which the price has not been paid, or in a case of a verbal sale, there is no fault whatsoever if the transaction proceeds without a formal agreement between the buyer and the seller. Thus says Nārada:
"This rule has been proclaimed for merchandise whose price has been paid;
in other cases, provided there is no agreement, there is no transgression on the part of the seller."

Furthermore, regarding a case where something is placed in the hand of the seller by the buyer so that the purchase might not be merely verbal, Vyāsa says that if the purchase fails due to a defect in the buyer, [the following applies]:
"If one who has given a down payment (*satyaṃkāra*) does not appear at the appointed time,
or if the merchandise has been relinquished and he refuses to accept it when it is being offered," [he shall forfeit it].

[371] Thus it is said. Here, the "relinquishing of the commodity" (paṇyadravya) is intended as the relinquishing of the earnest-money (satyaṃkāra-dravya). Regarding this very matter, when the sale fails due to a defect in the seller, Yājñavalkya says: "One should cause the person who provided the earnest-money to be made to return double the amount.
To prevent regret after having purchased, Manu states that certain types of commodities are unfit for sale:
"An object whose form is not mixed with another is not fit for sale;
nor one that is worthless, nor one that is deficient, nor one that is distant, nor one that is concealed. (MDh 8.203).
Thus ends the legal title of dispute known as *krayavikrayānuśaya* (rescission of purchase and sale).
[372] Now follows the procedure for disputes between owners and herdsmen;
regarding this, Manu has made a formal declaration concerning its exposition.
"I shall fully declare, according to the true principles of dharma, the dispute arising from the transgressions of both owners and herdsmen regarding livestock. (MDh 8.229).
"Dispute" here means the resolution of the dispute. Nārada states the duties of both the owner and the herdsman:
"The cowherd should bring back the cows every day at the end of the night;
having grazed and drunk, he should bring them back in the evening. Here, the mention of "cows" is intended as an illustration for all livestock. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya says:

"Just as a cowherd should return the cattle entrusted to him in the evening, so [should he return them in the morning]. (YDh 2.164) The meaning is that however many were entrusted in the morning, that same number must be returned in the evening. Nārada states the measure of wages for the protector of cows and other livestock:
"For every hundred cows, a young bull shall be the fee; for two hundred, a milch cow."

"Every year, O cowherd, the *saṃdoha* on the eighth day. This means that every year a two-year-old heifer (*vatsatarī*) is to be assigned as wages for the hired laborer; however, when the fee is two hundred [paṇas], a cow with her calf is to be assigned. Furthermore, the *saṃdoha*—meaning the milking of the entire herd—is to be assigned as wages on the eighth day; the meaning is that one who is hired by that cow shall receive all the milk on the eighth day. *Saṃdoha* refers to the milking of all [the cows]; from that cow hired as wages, one shall obtain the entirety of the milk on the eighth day.

This is because of the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of Bṛhaspati. And this arrangement regarding wages applies to cases where no specific wage has been stipulated; however, when a specific wage has been stipulated, that very amount must be given. Manu, however, describes wages in another manner:
"A cowherd who is paid with milk may, with the consent of the owner of the cattle, milk the best cow out of ten; that shall be the wage for a herdsman if no other wage is provided. (MDh 8.231)

From among ten cows that yield milk, one should take the best and most excellent cow for oneself and receive its milk as wages; however, for those cows that are devoid of milk, the wages should be calculated according to the value of their milk. This means that if he has been hired for another kind of labor, this specific wage does not apply. Regarding the servant who, having accepted such a stipulated salary while tending the animals, kills or destroys them through his own negligence, Yājñavalkya says: "One who has received wages must make good the animals lost or destroyed through negligence" (YDh 2.164).
The mention of "negligence" (*pramāda*) is intended to indicate the faults of the keeper. Negligence has been clearly defined by Manu:
"But the keeper alone shall restore what is lost, destroyed by worms, seized by dogs, killed in a dangerous place, or deficient in human effort" (MDh 8.232).

One who has been forcibly carried off by thieves need not be made to pay restitution. And so says that same author: "But a herdsman is not liable to pay for what has been carried off by thieves after they were publicly proclaimed, provided he announces it to his master at the proper place and time" (MDh 8.233).
Vyāsa also says:
"In the case of seizure by predators, destruction of the village, or likewise in the upheaval of the kingdom,
whatever may be lost or stolen, there is no fault in the herdsmen in this regard."

This should be understood as applying when one performs human effort (*puruṣakāra*). However, if one fails to perform such effort, one certainly becomes a sinner. The nature of human effort has been shown by Nārada:
"One should protect [the cattle] from the fear of worms, thieves, tigers, caves, and pits;
one should exert oneself according to one's ability, cry out [for help], and report it to the owner. Thus it is said.
"One should strive" means one should exert effort for the purpose of preventing [the loss]. He says the following regarding him who does not strive for the matter at hand:
"If he does not strive, does not cry out, or does not inform his master, the cowherd must bear the value of that [lost animal] as well as a fine to the king. Thus it is said.
Yājñavalkya states the authoritative rule regarding discipline:
"In the case of destruction due to the fault of the keeper,
a fine is prescribed for the keeper, amounting to twelve and a half paṇas, as well as the value of the property itself" (YDh 2.165).
"Thirteen and a half paṇas" means twelve and a half kārṣāpaṇas. Regarding the fault of the herdsman, Manu says:
[376] "But when goats and sheep are hemmed in by wolves and the herdsman does not come to their aid, whatever wolf may forcibly kill shall be the herdsman's fault. (MDh 8.235)

"Anāyati" means not coming back, for the purpose of removing danger; that is, [the animal] does not return. This refers to the case of animals of the goat or sheep species when they are in an accessible place. However, he himself states that there is no fault in the case of an inaccessible place: "If, among those [animals] being kept and grazing together in the forest, a wolf should kill one by leaping upon it, the herdsman is not culpable therein. (MDh 8.236)
The meaning is: those that have been kept penned together by a herdsman. Furthermore, in the case of those that died of natural causes, the ears and so forth must be shown. Thus Manu says:

"Upon the death of animals, one should give the ears, hide, tail-hairs, the bladder, bones, sinews, and the yellow pigment (rocana) to the owners; one should show these parts [to prove the cause of death]. (MDh 8.234)
[377] Thus it is said. There is also another Smṛti text:
"The ears, the hide, the tail-hairs, the horns, the sinews, the bones, and the fat—one should give these to the owners of the animals; however, when they have died, one should show the limbs."

Yājñavalkya states regarding the pasture land for cattle: "The pasture for cattle may be [determined] by the will of the village, or even by the will of the king" (YDh 2.116). Depending on whether the village is small or large, or by the will of the king, an unploughed portion of land—even if it is a wasteland—should be set aside for the purpose of the cattle grazing on grass and the like. He further states the distance between the village and the fields for the sake of providing convenient space for the cattle's movement and resting: [The text continues with the verse: "Between the village and the field, there should be a space of one hundred *dhanus* for the pasture; beyond that, the field belongs to the owner. (YDh 2.158) A *dhanus* is equal to four *aralīs*, and an *aralī* is equal to twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgulas*). Thus, the distance from the village to the field should be four hundred *dhanus*. Beyond this, the field is the property of its owner. This is the rule concerning pasture land. Regarding the rules for the grazing of cattle, he says: "Having entered the pasture, they should graze until the sun has risen; having grazed, they should return before sunset. (YDh 2.160) They should enter the pasture at dawn and graze until sunrise. Having grazed, they should return before sunset. If they do not return by sunset, the following penance applies: "If they do not return by sunset, the master of the herd shall perform a *prājāpatya* penance. (YDh 2.161) If the cattle do not return by sunset, the owner of the herd must perform the *prājāpatya* penance. If the cattle stray onto another's field and eat the crops, the following applies: "If they eat the crops of another, the owner of the herd shall pay the value of the damage, or else perform a *prājāpatya* penance. (YDh 2.162) If the cattle eat the crops of another person, the owner of the herd must pay the value of the damage, or else perform the *prājāpatya* penance. If the cattle stray onto a field belonging to the king, the following applies: "If they stray into the king’s field, the owner of the herd shall pay a fine of one *māṣaka*. (YDh 2.163) If the cattle stray into a field belonging to the king, the owner of the herd shall pay a fine of one *māṣaka*. If the cattle stray into a field belonging to a Brahmin who is learned in the Vedas, the following applies: "If they stray into the field of a Brahmin learned in the Vedas, the owner of the herd shall perform a *prājāpatya* penance. (YDh 2.164) If the cattle stray into the field of a Brahmin who is learned in the Vedas, the owner of the herd shall perform the *prājāpatya* penance. If the cattle stray into the field of a Brahmin who is not learned in the Vedas, the following applies: "If they stray into the field of a Brahmin who is not learned in the Vedas, the owner of the herd shall give a cow as a gift. (YDh 2.165) If the cattle stray into the field of a Brahmin who is not learned in the Vedas, the owner of the herd shall give a cow as a sacrificial gift. If the cattle stray into the field of a Śūdra, the following applies: "If they stray into the field of a Śūdra, the owner of the herd shall give a load of grain. (YDh 2.166) If the cattle stray into the field of a Śūdra, the owner of the herd shall give a load of grain. If the cattle stray into the field of a Vaiśya, the following applies: "If they stray into the field of a Vaiśya, the owner of the herd shall give half a load of grain. (YDh 2.167) If the cattle stray into the field of a Vaiśya, the owner of the herd shall give half a load of grain. If the cattle stray into the field of a Kṣatriya, the following applies: "If they stray into the field of a Kṣatriya, the owner of the herd shall give a quarter of a load of grain. (YDh 2.168) If the cattle stray into the field of a Kṣatriya, the owner of the herd shall give a quarter of a load of grain. If the cattle stray into the field of a Vaiśya who is learned in the Vedas, the following applies: "If they stray into the field of a Vaiśya learned in the Vedas, the owner of the herd shall perform a *prājāpatya* penance. (YDh 2.169) If the cattle stray into the field of a Vaiśya who is learned in the Vedas, the owner of the herd shall perform the *prājāpatya* penance. If the cattle stray into the field of a Kṣatriya who is learned in the Vedas, the following applies: "If they stray into the field of a Kṣatriya learned in the Vedas, the owner of the herd shall fast for three days. (YDh 2.170) If the cattle stray into the field of a Kṣatriya who is learned in the Vedas, the owner of the herd shall fast for three days. If the cattle stray into the field of a Śūdra who is learned in the Vedas, the following applies: "If they stray into the field of a Śūdra learned in the Vedas, the owner of the herd shall fast for one day. (YDh 2.171) If the cattle stray into the field of a Śūdra who is learned in the Vedas, the owner of the herd shall fast for one day. If the cattle stray into the field of a Vaiśya who is not learned in the Vedas, the following applies: "If they stray into the field of a Vaiśya who is not learned in the Vedas, the owner of the herd shall give a *droṇa* of grain. (YDh 2.172) If the cattle stray into the field of a Vaiśya who is not learned in the Vedas, the owner of the herd shall give a *droṇa* of grain. If the cattle stray into the field of a Kṣatriya who is not learned in the Vedas, the following applies: "If they stray into the field of a Kṣatriya who is not learned in the Vedas, the owner of the herd shall give half a *droṇa* of grain. (YDh 2.173) If the cattle stray into the field of a Kṣatriya who is not learned in the Vedas, the owner of the herd shall give half a *droṇa* of grain. If the cattle stray into the field of a Śūdra who is not learned in the Vedas, the following applies: "If they stray into the field of a Śūdra who is not learned in the Vedas, the owner of the herd shall give a *prastha* of grain. (YDh 2.174) If the cattle stray into the field of a Śūdra who is not learned in the Vedas, the owner of the herd shall give a *prastha* of grain. If the cattle stray into the field of a Vaiśya who is not learned in the Vedas and eat the crops, the following applies: "If they eat the crops of a Vaiśya who is not learned in the Vedas, the owner of the herd shall give a *droṇa* of grain. (YDh 2.175) If the cattle eat the crops of a Vaiśya who is not learned in the Vedas, the owner of the herd shall give a *droṇa* of grain. If the cattle eat the crops of a Kṣatriya who is not learned in the Vedas, the following applies: "If they eat the crops of a Kṣatriya who is not learned in the Vedas, the owner of the herd shall give half a *droṇa* of grain. (YDh 2.176) If the cattle eat the crops of a Kṣatriya who is not learned in the Vedas, the owner of the herd shall give half a *droṇa* of grain. If the cattle eat the crops of a Śūdra who is not learned in the Vedas, the following applies: "If they eat the crops of a Śūdra who is not learned in the Vedas, the owner of the herd shall give a *prastha* of grain. (YDh 2.177)
"The circumference of a village boundary should be one hundred bows;
that of a *kharvaṭa* should be two hundred, and that of a city four hundred. (YDh 2.167)

The distance between a village and a field shall be one hundred *dhanus*; the crop must always be protected according to the prescribed rule. For a *kharvaṭa*—a village abounding in thorny thickets—the crop should be protected at a distance of two hundred [bow-lengths]. And for a city crowded with many people, the crop should be protected at a distance of four hundred [bow-lengths]. Regarding this, Kātyāyana states that a fence should also be constructed there to ward off cattle:
"One should always provide a barrier even when the crops have already grown;
for wild animals, having once tasted their sweet flavor, are difficult to turn away."
Nārada also says: "On the road or in the field, a fence should be made such that a camel cannot look over it, nor can a beast, a horse, or a boar leap over or break through it."

And Manu has said that even when such measures have been taken to ward off the animals, if they nevertheless bypass them and destroy the crops and so forth: "In the case of a field enclosed by a fence, or one situated on the outskirts of a village, the keeper is liable to a fine of one hundred [paṇas] if the animals enter; however, he should drive away the cattle if they are unattended. Thus it is stated.

When a field on a path is enclosed by a fence, if the crop is damaged by cattle that have bypassed that fence, the keeper is liable for a fine of one hundred *paṇas*. Likewise, when a field near a village boundary is enclosed, if the crop is damaged by bypassing that fence, the keeper is worthy of a fine of one hundred *paṇas*; the meaning is that the owner of those cattle should be punished with a fine of one hundred *paṇas*. The owner of the field should ward off the unattended cattle with a staff or other means. Nārada also says:
"Where the destruction of crops by cows and other animals occurs after they have bypassed the fence..."
"The guardian shall be subject to punishment there if he does not prevent [the damage] by his power.
Regarding the destruction of uncultivated fields, that same author says:
"And that field which is near a village, at the edge of a pasture, or on a great road..."

"If it is unenclosed, there is no transgression on the part of the guardian upon its destruction. By the term *vivīta*, a region belonging to another that is rich in grass and wood is meant. By the prohibition of transgression, the absence of punishment is indicated by implication. Thus, by this, the absence of punishment for the guardian regarding an unenclosed area is indicated. Manu, however, explicitly prohibits the punishment: "If cattle should damage grain that is not enclosed... [380]

"The king shall not inflict punishment upon cattle-herders in that case" (MDh 8.238). This refers to cases where the cattle have been grazing for a short time; however, they deserve punishment if they have grazed for a long time. For this very reason, Viṣṇu states that there is no fault when the grazing is for a short duration: "There is no fault on a path or at the edge of a village if it is for a short time" (ViDh 3.15). As for the measure of the fine according to the specific type of animal, Yājñavalkya has shown it:
"A buffalo that causes damage to the crops [should pay] eight māṣas."
For that offense, however, a cow is subject to a fine of one [paṇa], while a goat or sheep is subject to half of that.
"For those who have eaten and are sitting [there], the fine is double as previously stated;
for these same animals, even in a pasture (*vivīta*), the penalty for a donkey or a camel is equal to that for a buffalo.

(YDh 2.159–60) The owner of a buffalo that destroys another's crop should be fined eight *māṣas* per buffalo; the owner of a cow, four *māṣas*; and the owner of a sheep, two *māṣas* each. For these same animals, if they remain unconfined from the time they begin eating the crop until they go to sleep, their owner shall be fined double the aforementioned amount.

[381] When grass and other vegetation in a pasture (*vivīta*) are damaged, the owner of the cattle is to be punished like one who damages a field of grain. The owner of donkeys or camels is to be punished like the owner of a buffalo-cow. This refers to cases of ignorance. However, for a cow, the fine is two quarters of a *paṇa*; for a buffalo, it is double that; and likewise, for goats, sheep, and calves, a quarter of a *paṇa* is declared as the fine.

This is to be understood as stated in another *smṛti*. Furthermore, in this context, a *māṣa* is one-twentieth of a copper *paṇa*, according to the traditional teaching of Nārada: "A *māṣa* is declared to be the twentieth part of a *paṇa*. Regarding the case of one who sits down after having eaten [the cow] along with its calf, the fine is fourfold compared to what was previously stated. This has been said in another *smṛti*:
"For calves, it is declared to be double; for cows with their calves, it is fourfold.
Furthermore, as stated by Nārada:
"One should cause a cow to pay a fine of one māṣa, and likewise a buffalo two māṣas."
Likewise, for goats, sheep, and calves, the fine shall be half a māṣa.

[382] Thus, this refers to the case of grazing for only a moment. For this very reason, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "A cow grazing at night [incurs a fine of] five māṣas; during the day, three; for a muhūrta, one māṣa; and for a single mouthful, a daṇḍa. However, regarding cattle that are afflicted by illness, Nārada states that there is no fine:
"Whether seized by the king's officers, or struck by lightning and thunderbolts, or bitten by a serpent, or fallen from a tree—"
"Even if [an animal] is killed by tigers and the like, or afflicted by diseases,
there is no fault on the part of the keeper, nor is there any fault on the part of the owners.
Thus he [Yājñavalkya] states that there is no punishment even in the case of certain animals that are not ill.

A cow that has recently calved, for ten days; a large bull; and horses and elephants—these should be restrained with great effort [from causing damage], and their owner shall not be subject to punishment.
Thus [it is said]. Manu also says:

"Manu has declared that cows within ten days of calving, a cow that has recently given birth, bulls, and animals dedicated to the gods—whether they have a herdsman or are without a herdsman—are not subject to punishment. (MDh 8.242)
"Vṛṣā" means a large bull; or alternatively, those released according to the ritual procedure for the release of a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*). Yājñavalkya also says:

"Large bulls, animals released [in ritual], those that have recently given birth, newcomers, and so forth—those for which there is no keeper are not to be claimed [as lost], even when overwhelmed by fate or the king. (YDh 2.166)

An "outsider" (*āgantuka*) is one who has strayed from his own herd. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), those such as cows that have lost their calves are included. For this very reason, Uśanas states: "A cow that has lost its calf, one that is lame, diseased, or emaciated, an outsider, one that has recently calved, and one that is in heat—these are not to be punished."

"Cows are not to be punished during a festival, and likewise at the time of a *śrāddha* ceremony. Furthermore, when there is destruction of another's crops, not only is the owner to be fined, but he must also be made to pay for the crops. Thus says Bṛhaspati: "One should keep cows away from the crops; however, if they have grazed, two faults arise."
The owner shall be made to pay a fine of one hundred [paṇas], while the keeper deserves corporal punishment.
"And six hundred and sixty [paṇas] when the crop has been consumed along with its roots by *kārṣabhakṣita*.
For this very reason, Nārada says:
"But in the case of the destruction of a root-crop, the owner of that field shall incur a fine of one hundred [paṇas]."

"By killing [the cow], the herdsman may be released; he shall inflict the fine upon the owner. Thus, the "owner" refers to the owner of the grain, and the "share" (śada) is that which is determined by the neighbors and others to be paid. And likewise, that same [text] states: "The man who demands compensation for the grain eaten by cows..."
"Grain that has been consumed there should be given with the consent of the neighbors.
As for the prohibition against begging for compensation made by Uśanas, it is established by implication:
"The man who begs for grain destroyed by cattle [is not to be granted it]."
"His ancestors do not eat [the offerings], nor do the inhabitants of the triple heaven eat.
This refers to uncultivated fields located near villages and the like.
Thus concludes the legal title known as "Disputes between Owner and Herdsman."
Now follows the determination of boundary disputes.

In that regard, there are four kinds of boundaries: the boundary of a country (*janapada-sīmā*), the boundary of a village (*grāma-sīmā*), the boundary of a house (*gṛha-sīmā*), and the boundary of a field (*kṣetra-sīmā*). These, respectively, possess five characteristics. As stated by Nārada:
"The banner-bearing (*dhvajinī*), the fish-marked (*matsyanī*), the one established by deposits (*naidhānī*), and the one free from fear (*bhayavarjitā*)."
"And the boundary established by royal decree is recorded as being of five kinds.

Thus: *dvajinī* is characterized by banners, trees, and the like; *matsyinī* is endowed with water-marks; *naidhānī* consists of buried husks, charcoal, and so forth; *bhavarjitā* is established through the mutual agreement of the plaintiff and defendant in the absence of other marks; and *rājaśāsananītā* is established by the king's will in the absence of known witnesses or signs. And so Vyāsa says: "Where there are lofty trees upon the boundary between two villages..."
That which is raised up in the form of a banner is proclaimed as "dhvajinī" (the army).
Where there is a river flowing westward, with abundant water, moving at its own will, and filled with fish and tortoises— that is considered the boundary known as Matsyanī.

"The boundary should be marked by husks, charcoal, potsherds, jars, and likewise by shrines; that is called the *naidhānī* [boundary]. As for the trees, they are the *nyagrodha* and others. Regarding this, Manu says:
"One should establish boundary trees such as the *nyagrodha*, *aśvattha*, *kiṃśuka*, *śālmali*, *sāla*, *tāla*, and milky trees (*kṣīrin*). (MDh 8.246).
By the phrase "flowing westward," ponds and other such visible markers are indicated; these have been shown by Bṛhaspati.
Reservoirs, wells, and ponds; shrines, groves, and temples; as well as high ground, low ground, river currents, reed-beds, thickets, mountains, and so forth.
"One should always cause these signs of demarcation to be made at the boundary.

The phrase "with husks, charcoal, and potsherds" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) that includes other concealed marks such as dried cow-dung and the like. These have been shown by that same author:
"Dried cow-dung, bones, husks, charcoal, gravel, stones, and potsherds..."
Sand, bricks, cow-hair, cotton, bones, and ashes.
"Having cast these into jars, one should have them deposited at the boundaries.
And those boundary markers should be shown to children by the elders; likewise, Bṛhaspati says:
"Thereafter, one should diligently show them to the children who are of school-going age (paugaṇḍa)."
And they should likewise show those children to the elderly.
"In this way, when [the tradition] is known through succession, no confusion regarding the boundary arises.
Thus Manu says that one should settle a dispute over a boundary by means of the aforementioned marks:
"By these marks the king should determine the boundary between two disputing parties."
And by the constant enjoyment of what was previously used, as well as by the arrival of water.
If there were doubt even upon seeing the marks,
the determination of the boundary dispute would depend solely on the testimony of witnesses.
"But in the absence of witnesses, four villages, including the neighboring inhabitants, shall, being purified, determine the boundary in the presence of the king. (MDh 8.252–53, 258)

First of all, the determination of a boundary dispute is made by means of the marks (*liṅga*) presented by the plaintiff and the defendant. If there is still no confidence in this matter, then the determination is made through the testimony of witnesses (*sākṣipratyaya*) concerning either the marks or the boundary itself. When witnesses are absent, the determination is made by the neighbors (*sāmanta*); such is the meaning, because Kātyāyana has stated: "In their absence, the neighbors [shall decide]. When it is asked who these neighbors are, he himself says:
"The immediate neighbors are the *saṃsaktaka*s; likewise, those adjacent to them are the *uttara*s."
"Those who are attached (*saṃsakta*), attached-to-attached (*saṃsaktasaṃsakta*), and attached-to-attached-to-attached (*saṃsaktasaṃsakta*) are proclaimed to be of the 'lotus' type.

Thus, for a field whose boundaries are disputed, those who enjoy the neighboring villages and so forth in the four directions are the "attached" ones; these alone are designated by the term *sāmanta* (neighboring witnesses). However, when such faultless "attached" persons do not exist, then the decision must be made by the "attached-to-attached," the "attached-to-attached-to-attached," and those beyond them. Regarding this, the same author says:
"And when the *sāmanta*s are found to be corrupt in the accomplishment of their own interests, [the decision should be made] because of the gravity of the matter."
However, those who are closely associated with him must perform the extraction; there is no doubt in this matter.
But those who are attached to the faults of those who are themselves attached are declared to be "associated with them";
however, a king who understands the Dharma should employ those who are free from such corruption.

"In their absence, the neighbors, the original owners, the elders, the excavators, and so forth—these must be made witnesses even in the case of the six types of immovable property; there is no doubt about this.
The definition of "elders" and the others has been stated by that same author:
Those endowed with excellent qualities who see what is being bound together—
whether they be old or even young— are proclaimed as truly "elders" (vṛddha).
Those who were formerly neighbors there but later went to another region are proclaimed by the seers as "original" (maula) because they are rooted in that [original territory].
"Because they are marked by the fear of being overheard, of sharing [the secret], and of the place [of the crime],
and because they are drawn out [from that state], they are therefore known as *uddhṛta*s. Thus,
Manu has stated regarding the absence of witnesses and all others down to the *uddhṛta*s:
But in the absence of neighboring boundary-witnesses of the primary villages,
he should also interrogate these men who frequent the forests.
"Hunters, fowlers, cowherds, fishermen, root-diggers, snake-catchers, gleaners, and others who roam the forest" (MDh 8.259–60).
By the word "and others" (*anyāṃś ca*), those who draw boundary lines are indicated. And so says Yājñavalkya:
In a dispute over a boundary, the neighbors, elders, and others, the cowherds, those who cultivate the land at the boundary, and all those within the range of hearing [should be consulted].
"They should establish the boundary, marked by landmarks such as mounds of earth, charcoal, husks, trees, embankments, anthills, depressions, bones, shrines, and so forth.
Thus [says Yājñavalkya]. Nārada also says:
"And those who live by agriculture outside the village boundaries, cowherds, fowlers, hunters, and others who dwell in the forest"—thus [it is said].
And they, having been bound by oaths, should deliver their verdict. Likewise, Bṛhaspati says:
"Bound by their respective oaths, they shall declare the determination of the boundary;
they shall also point out the marks, for that is the established rule regarding the authority of evidence.
Regarding the phrase "by their respective [oaths]":
The meaning is: "One should cause a Brahmin to swear by truth, and a Kṣatriya by his vehicles and weapons," as established by such worldly conventions. Manu also says:
"In the presence of the villagers and the families [of the boundary], the witnesses [should be questioned] at the boundary."
The boundary markers of those two litigants must be questioned.
"But once they have been questioned, one should demarcate the boundary exactly as all of them unanimously declare it, and record them all by name. (MDh 8.254–55).
Bṛhaspati, however, states the defining characteristics of the witnesses to the boundary:

"Those who know the title-deed, the means of proof, the possession, the desire, the name, and the characteristics of the plot of land—they are the witnesses in this matter. "Or the neighboring lords of the land, four, eight, or even ten, all together, wearing red garlands and garments, shall go to establish the boundary. (YDh 2.152)

The phrase "or the neighbors" is an alternative expression intended to include witnesses and others mentioned in other legal treatises (*smṛti*). The inhabitants of the entire village, or those from the neighboring villages—four, eight, or ten in number, being equal in count—should display the boundary while wearing red garlands and red garments, with clods of earth placed upon their heads. Having been sworn by their respective oaths, they should lead [the parties] along the boundary. And so Manu says:
"Wearing garlands and red clothes, they shall hold the earth upon their heads."
"Bound by their own good deeds, they should determine the matter correctly. (MDh 8.256).
Although the plural number in "they should determine" (*nayeyuḥ*) is not intended to be significant, for Bṛhaspati has shown that even a single person may indicate the boundary:
"Even a single virtuous man, approved by both parties, [may do so] in the absence of witnesses and marks."
Wearing red garlands and garments, he took earth upon his head.
"A man who is devoted to truth and has observed a fast shall indicate the boundary. As for that which was stated by Nārada:
"A man, even if he is trustworthy, should not determine the boundary alone."
"Because this matter is of great importance, this procedure is established for many [cases].

This refers to cases other than those where both parties agree upon a knower of the law (*dharmavid*). Regarding the specific means for determining boundaries even in the absence of marks such as mounds and the like, Nārada says:
"In lands where boundary marks have been swept away by river waters, abandoned, or destroyed..."
"And because of the inference from that region, and because of the observation of experience through valid cognition. Thus [it is said].

The meaning is that they should determine [the boundary] by means of the following: (1) from the removal by a river flowing downwards, [objects] cast away, lost, or displaced from their original locations; (2) from the observation of visible marks in those specific regions according to the estimation of the local area; (3) from usage, such as the measurement starting from a village, namely "a field measuring one thousand *daṇḍas* constitutes the western portion of this village"; and (4) from the observation of possession, either through undisputed enjoyment witnessed by the opposing party or through possession characterized by a period beyond the limits of memory (*asmārta-kāla*). If, among these witnesses, neighbors, and others, no calamity caused by the king or by fate occurs for three fortnights starting from the day of the boundary-marking, then the determination of the boundary shall be made based on their testimony. And so says Kātyāyana:
"In the case of crossing a boundary, a treasury, or likewise touching with the foot [a corpse],
a period of three fortnights, five, or seven days is prescribed for divine and royal calamities. As for the prohibition stated therein in another Smṛti:

"One should avoid divine ordeals in cases of verbal abuse and disputes over land"—this [rule] refers to a situation where persons possessing the aforementioned characteristics are absent; thus, there is no contradiction. When it is asked how a decision is reached in such a case, Nārada says:
"But when there are no knowers [of the boundary] and no marks of the boundary..."
"Then the king himself may establish the boundary between the two as he desires. Here, "as he desires" means according to his will. Yājñavalkya also states:
"In the absence of witnesses and marks, the king is the establisher of the boundary. (YDh 2.153)

In the absence of witnesses such as neighbors or of boundary markers such as trees, the king alone shall establish the boundary. He should divide the land situated between two villages—which has become the subject of dispute—equally and hand it over to both villages; then, he should have boundary markers established in the middle of that land. At that time, if a superior utility for the land is observed on one side, then the entire land should be assigned to that very village. Thus says Manu: "When a boundary is impossible to determine, the king himself, knowing the law, [shall decide]."

"He should assign land to some on account of their services; such is the settled rule" (MDh 8.265). "In the case of an impassable [boundary]" means one that is devoid of witnesses or those who can identify it. The determination of a boundary, like the settlement of a debt and other matters, should not be carried out immediately following the formal complaint; rather, it should be done when embankments and other markers are visible. To this effect, the same author says:
"When a dispute has arisen regarding a boundary between two villages..."
"In the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should determine the boundary where the landmarks are clearly visible. (MDh 8.245).
The mention of "village" (*grāma*) is intended as an illustration for cities (*nagara*) and other such settlements as well. For this very reason, Kātyāyana states:
"One should determine the boundaries of fields and the like by means of neighboring neighbors residing on the edge of the border."
"Likewise for village boundaries and so forth, as well as for cities and districts.
He [Yājñavalkya] himself states that when witnesses to the boundary do not reach a decision due to the influence of passion, greed, and the like, they are to be punished:
"But if, among many who have been summoned, there is no determination of the boundary..."
"Whether out of fear or greed, they should be made to pay the highest fine. This refers to cases where [the neighbors] act intentionally. However, regarding cases of ignorance, Nārada says:
"Now, if the neighbors should speak falsely in the determination of a boundary..."
All of them shall be punished individually by the king with the middle amercement.
Those who are adjacent to the neighbors beyond, as well as those connected to them through false statements—
namely, the *saṃsakta*, *sakta*, and *saktasakta*— are to be fined the first amercement.

"But others, such as the *maulavṛddha* and so forth, shall each be made to pay a fine; they are to be disciplined by the first *sāhasa* alone, as established by law. Thus Kātyāyana states the punishment for witnesses when they give contradictory testimony to one another.

"If there should be a discrepancy when it has been proclaimed, they shall be punished with the highest fine. Thus he stated. He also declared the punishment for those who trespass upon the boundary: "Those who lead [the boundary] according to what was stated are purified as truthful witnesses."
"But those who lead [the case] erroneously shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred.
Thus, when witnesses and others have spoken falsely through ignorance, they should be punished and the investigation should be conducted again. And so says Kātyāyana:
"Having punished those who spoke out of ignorance, one should investigate the boundary once more."

"Having excluded wicked neighboring landowners, one should have the boundary determined by those who are hereditary residents and others; thus do those who know the Dharma declare. Regarding the determination of a field abandoned by a river, Bṛhaspati says:
When land has been brought from another village and given to him by a great river or by a king, how is the legal decision to be made in that case?
Land granted by a king or left by a river belongs to that very person alone;
otherwise, men would have no gain resulting from either kings or fate.
The decline, rise, and very life of men depend upon fate and the king;
therefore, in all undertakings, one should not obstruct what has been ordained by them.
Wherever a river is established as the boundary between two villages,
it effects the giving and taking [of land] for men according to their fortune or misfortune.

"One should not disturb that [embankment] which one constructs on a riverbank, causing it to fall into the water in one place while remaining stable in another.
