"That which was taken by a king through anger, greed, fraud, or injustice, but subsequently given away by him out of satisfaction to another, shall not attain validity. And this refers to the case of land, as it possesses the means of proof for ownership; however, regarding the absence of such proof, he himself says:
"One should not displace from his land a person who enjoys a plot of ground that lacks a title, provided that land was seized from someone or given to one superior in merit.
Thus, the decision regarding houses and other such matters has been shown by that very same [author].
From the time of its construction, whatever house, enclosure, shop,
or other property has been used by someone to a certain extent and in a certain manner, that shall not be altered for him.
[400] “One should not disturb the windows, the water-channels, nor the turrets and altars;

one should not disturb the four-sided courtyard or the drainage ditch established in front. Here, *vātāyana* means a window. *Praṇālī* is a means for the exit of water made of wood and so forth. *Niryūha* refers to a corner of the house or a peg (*nāgadantaka*). *Vedikā* is an elevated ground prepared in areas such as the street. *Catuḥśāla* is the collection of four halls. From that [courtyard], the *syandanikā* is the falling of rainwater.
Kātyāyana states that after the time of settlement, one must not construct windows or similar structures that cause annoyance to the neighbors:
"After the time of settling, these [structures] should never be employed;
one should not create sight-lines or drainage channels directed toward the houses of others."
A window is a "falling of the gaze. [One should not look] toward the houses of others. Bṛhaspati also says:
"A place for excrement, a fire-pit, or a pit for pouring out leftover water should never, under any circumstances, be made too close to another's wall."
Kātyāyana states that [the wall] should be constructed leaving a space of two *aratnis*:
"One should construct walls against those of others, leaving a space of two *aratnis* for the passage of feces, urine, water, and wheels, as well as for smoke and air."
Nārada states that one should not obstruct a crossroads and the like with refuse heaps and so forth:
"One should not obstruct crossroads, shrines of the gods, or royal roads with refuse heaps, earthen mounds, pits, cesspools, drains, and the like. [401]
Bṛhaspati says: "That by which people and cattle pass to and fro without obstruction is called *saṃsaraṇa* (the thoroughfare); it must not be blocked by anyone."
Regarding one who creates a pit or the like on a public road, that same author states the punishment:
"If anyone there on a public road should out of desire make a pit, plant a tree, or void excrement, his fine shall be one *māṣaka*. Thus it is said.
Manu has declared the punishment for one who voids excrement on the royal highway:
"He who, except in times of distress, should discharge impurity upon the royal highway,
shall pay two kārṣāpaṇas and must immediately clean away that impurity."

“Furthermore, one who has fallen into calamity, an elderly person, a pregnant woman, or even a child deserve only a verbal reprimand, and that [offense] must be cleared away; such is the settled rule. (MDh 9.282–83).
Regarding those who cause defilement in tanks and other water bodies by means of impure substances and the like, Kātyāyana states the following punishment:
He who destroys tanks, gardens,
or sacred bathing places with impure matter shall first have that impurity cleared away and then be fined the lowest amercement.

"One who defiles sacred sites established by great souls— sites that are meritorious and purifying— shall incur the punishment for a prior violent crime. Regarding the breaking of boundaries and similar offenses, Yājñavalkya states the following penalty:
"In cases of breaking a boundary mark, as well as crossing a boundary line, and in the seizure of a field, the punishments are low, high, and middling, respectively. (YDh 2.155)

The common ground that demarcates many fields is the boundary (*maryādā*). For its excessive breach—that is, for plowing beyond the limit or seizing a field by displaying contemptuous gestures—the punishments of the lowest, middle, and highest fines (*sāhasa*) are to be understood respectively. The mention of "field" is intended to include houses, gardens, and so forth. When a field or such is seized through ignorance, only the lowest fine is to be understood. Therefore, Manu says: "One who seizes a house, a tank, a garden, or a field by means of intimidation..."

"One who steals land by force should be fined five hundred [paṇas], while for stealing through ignorance, the fine shall be two hundred. (MDh 8.264) [404]. However, for those who forcibly seize lands such as fields and the like, the highest amercement must be imposed. As for the highest amercement, it is: "execution, confiscation of all property, banishment from the city, and branding."
In that case, the cutting off of a limb is one punishment, namely the highest amercement.

This is because of such a traditional rule (*smaraṇa*). As for the increased penalty stated by Śaṅkha and Likhita regarding the transgression of a boundary—namely, "But in the case of crossing a boundary, [the fine is] eight thousand"—that refers to the case of crossing an entire boundary. Regarding trees grown at the junctions of boundaries, Kātyāyana states:
"One should declare that for trees grown in the middle of a boundary between two fields, the fruit and the flowers belong in common to the owners of the fields."

Regarding trees and other such things grown on another's field, that same rule applies. However, as for those grown on another's field whose branches extend elsewhere, one should know them to belong to the owner in whose field they are established. Thus it is said.
A bridge, well, or similar structure being constructed on another's field at the request of the owner shall not be prohibited by the owner of that field. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
"A bridge that causes little harm and brings about welfare shall not be prohibited;
likewise, a well that takes up little of another's land but provides abundant water. (YDh 2.156)

A field or similar property that causes little harm and provides great benefit should not be obstructed by its owner. However, that which causes much harm and provides little benefit must be obstructed. Nārada also says: "A watercourse for another's field should not be blocked if it possesses great utility and causes little harm; indeed, an increase is desired even when there is a decrease [in one's own land]."
And the embankment is of two kinds. Thus he himself says:
"The embankment should be known as being of two types: one to be cleared away and likewise one to be bound.
It is to be cleared away by causing water to flow through it; it would be bound by stopping that flow. Thus.
Regarding the subject of constructing embankments and other such works, Nārada states:
"He who should construct an embankment that was previously begun but has fallen into ruin, without having consulted the owner, shall not partake in its fruit."
"But when the owner has died, or even when a descendant of his lineage is no longer a human being,

one should then undertake that work of constructing a dam after consulting the king. Thus says Yājñavalkya regarding the undertaking of dams and the like, either without obtaining the consent of the field-owner or, in his absence, with the king.

"Whoever constructs a watercourse on another's field without first informing the owner, the enjoyment of the produce belongs to the owner; in his absence, it belongs to the king. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.157). The intended meaning of this is that one should construct a watercourse on another's field only after having obtained permission through a request or by the gift of wealth. It does not, however, intend to prohibit the constructor from receiving a share of the fruit, for such a prohibition would be irrelevant since no such entitlement had arisen. Alternatively, let the intent be to prohibit the enjoyment of the fruit consisting of visible worldly gain. Kātyāyana also says:
But he who performs a consecration for a house, garden, or pond without the consent of the owner does not obtain any [right] to that which was consecrated.

"If expenses have been incurred and the owner has arrived, [the cultivator] shall not report them to the king; however, if he reports them and they are authorized, he recovers those expenses. Regarding one who, having first agreed with the landowner, "I shall cultivate this field," subsequently does not cultivate it himself or does not have it cultivated by another, Yājñavalkya says: [The following verse from Yājñavalkya-smṛti 2.156 applies: "If, having accepted [the lease], he does not cultivate [the field] himself or cause it to be cultivated by another, he shall pay the value of the crop to the owner and be fined the same amount. Thus, having promised to the owner of the field, "I will plow this field," if he afterwards neither plows it himself nor causes it to be plowed by another, Yājñavalkya addresses him as follows.

"Even a field that has been ploughed, he who neither cultivates it himself nor causes it to be cultivated shall be made to pay the fruit of the cultivation; another shall cause it to be cultivated. (YDh 2.158) Although "ploughed" (*phālāhata*) means merely slightly torn by the plough and not yet fit for the sowing of seeds, nevertheless, this person must be made to pay the owner the full extent of the fruit of an uncultivated field that would have been capable of production there, as determined by the neighbors and others. And that field, having been taken away from the previous cultivator, he shall cause it to be cultivated by another. Bṛhaspati also says:
"Whoever, having taken a field, neither cultivates it nor causes it to be cultivated,
shall be made to pay the produce to the owner and a fine equal to that to the king.
When it is asked how much produce should be given to the owner, he himself says:
"When left fallow for a long time, [the cultivator] shall be made to pay a tenth part; likewise, an eighth part when [the field] has been ploughed;

but when well-prepared, a sixth part shall be paid, having determined it according to the rule. (Nārada) The meaning is as follows: "Left fallow for a long time" (*cirāvasanna*) refers to a field that has not been cultivated for a long duration and was neglected after being accepted [for cultivation]. Whatever fruit is obtained from such a field before it is neglected, a tenth part thereof shall be made to be paid [to the owner]. However, when it has been ploughed (*kṛṣyamāṇe*)—that is, when it was neglected after being accepted despite having been left fallow for a very long time—an eighth part shall be made to be paid. But when the field was well-prepared (*susaṃskṛte*) and then neglected, a sixth part shall be made to be paid. Regarding fields that are incapable [of cultivation], abandoned by death, or lost, Nārada says:
If someone should cultivate a field when the owners are incapacitated, deceased, or lost, he shall enjoy the fruit thereof without being hindered.

"When the fields are being ploughed, the owner may return; having paid for all the expenses related to the fallow land (*khila*), he shall recover the field. Here, "expenses related to the fallow land" refers to the costs incurred for the purpose of reclaiming the fallow ground. To determine the extent of those expenses, that same author states the following regarding their assessment:
"In one year, half of it becomes waste; in three years, the whole becomes waste;
but a field neglected for five years becomes equal to a forest.
Furthermore, Kātyāyana says this even when the owner does not provide the treatment required for waste land:
If, due to incapacity, he does not pay what was spent for the purpose of clearing the land,
the cultivator shall receive the fruit of his labor minus one-eighth.
"He shall be the enjoyer for eight years; thereafter, it belongs to the owner.
Thus ends the determination of disputes concerning boundaries. Now begins the section on assault (*daṇḍapāruṣya*).
The nature of that [assault] was stated by Nārada: "Inflicting injury upon the bodies of others with hands, feet, weapons, and so forth,
or by throwing ashes and other substances, is called *daṇḍapāruṣya* (physical assault)."

[410] Thus: "Upon the limbs of others," meaning upon various substances such as stationary and moving things; "by means of hands, feet, weapons, and so forth"—the inclusion of "and so forth" (ādi) refers to stones and the like; "injury" (droha) is the act of harming. Likewise, "assault" (upaghāta) by means of ashes and so forth—meaning by ashes, dust, mud, excrement, and the like—is the production of mental suffering in the form of physical contact. Both of these constitute *daṇḍapāruṣya* (assault). He himself states its threefold nature: "Its threefoldness is also observed according to the sequence of low, middling, and high, through threatening, striking without hesitation, and the display of wounds."

"Because there is no deviation from the categories of inferior, middling, and superior objects, they say that there are exactly three *sāhasas* (acts of violence); therein lies the purification of thorns. "Falling without hesitation" means striking without hesitation. The meaning is that there are exactly three *sāhasas*, which are acts of violence (*sāhasīkṛta*) consisting of physical assault (*daṇḍapāruṣya*). Five types of rules regarding physical assault have been stated by that same author.
The procedure for both of these is said to be fivefold when verbal abuse has occurred, arising from agitation between two parties who have become disturbed.
He who endures is honored, while he who transgresses receives the rod of punishment;
however, he who first initiates an accusation shall certainly be the one to bear the blame.
Furthermore, he who is disrespectful later, whereas discipline was formerly his teacher—
of two such persons fallen into equal misfortune, he binds himself with greater [consequence].
He who is the first, or even he who is the second,
incurs the punishment when both are simultaneously engaged in an outburst of harshness, being shrouded by the fault of verbal abuse.
If no distinction were perceived, discipline would apply equally to both [the ordained and the laity],
including outcastes, eunuchs, heretics, the deformed, and the deaf.
In the case of elephants, outcasts, and slaves, as well as toward one's elders and teachers,
the only disciplinary measure for transgressing established bounds is immediate corporal punishment.
For if a man among men, being base himself, should overstep one who is truly humble, he alone commits the offense of discipline; the king does not share in that lack of discipline.
"For these are indeed the stains of men; their wealth is of the nature of stain.
Therefore, the king should have them executed; he should not punish them with a fine.
As for the absence of guilt in one who subsequently engages [in good conduct], that has been shown by Bṛhaspati:
"But a man who, having been dragged away, reviles [his assailant], or having been struck, strikes back,
or even having killed an offender, shall not be considered guilty.
This is the punishment for one who acts subsequently, as shown by Kātyāyana.
"But that man who strikes with a weapon that is not terrifying, whether he was the first aggressor or the one who was previously injured, is declared to be liable for punishment.

This [statement] also serves the purpose of imposing a lesser punishment than the standard penalty for assault already set forth. Yājñavalkya states the grounds for a decision when there is doubt regarding the severity of the assault:
"But when a case is struck down by lack of witnesses, it must be examined through marks, logical reasoning, and scripture, for [a litigant] might have committed forgery out of fear. (YDh 2.212)

When someone reports to the king in secret, "I have been struck by this person," then an investigation must be conducted—based on marks such as fatigue on the body, logical reasoning consisting of an examination of causes and motives, scriptural authority, public rumor, oral testimony, and divine means—out of fear that the mark might have been forged. He (Yājñavalkya) himself states the specific punishment according to the particular substance used for the royal edict:
"For contact with ash, mud, or dust, a fine of ten paṇas is prescribed;
for contact with impure matter, the heel, or spittle, double that is prescribed."

"In the case of women of equal status, the penalty is the same; for those of higher status, it is double; for those of lower status, it is half. There is no punishment if [the act] occurs through delusion, intoxication, and so forth. (MDh 2.213–14). By the word *amedhya* (impure substance), phlegm, nails, earwax, dūṣikā (eye-secretion), semen, remnants of food, and the like are included. Regarding contact with feces and other such substances, Kātyāyana states:
If [polluted] by vomit, urine, feces, and so forth, the penance is fourfold for the feet and other lower parts;
it is sixfold for the middle of the body, and it is traditionally taught to be eightfold for the head.

[414] Thus. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), fat, semen, blood, and marrow are included. Regarding the punishment for raising a hand to strike and for actually striking, that same author states: "When the hand is merely raised, the fine shall be twelve *kārsāpaṇas*;
for those of the same caste, it is declared to be double that amount when the blow is dealt. Thus.

Yājñavalkya also says: "If one merely raises a hand or a foot, the fines shall be ten and twenty [paṇas] respectively; but for all [offenses] involving a weapon against one another, the middle amercement applies. (YDh 2.216)

When a hand or a foot is raised for the purpose of striking, the fines shall be ten and twenty *paṇas* respectively. When a weapon is raised for the purpose of mutual killing, the meaning is that a fine of the middle amercement (*madhyama-sāhasa*) applies to all castes. The same applies to striking with wood and similar materials:
"A man who causes pain with wood and such, without drawing blood, shall be fined thirty-two *paṇas*; if blood is seen, the fine shall be double. (YDh 2.218)
Manu states the punishment for piercing the skin and so forth:
"One who pierces the skin shall be fined one hundred [paṇas], as shall one who causes blood to flow;
for cutting flesh, one shall be fined a hundred niṣkas, but one who breaks a bone shall be banished" (MDh 8.284).
Regarding the dragging by the feet and so forth, Yājñavalkya states:
"For pulling at the feet, hair, garment, or hands, the fine is ten paṇas;
for dragging by the mass [of hair], wrapping with a garment, or placing the foot [upon another], the punishment is one hundred [paṇas]."
For breaking or cutting off a hand, a foot, a tooth, an ear, or a nose, the middle amercement is the punishment;
likewise for piercing a wound or for striking someone who is nearly dead.
In cases of obstructing movement, food, or speech; piercing the eyes or other organs;
or breaking the neck, arms, or thighs, the middle amercement shall be imposed.
"For those who kill one person or many, the fine shall be double that which has been prescribed. (YDh 2.217–218)

He who, having disregarded [the woman], seizes her by the hair and pulls her away suddenly, shall be fined ten *paṇas*. Furthermore, he who, having enveloped her with a garment, squeezes her tightly, drags her, and strikes her with his foot, shall be fined one hundred *paṇas*. For the breaking of each of the hands, feet, or teeth, for the cutting off of the ears or nose, and for striking her so that she is nearly dead, the punishment is the middle *sāhasa* fine. For obstructing her movement, eating, or speech, for piercing the eyes, and for breaking a wound on the neck or hand, the punishment is the middle *sāhasa* fine. The meaning is that when many people together cause the breaking of a single limb, the punishment prescribed for a single offense against one person should be understood to apply to each of them, doubled. Kātyāyana also says:
According to Bhṛgu, for the cutting off of the ears, lips, nose, feet, tongue, nostrils, or hands, the highest fine is prescribed; for their piercing, the middle fine.
"When a blow is struck against humans or animals for the purpose of causing pain,
the punishment shall be inflicted in proportion to the pain that may have been caused.
Regarding a blow struck in the reverse direction (i.e., against one's own body), Yājñavalkya states the following concerning the punishment:

"But the limb of a non-Brāhmaṇa that causes injury to a Brāhmaṇa shall be cut off; if he merely raised [his weapon], the first amercement is the punishment, but for actual contact, it is half of that. (YDh 2.215) The limb—such as a hand or a foot—of a non-Brāhmaṇa, such as a Kṣatriya or others, which causes injury to a Brāhmaṇa, must be severed. The mention of "Brāhmaṇa" is intended to indicate any member of the highest caste. For this very reason, Manu says:

"If a person of the lowest caste should injure a superior by any limb whatsoever, that very limb of his shall be cut off; such is the instruction of Manu. (MDh 8.279) Thus, when a weapon or similar object is raised for the purpose of killing, it should be understood as the first *sāhasa* (fine); even in that case, for a Śūdra, there must be the amputation of the hand or other limb. Regarding this, Manu says:
"Raising his hand or a staff, he deserves the cutting off of his hand;

striking with his foot out of anger, he deserves the cutting off of his foot. (MDh 8.280). For the mere brandishing of a weapon or the like, half the fine of the first *sāhasa* should be understood as the penalty. However, for touching with ashes and the like, the fine is double that prescribed for insults against Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas when committed in the reverse order of castes (*prātilomya*). As Yājñavalkya has said:

"In cases of defamation involving the reverse order of castes, the fines are double and triple; for the castes in the direct order, they are reduced by half and half again respectively. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.207).
The punishment should be determined according to the principles stated regarding verbal abuse. Kātyāyana says:
"Just as it has been stated regarding verbal abuse, both in the inverse and direct order,
so too shall punishment be inflicted in cases of physical assault according to the sequence.
Regarding that, Manu states a specific rule concerning the Śūdra:
The king shall cause the two lips of one who spits out of arrogance to be cut off;
likewise, he shall have the penis of one who urinates [upon him] cut off, and the anus of one who passes wind [upon him].
[419] One who seizes him by the hair should have both hands cut off without hesitation; likewise for seizing him by the feet, the beard, the neck, or the testicles.
"One born of a lower caste who seeks to sit on the same seat as one of a superior caste shall be branded on the hip with a mark, banished, and have his buttock cut off. (MDh 8.281–83).
Regarding specific details concerning the amputation of limbs and other punishments, Kātyāyana states:

"But when one inflicts a punishment for the destruction of the body or the sense organs, then the wise should provide what brings satisfaction as well as the means for recovery (*samutthāna*). Here, "what brings satisfaction" refers to that which satisfies the wound; "means for recovery" refers to the healing of the wound. Furthermore, the expenses incurred on its account—both for medicine and for the cost of treatment—should be paid by the wise according to the severity of the wound, in accordance with the prescribed measure for the purpose of healing the wound.
"He shall provide for the healing of the wound, including its arising and its subsiding," because it has been stated by that very same authority. Bṛhaspati also says:
"In the case of crushing a limb, as well as in cutting or injuring it..."
"He shall be made to pay the expenses of the expedition and whatever was taken away during the quarrel.
Yājñavalkya also says: "That which was taken away during a quarrel must be restored, and likewise a fine double that amount shall be imposed."
"He who causes pain shall be made to pay for the injury and the expenses incurred; and he shall also be made to pay the fine prescribed for that particular quarrel. (YDh 2.221–22)

Viṣṇu states the punishment for injury to domestic animals: "For the killing of a domestic animal, one shall be fined one *kārṣāpaṇa*; however, he shall also pay its value to the owner of the animal. The payment of the value refers specifically to the case of a dead animal; in the absence of death, however, he shall pay the expenses incurred for recovery. Thus, the same author says: "All those who cause injury to humans and those who cause injury to domestic animals shall be made to pay the expenses incurred for recovery" (4.121). Manu states that the punishment occasioned by the killing of a living being does not apply in certain cases where it is impossible to provide a remedy.
When the nose-rope is severed, when the yoke is broken, when the animal turns sideways or faces the opposite direction,
when the axle of the vehicle breaks, and likewise when the wheel breaks;
"Manu has declared that there is no punishment for one who cuts the harnesses, the traces, or the reins, or who cries out 'Move aside! (MDh 8.291–92).
He [Manu] himself states the punishment for one who neglects what can be remedied:

"Where a vehicle turns off course due to the negligence of the driver, the owner shall be liable for the damage and must pay a fine of two hundred panas. (MDh 8.293) Here, the *prājaka* is the driver of the cart or similar vehicle. *Vaiguṇya* means incompetence or incapacity, which may have been consented to by the owner for the sake of reducing wages. Where injury to living beings occurs through the fault of a capable driver, there is no punishment for the owner, but rather for the driver alone; thus says the same author:
"If the driver be capable, the driver deserves the punishment" (MDh 8.294).
"Capable" means competent. Yājñavalkya states the punishment for injury to livestock:
"In the case of causing pain, drawing blood, or likewise the cutting off of a limb or a tail..."
But for small animals, the fine shall start from two paṇas and increase in sequence.
"In the case of cutting off the male organ or killing [the animal], the middle amercement shall be imposed, as well as its value;
for these great animals, the fine in these instances is double. (YDh 2.225–26)

Regarding small animals such as goats, sheep, and the like: for causing them pain, for drawing their blood, or for cutting their limbs—by the word "limbs" (*śākhā*), horns and so forth are indicated; by "members" (*aṅga*), hands, feet, and so forth are meant—the punishment shall be two *paṇas* and so on, respectively. That is to say, it takes the form of two *paṇas*, four *paṇas*, six *paṇas*, eight *paṇas*, and so forth. For cutting off their genitals or causing their death, the middle amercement (*madhyama-sāhasa*) is the punishment, along with the payment of their value. Regarding large animals such as cows, elephants, horses, and the like, the meaning is that in these same circumstances, a double penalty compared to what was stated above should be understood. In the context of the recurring phrase "a fine of one hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*," Viṣṇu also states: "One who destroys the virility of animals, as well as one who kills an elephant, horse, camel, or cow, shall pay one quarter of a fine. A seller of meat shall pay the value of the animal. One who kills a wild animal shall pay fifty *kārṣāpaṇas*. A killer of birds or fish shall pay ten *kārṣāpaṇas*. A destroyer of insects shall pay one *kārṣāpaṇa*. Kātyāyana also says:
"A fine of two paṇas for killing deer or birds, but twelve paṇas for killing snakes, cats, mongooses, dogs, or pigs, as well as humans. Thus says Manu as well.

One who, out of recklessness, drives a young cow, a deity, or a sacrificial animal, as well as a bull that is incapable of work, shall first incur the punishment for violence; in the case of killing, he shall incur the highest penalty.
In the case of killing a human being, the guilt is immediate and equal to that of a thief;
for large living beings such as cows, elephants, camels, horses, and so forth, it is half [the guilt].
For the killing of small animals, the fine shall be two hundred;
however, for auspicious beasts and birds, the punishment shall be fifty.
"But for donkeys, goats, and sheep, the fine shall be five *māṣas*;
however, the fine for killing a dog or a pig shall be one *māṣa*" (MDh 8.296–98).
Kātyāyana states that, just as the king receives the fine, the owner should pay a corresponding amount or the value of the animal.

"Upon killing living beings, one should provide a substitute for them, or pay its equivalent value; so Manu has declared. Thus, Manu states the punishment for those who cause injury to stationary living beings.
"According as the utility of all forest trees [is determined], so must punishment be inflicted for injury to them; such is the settled rule. (MDh 8.285)

[426] Thus, fines such as the highest, middle, and so forth, should be determined in accordance with the degree of enjoyment of the fruits and flowers. And likewise, Viṣṇu states, following the recurring term "one who deserves punishment": "One who cuts down a tree that provides fruit or flowers shall pay the highest amercement; one who cuts down a tree that provides flowers shall pay the middle amercement; one who cuts down a creeper, shrub, or climbing vine shall pay one hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*; and one who cuts down grass shall pay one. Furthermore, all of them shall restore the produce to the owners. The implication is that those who cut down trees providing fruit or flowers must pay the owners the value of the produce until the time when the re-planted tree again yields fruit and other benefits. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states a specific rule:
For the cutting of branches, trunks, or all parts of trees that bear shoots,
as well as for trees that provide livelihood, the fine shall be double that prescribed for twenty [small trees].
[427] At a shrine, a cemetery, a boundary, a place of merit, or a temple, the fine for trees that have grown there is double; the same applies to a tree that is well-known.

"For the cutting of shrubs, clusters, bushes, creepers, spreading plants, medicinal herbs, and climbing vines, the fine shall be half of that prescribed previously for the aforementioned locations. (YDh 2.227–29)

In the case of trees that grow by sprouting branches, such as the *vaṭa* and others, for cutting their branches or their trunks, starting from a fine of twenty *paṇas*, each subsequent fine is double the preceding one—namely, twenty, forty, and eighty *paṇas*. For trees that do not grow by sprouting branches, such as the *āmra* and other trees useful for livelihood, or those grown in the aforementioned places such as sacred groves (*caitya*) and so forth; and for trees like the *aśvattha* and *palāśa* when their branches and so on are cut, the fine is double that previously mentioned. *Gulmas* are plants such as the *mālatī*; *gucchās* are such as the *kuraṇḍaka*; *kṣupas* are such as the *karavīra*; *latās* are such as the *drākṣā* and *atimuktā*; *pratānas* are those devoid of lateral shoots; *oṣadhis* are those that perish after the ripening of their fruit, such as *śāli* rice and the like; and *vīrudhas* are such as the *guḍūcī*. For cutting these in the aforementioned places, half of the previously mentioned fine should be understood to apply. Yājñavalkya states the punishment for striking a wall or throwing thorns and the like into a house: *kuḍyam bhitvā tu yaḥ kaścit gṛhe kaṇṭakam utsṛjet | dvātriṃśatpaṇiko daṇḍas tasya kāryo vicakṣaṇaiḥ ||* "But whoever, having broken a wall, should throw thorns or the like into a house, a fine of thirty-two *paṇas* should be imposed upon him by the wise. *kuḍyam bhitvā tu yaḥ kaścit gṛhe kaṇṭakam utsṛjet | dvātriṃśatpaṇiko daṇḍas tasya kāryo vicakṣaṇaiḥ ||* "But whoever, having broken a wall, should throw thorns or the like into a house, a fine of thirty-two *paṇas* should be imposed upon him by the wise. *kuḍyam bhitvā tu yaḥ kaścit gṛhe kaṇṭakam utsṛjet | dvātriṃśatpaṇiko daṇḍas tasya kāryo vicakṣaṇaiḥ ||* "But whoever, having broken a wall, should throw thorns or the like into a house, a fine of thirty-two *paṇas* should be imposed upon him by the wise. *kuḍyam bhitvā tu yaḥ kaścit gṛhe kaṇṭakam utsṛjet | dvātriṃśatpaṇiko daṇḍas tasya kāryo vicakṣaṇaiḥ ||* "But whoever, having broken a wall, should throw thorns or the like into a house, a fine of thirty-two *paṇas* should be imposed upon him by the wise. *kuḍyam bhitvā tu yaḥ kaścit gṛhe kaṇṭakam utsṛjet | dvātriṃśatpaṇiko daṇḍas tasya kāryo vicakṣaṇaiḥ ||* "But whoever, having broken a wall, should throw thorns or the like into a house, a fine of thirty-two *paṇas* should be imposed upon him by the wise. *kuḍyam bhitvā tu yaḥ kaścit gṛhe kaṇṭakam utsṛjet | dvātriṃśatpaṇiko daṇḍas tasya kāryo vicakṣaṇaiḥ ||* "But whoever, having broken a wall, should throw thorns or the like into a house, a fine of thirty-two *paṇas* should be imposed upon him by the wise. *kuḍyam bhitvā tu yaḥ kaścit gṛhe kaṇṭakam utsṛjet | dvātriṃśatpaṇiko daṇḍas tasya kāryo vicakṣaṇaiḥ ||* "But whoever, having broken a wall, should throw thorns or the like into a house, a fine of thirty-two *paṇas* should be imposed upon him by the wise. *kuḍyam bhitvā tu yaḥ kaścit gṛhe kaṇṭakam utsṛjet | dvātriṃśatpaṇiko daṇḍas tasya kāryo vicakṣaṇaiḥ ||* "But whoever, having broken a wall, should throw thorns or the like into a house, a fine of thirty-two *paṇas* should be imposed upon him by the wise. *kuḍyam bhitvā tu yaḥ kaścit gṛhe kaṇṭakam utsṛjet | dvātriṃśatpaṇiko daṇḍas tasya kāryo vicakṣaṇaiḥ ||* "But whoever, having broken a wall, should throw thorns or the like into a house, a fine of thirty-two *paṇas* should be imposed upon him by the wise. *kuḍyam bhitvā tu yaḥ kaścit gṛhe kaṇṭakam utsṛjet | dvātriṃśatpaṇiko daṇḍas tasya kāryo vicakṣaṇaiḥ ||* "But whoever, having broken a wall, should throw thorns or the like into a house, a fine of thirty-two *paṇas* should be imposed upon him by the wise. *kuḍyam bhitvā tu yaḥ kaścit gṛhe kaṇṭakam utsṛjet | dvātriṃśatpaṇiko daṇḍas tasya kāryo vicakṣaṇaiḥ ||* "But whoever, having broken a wall, should throw thorns or the like into a house, a fine of thirty-two *paṇas* should be imposed upon him by the wise. *kuḍyam bhitvā tu yaḥ kaścit gṛhe kaṇṭakam utsṛjet | dvātriṃśatpaṇiko daṇḍas tasya kāryo vicakṣaṇaiḥ ||* "But whoever, having broken a wall, should throw thorns or the like into a house, a fine of thirty-two *paṇas* should be imposed upon him by the wise. *kuḍyam bhitvā tu yaḥ kaścit gṛhe kaṇṭakam utsṛjet | dvātriṃśatpaṇiko daṇḍas tasya kāryo vicakṣaṇaiḥ ||* "But whoever, having broken a wall, should throw thorns or the like into a house, a fine of thirty-two *paṇas* should be imposed upon him by the wise. *kuḍyam bhitvā tu yaḥ kaścit gṛhe kaṇṭakam utsṛjet | dvātriṃśatpaṇiko daṇḍas tasya kāryo vicakṣaṇaiḥ ||* "But whoever, having broken a wall, should throw thorns or the like into a house, a fine of thirty-two *paṇas* should be imposed upon him by the wise."
[428] In cases of striking, cutting, piercing, or causing a wall to collapse,
one shall be made to pay five, ten, or twenty paṇas, as well as the cost of the damage.

"Property in the home that causes suffering, as well as that which is life-threatening—one who throws such things [at another] shall be made to pay sixteen *paṇas* for the first offense, and for the second, the middle fine. (YDh 2.223–24)

In the case of striking a wall with a mallet or similar object, or tearing it apart, or splitting it into two, the fines shall be five *paṇas*, ten *paṇas*, and twenty *paṇas* respectively. Furthermore, if the wall collapses, the three aforementioned fines are to be combined; additionally, the cost of repairing the wall must be paid. For throwing thorns or other harmful objects into another's house, the fine is sixteen *paṇas*. For throwing poison, snakes, or similar things, the middle amercement (*madhyama-sāhasa*) is the penalty—this is the meaning. Thus ends the section on physical assault; now follows verbal assault.
Its definition was stated by Nārada:
"Speech that is contrary in meaning, joined with abuse or censure regarding country, caste, family, and so forth— that is called verbal cruelty (vākpāruṣya)."

"The Gaudas are fond of quarreling" is an insult directed at a region (*deśākrośa*). "The Brahmins are excessively greedy" is an insult directed at a caste (*jātyākrośa*). "The Vaiśvāmitras are cruel-hearted" is an insult directed at a family (*kulākrośa*). [429] An insult (*ākrośa*) is speaking loudly; it is a disparaging and blameworthy statement. The meaning is that verbal abuse (*vākpāruṣya*) is speech characterized by both of these qualities and intended to produce distress. He himself states its threefold nature: "Because of being harsh, vulgar, and extreme, it is also recorded as being of three kinds.
According to the sequence of gravity, the punishment here also increases accordingly."
"Reproachful speech is to be known as harsh; that which is accompanied by a physical defect is called vulgar; and the wise say that speech involving censure with grounds for expulsion is 'severe'.
Thus [says] Kātyāyana as well.
When one, by means of arguments characterized as unreal— whether they be baseless or even seemingly grounded— somewhat reviles another,
that is known by the wise as harsh speech.
When one, out of anger, uses speech to cause the humiliation of another's livelihood,
country, or family, that is considered by the wise to be *aślīlā* (obscene or vulgar).
"That speech which binds one with great sins, which produces passion and hatred, or which causes loss of caste— that indeed is known as 'intense' (tīvrā) speech.
Thus Bṛhaspati states its threefold division according to the distinctions of inferior, middling, and superior.
The reviling of regions, villages, families, and so forth, by associating them with sin,
when not preceded by a specific grievance, is called the first form of verbal abuse.
[430] Speaking of a sister, a mother, or their relatives, as well as reviling them, is declared by those who know the scriptures to be middling verbal *upapātaka*.

"The discussion of forbidden foods and drinks, the defilement by a mortal sin (mahāpātaka), and harshness— defined as intense piercing of the vital spots— is declared to be the highest [degree of verbal abuse].
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states the punishment for cruel abuse:

"If one insults those who have deficient limbs, sensory impairments, or diseases by means of praise that is true, false, or otherwise, he shall be fined twelve and a half *paṇas*. (YDh 2.204) He who threatens those with deficient limbs and so forth with praise that is true, false, or otherwise shall be punished with a fine of twelve and a half *paṇas*. This rule pertains to cases involving persons of equal caste and qualities. And so says Bṛhaspati:
"But when persons of equal caste and qualities engage in mutual verbal abuse,
the fine prescribed in the treatise is twelve and a half paṇas.
As for the statement of Manu:
[431] "Whether one says of another that they are one-eyed, lame, or otherwise similarly deformed—even if it be the truth—one shall be made to pay a fine of at least one *kārṣāpaṇa*. (MDh 8.274).
This rule also refers to those of wicked conduct. Regarding one who insults his mother and others, Manu says:

"One who slanders a mother, a father, a wife, a brother, a mother-in-law, or a teacher shall be made to pay a fine of one hundred [paṇas], as shall one who does not yield the path to a teacher. (MDh 8.275).
This should be understood to apply when the mother and others are offenders, or when the wife is innocent. Bṛhaspati states the punishment for insulting a sister and others:
"Insulting one's sister or other female relatives, one shall pay a fine of fifty paṇas.
Thus Manu states the punishment for verbal abuse according to the inverse and natural orders of the castes:
"A Kṣatriya, having insulted a Brāhmaṇa, deserves a fine of one hundred [paṇas]."
A Vaiśya deserves fifty or two hundred [strokes], but a Śūdra deserves corporal punishment.
"A Brāhmaṇa should be fined fifty [paṇas] for falsely accusing a Kṣatriya;
in the case of a Vaiśya, it should be forty-five, and for a Śūdra, the fine is twelve.
Thus says Bṛhaspati as well.
A Vaiśya who reviles a Kṣatriya should be made to pay a fine;
a Kṣatriya who insults a Vaiśya deserves punishment equal to half of that.
For insulting a Śūdra, the fine for a Kṣatriya is twenty-five [paṇas];
if the insult is grave, it is declared by those who know the scriptures that the fine there is double.
"A Śūdra who insults a Vaiśya shall be made to pay the first amercement;

[if he insults] a Kṣatriya, the middle amercement; and [if he insults] a Brāhmaṇa, the highest amercement. Thus says Yājñavalkya regarding the cutting off of arms and other limbs, and harsh verbal abuse.
For verbal injury involving the destruction of the arms, neck, eyes, or thighs, the fine is one hundred [paṇas];
for those involving the feet, nose, ears, hands, and so forth, it is half of that.
"But one who is incapable, if he speaks thus, should be fined ten *paṇas*;
likewise, one who is capable should be made to provide a surety for his security. (YDh 2.208–09)

If, upon the destruction of arms or other limbs, one declares with words, "I shall cut off your arms," the fine for each such instance is one hundred *paṇas*. However, in the case of the feet, nose, and so forth, the verbal fine is half of that, consisting of fifty *paṇas* and so on. One who is incapable of such an act, yet speaks thus, should be fined ten *paṇas*. On the other hand, one who is capable but speaks thus to someone whose power is diminished should pay a fine of one hundred *paṇas* or more and provide a guarantor for that person's safety; this is the meaning. The same author states the fine for using vulgar speech: "I shall violate your sister or your mother."
"The king shall cause one who utters a curse to pay a fine of twenty-five [paṇas]. (YDh 2.205).
He himself states the punishment for severe abuse:
"For an insult involving a charge of an act that causes loss of caste, the punishment is the middle amercement."
"But one who is guilty of a minor offense (upapātaka) shall be made to pay the first amercement" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.210). Manu also says:
"Those who speak of sins and minor offenses, and those who proclaim a mortal sin (mahāpātaka)..."
"However, these [classes] shall pay the first, middle, and highest fines respectively. (MDh 8.269).

Regarding verbal abuse directed toward those possessing the three Vedas and others, Yājñavalkya states: "Verbal abuse directed toward those who possess the three Vedas, the king, or the gods is the highest amercement."

"The middle [fine] for groups of castes (*jāti-pūga*), and the first for villages and districts. (YDh 2.211) "Castes" (*jāti*) refers to Brāhmaṇas and so forth; "groups" (*pūga*) refers to associations (*saṅgha*). With reference to a Śūdra, Manu and Nārada both state:
"A once-born man who insults twice-born men with harsh speech..."
He would suffer the cutting off of his tongue, for he is one of low birth.
"For one who, out of malice, utters the names or castes of groups of people, of a village,
or of a district, a ten-finger-long iron spike shall be driven into his tongue while it is still alive. (MDh 8.270–71)
Bṛhaspati also says:
"If he imparts instruction on dharma to these Brahmins in a manner contrary to dharma,
the king shall pour boiling oil into his mouth and his ears."
In some places, that same author states an exception regarding verbal abuse and punishment:
"This discipline has been prescribed for a virtuous Śūdra who is innocent; however, a Brāhmaṇa should not inflict punishment for verbal abuse upon one who is devoid of merit. Thus it is said.
Thus ends harsh speech;
now, theft.
Manu states the definition of that [sāhasa]:
"Sāhasa is an act committed by force when there is a connection [to the owner];
it becomes theft (steya) when it is done without such connection, provided that after taking it, one denies the act. (MDh 8.332)

The meaning of this is as follows: *sāhasa* (violence) is that which is committed by means of physical force in the presence of the owner of the property, the king, or officials, such as the seizure of another's goods. *Steya* (theft), on the other hand, is the taking of another's property by deceiving them while they are not present. Furthermore, even if one has brought the property before the king or officials and then denies it out of fear, saying "I did not take this," that also constitutes *steya*. For this very reason, Nārada says: "The removal of these [goods] after having deceived them by various means..."

"The wise declare that theft consists of taking from those who are asleep, intoxicated, or heedless. This [theft] is also threefold, depending on whether the object is of low, middling, or superior quality. As he himself said:
"That too should be known as threefold by the wise, according to the objects involved:
through the seizure of objects that are low, middling, or principal."
Hārīta has described the inferior, middling, and superior objects:
"Earthenware vessels, seats, beds, straw, husks, skins, grass, and the like,
as well as leguminous grains and prepared food— these are declared to be inferior objects."
Clothing, excluding silk; likewise cattle, excluding cows;
metals, excluding gold; and liquor, rice, barley, and so forth.
"Gold, jewels, silk garments, women, men, elephants, and horses—these are to be known as the most excellent property belonging to gods, Brahmins, and kings. Thus [it is said].
Yājñavalkya states the means for detecting thieves:
A thief is apprehended by pursuers through his stolen goods, or by his tracks,
or because of his prior criminal record, or likewise because he stays in an unclean place.
Others also should be apprehended with suspicion on account of their concealing their birth, name, and so forth;
as well as those addicted to gambling, women, and drinking, and those whose faces and voices appear parched and altered.

Those who inquire about the property or houses of others while moving about in secret, those who have no income yet have great expenditures, and those who sell goods that do not belong to them; (YDh 2.266–68)

[437] Thus: Suspects should be apprehended by royal officers using stolen goods—such as vessels and the like—as signs of theft, either by following the thief's tracks from the location where the lost property was found or by pursuing the thief’s footprints. A "guilty of prior acts" is one previously notorious for thievery. An "impure dweller" is one who resides in an unknown place. One who "conceals his caste" says, "I am not a Śūdra. One who "conceals his name" says, "I am not Ḍittha. By the use of the word "etcetera," one's own country, village, family, and so forth are indicated. Those who "sell lost property" are those who sell items such as broken vessels or worn-out clothes whose owners are unknown. Having arrested men on the basis of such signs, one should carefully examine whether they are thieves or not; one should not conclude that a person is a thief based on that alone. Regarding this, Nārada says:
One should carefully examine a stolen object that has fallen from another's hand, or risen to the ground unintentionally, even if it has been seized by a thief.

"Unreal things appear like the real, and real things appear like the unreal; various entities are seen in this way, therefore investigation is appropriate. Thus it is said. A thief, moreover, is of two kinds. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
Thieves are recorded as being of two kinds: those who act openly and those who act in secret;
yet through their intelligence, skill, and guile, they are divided into a thousand varieties.
[438] Merchants, physicians, gamblers, members of an assembly, those who take bribes, deceivers, those who know omens and portents, fortune-tellers, craftsmen, and counterfeiters;

"Those who do not perform their duties, those who remain indifferent, false witnesses, open thieves, and likewise those who live by deception"— the term *pratirūpakāḥ* means "those who manufacture counterfeits. And so says Nārada:
There, those who deceive by means of light, those who rely on fraudulent measures and scales,
bribe-takers, those who use fraudulent weights, gamblers, and prostitutes [are found].
"Those who produce counterfeit goods and those who subsist on the practice of fortune-telling—such as these are to be known as open thieves on earth. Thus [it is said].
Bṛhaspati states the nature of concealed thieves:
"Those who break through walls, those who rob travelers, those who seize bipeds and quadrupeds,
those who steal crops, and those who take by stealth— these should be known as hidden thieves.
Thus says Vyāsa as well.
Endowed with the means of accomplishment, they roam at night unobserved;
their dwellings unknown, they are to be recognized as hidden thieves.

"The thrower [of stones], the breaker of joints, the one who plunders travelers, the one who unties knots, and so forth; the thief of women or men, and the thief of livestock—these are recorded as the nine kinds of thieves."

The *utkṣepaka* is one who, having ascertained the wealth of the wealthy, cuts off that wealth and seizes it. The *saṃdhibhettr̥* is one who, standing at the junction of two houses, breaks through the wall situated there. The *pāntha* is one who openly robs travelers in deserts and similar places. The *udgranthika* is one who unties a knot in order to seize wealth tied within a garment or the like. Bṛhaspati states the punishment for open thieves such as merchants and others: "Those identified by royal officers through their associations, physical marks, or appearance..."
They shall be made to restore what was stolen and be punished with the penalties prescribed by the scriptures.
A merchant who conceals a defect, adulterates goods, or restores them after alteration shall be made to pay double the price of that merchandise and be fined an amount equal to it.
But that physician who, ignorant of medicines and mantras and lacking true knowledge of disease,
takes wealth from the sick, shall be punished like a thief.
Those who play with false dice, the base, those who seize the wives of kings, fraudulent astrologers, and cheats— these gamblers are declared to be punishable.
Those members of the assembly who speak unjustly, as well as those who live on bribes and those who betray the trust placed in them— all of these must be banished.
Those who, out of greed for wealth, proclaim to people knowledge of astrology and portents without actually understanding them, should be restrained with great effort.
Those who display themselves as being equipped with staffs, antelope skins, and so forth,
while secretly harming men through deceit, are to be executed by the king's officers.
Those who, by means of processing, turn an article of small value into one of great value,
and those who deceive women and children, shall be punished according to the amount of the wealth involved.
[440] Those who manufacture artificial gold, gems, coral, and the like,
shall be made by the king to pay the purchaser the price and a fine double that amount.
"When neutral witnesses deceive one party out of affection, greed,
or other such motives, and when witnesses speak falsely, they shall be made to pay a fine double the amount [in dispute].
He [Yājñavalkya] himself states the punishment for those who are secret thieves and those who break through walls or dig tunnels:
Having identified one who has severed a joint [of a corpse], the lord shall cause him to be impaled on a stake;
likewise, one who plunders travelers shall have his neck tied to a tree and be suspended therefrom.
Those who carry off human beings should be burned by the king with a fire of straw;
one who steals a cow should have his nose cut off, or, having been bound, he should be submerged in water.
"But the one who picks pockets should be torn apart with pincers by the king's men;
the stealer of grain should be made to pay ten times [the value] as a double fine.
Thus Manu states the punishment for a cutpurse.
"In the first instance of breaking a seal, one should have the fingers of the thief cut off;
in the second, his hands and feet; in the third, he deserves death" (MDh 9.277). Here, "fingers" refers to the index finger and the thumb. For this very reason, Nārada says:
"In the first [case of] breaking a knot, there shall be the cutting off of the fingers and the thumb;
in the second, likewise, whatever remains; in the third, one deserves death. Thus [Yājñavalkya] states the punishment for those who seize prisoners. Yājñavalkya says:

"A man who forcibly seizes robbers, or those who carry off horses and elephants, or those who kill [others] by force, shall be impaled on a stake" (YDh 2.273). This punishment, which culminates in the severing of fingers or ends in death, applies to cases involving property of a value that merits the highest fine (*uttamasāhasa*).

"Killing, confiscation of all property, banishment from the city, branding, and the amputation of limbs— these are declared to be the punishments for the highest degree of violence (*uttama-sāhasa*)," according to the traditional teaching of Nārada. Thus, Nārada has shown the rule regarding the imposition of punishments in the form of first, middle, and highest degrees of violence (*sāhasa*) with respect to inferior, middling, and superior objects.
"The same punishment which has been prescribed by the wise for the three types of violent acts (sāhasa) applies also to theft, according to the sequence of the three kinds of property.
Thus Manu declares the gradations of punishment based on distinctions such as caste and so forth.
In the case of theft, the guilt of a Śūdra becomes eightfold;
that of a Vaiśya is sixteenfold, and that of a Kṣatriya is thirty-twofold.
"For a Brahmin, it may be sixty-four, or even a full hundred, or twice sixty-four; for he is indeed one who knows the merits and defects of those [weights]. (MDh 8.337–38).
"For one who steals more than ten *kumbhas* of grain, the punishment is death."
In other cases as well, he shall be made to pay eleven times [the value], and that wealth shall belong to him.
For gold, silver, and the like, as well as for the finest garments and all kinds of gems, the penalty is death for a value exceeding one hundred.
[443] But for an amount exceeding fifty [paṇas], the cutting off of the hand is prescribed;
for the remainder, however, one should determine a fine eleven times the value.
"For the abduction of men of noble birth, and especially of women, as well as for the theft of the most precious gems, one deserves the death penalty. (MDh 8.320–323)

Whatever punishment has been prescribed for a particular theft shall be eightfold when committed by a Śūdra, sixteenfold when committed by a Vaiśya, thirty-twofold when committed by a Kṣatriya, and sixty-fourfold—or a hundredfold, or one hundred and twenty-eightfold—when committed by a Brāhmaṇa. In other cases involving items of small value, one should determine a fine eleven times the value of the property. For petty articles of less than one *māṣa* in value, the fine shall be five times their value. And so says Nārada:
"In the case of wooden vessels, grass, and the like, as well as earthenware..."
Likewise, [the sounds] of bamboo, bamboo vessels, sinews, bones, and skins.
"For the theft of leafy vegetables with fresh roots,
of fruits and roots, of cooked foods, of prepared foods, of fish, and of meat—
as well as for all items of low value— the fine shall be five times their value. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, that which was stated by Manu:
"Of thread, cotton, fermenting agent, cow-dung, and molasses;
of curd, milk, buttermilk, water, and grass..."
For the theft of bamboo and bamboo vessels,
as well as salts,
and likewise for the theft of earthenware, earth, and ashes;
Of goats and birds, of oil and clarified butter,
of meat and honey, and whatever else originates from animals;
Regarding the statement, "For other such intoxicating drinks, for cooked rice,
and for all kinds of prepared foods, the fine shall be double their value" (MDh 8.326–29),
that refers to cases involving items of minor utility. Manu states that there is no punishment for travelers and others in the case of theft of goods of very little utility.
A twice-born man traveling on a journey whose provisions are exhausted, taking two stalks of sugarcane and two roots from another’s field, does not deserve to be punished.
[Likewise for taking] chickpeas, rice, wheat, barley, mung beans, and black gram. (MDh 8.341)
Those standing on the road may take a single handful of grain, provided it is not forbidden.
"Likewise, having fasted for six meals during the seventh meal-time,
one may take [wealth] from a person of low conduct according to the rule of not providing for the morrow.
Regarding even a grave offense, Yājñavalkya states that there is no punishment of death for a Brāhmaṇa.
"Having branded the Brāhmaṇa, he should banish him from his own kingdom;
even though he be a perpetrator of a great crime, he shall never cause a Brāhmaṇa to be killed. (YDh 2.279).
Rather, having made a mark upon his forehead, he should expel him from his own country. And so says Manu:

"For violating the Guru's bed, the mark of a female organ shall be made; for drinking liquor, the sign of a tavern-flag; for theft, the mark of a dog's foot; and for killing a Brahmin, the mark of a headless man" (MDh 9.237).
This branding and so forth is a penance for those who do not perform penance after the imposition of punishment, but not for those who desire to perform penance. And thus says Manu:
"But all castes who perform penance as prescribed shall not be branded on the forehead by the king; rather, they should be made to pay the highest fine" (MDh 9.240).
Regarding one who assists a thief by providing food, shelter, and so forth, Yājñavalkya says:

"Having provided lodging, food, fire, water, weapons, or implements for a thief or a murderer, if one knows [of their intent], the highest fine shall be imposed. Thus says Yājñavalkya (YDh 2.276). Kātyāyana also says:
Those who provide food for thieves, as well as those who supply fire and water,
those who purchase their goods, and those who accept them in exchange;
"For these are declared to be equally punishable, as are those who conceal them.
Thus says Nārada regarding one who neglects a thief:
"Those who, though capable, neglect [to act], they too share in the guilt thereof."
While the people were crying out as their wealth was being carried away in that manner.

"Those who, having heard [of the crime], do not run to [the aid of] it, they too share in that fault. Regarding the means of recovering property when thieves are not seen, Yājñavalkya says: "When [property] has been destroyed or stolen, the fault lies with the village headman if [the thieves] have not departed."
But for one who maintains a pasture on the road, there is no fine for cattle stolen from that pasture, provided they were recovered by thieves.
"A village shall provide [the way] within its own boundaries, or wherever the footstep goes;
or else, five villages beyond the *krośa*, or even ten villages. (YDh 2.271–72)

This is the meaning: when a killing or the theft of property occurs even within the midst of a village, then the fault of negligence regarding the thief lies solely with the village headman (*grāmapati*). To avoid that liability, the village headman himself must seize the thief and hand him over to the king. If he is unable to do so, he must restore the stolen property to the owner, provided he does not show the thief's tracks leading out from his own village. However, if he does show those tracks, then the ruler of the territory into which those tracks enter must deliver both the thief and the wealth. And so says Nārada:
[448] He whose property is stolen from his domain must diligently apprehend the thief, or else be made to pay the value of the goods, provided that the thief has not escaped with the tracks.
"If, moreover, what has gone forth from this does not go elsewhere, one should cause it to be given to the neighboring guardians of the roads and the guardians of the directions. Thus [it is said].

In the case of theft from a pasture (*vivīta*), the fault lies with the owner of the pasture alone. However, when the theft occurs on the road itself, or in a place that is not a pasture, or in a field other than the pasture, then the offense belongs to the thief-catcher, the guardian of the road, and the guardian of the region. Furthermore, when a crime occurs in a field outside the village, at the edge of its boundary, then the inhabitants of that very village must make restitution, provided the tracks of the thieves have not gone beyond the boundary. If they have gone beyond, then the village into which those tracks enter shall perform the delivery of the thieves and so forth. When, however, a robbery or similar act occurs in a location more than a *krośa* away from the center of several villages, and the trail of the thieves is lost due to the crush of people, then five or ten villages shall make restitution. This alternative arrangement is determined according to proximity and other such factors. When the king is unable to compel payment, he himself shall pay it. Thus says Gautama: "Having recovered what was stolen by thieves, he should restore it to its proper place, or he should give it from his own treasury. Vṛddha-Manu states the means for reaching a decision when there is doubt regarding theft:

"If, while that [stolen property] is being restored, there should be doubt regarding the theft, the one who claims to have been robbed shall be made to take an oath, or he may establish [his claim] through his kinsmen. Thus [it is said]. Nārada states the specific manner of executing thieves:
"Whichever thieves he may seize there, having beaten them and bound them,
and having dragged them out, he shall execute them everywhere by various means of capital punishment.
Thus ends the section on theft (*steya-prakaraṇa*).
Then, the nature of that rashness was described by Nārada:
"Whatever action is performed impulsively by those arrogant of their strength is [called] rashness."
"That is called *sāhasa* (violence); here, *saha* is said to mean strength.
Now, one might object: "But *sāhasa* is not distinct from theft, verbal and physical assault, and adultery, since it is merely a sub-variety of those. And so says Bṛhaspati:
'Killing a human, theft, violating another's wife, ... [450]

"Harshness and both [types of] violence are fourfold. This being so, how is it that this [violence] constitutes a separate head of litigation (*vyavahārapada*)? True; nevertheless, because it differs from those [other categories] by the qualifying condition of relying on force and arrogance, it is mentioned separately for the purpose of imposing a heavier punishment. Alternatively, it is mentioned separately because the form of violence consisting of the killing of a human being exceeds those [other forms]. Regarding its threefold nature, Nārada says:
Furthermore, that [discipline] is to be known as threefold—namely, the initial, the intermediate, and likewise the superior; its specific characteristics have been stated separately in the treatises.
The destruction, seizure, or trampling of fruits, roots, water, and other such items that serve as field-appurtenances is declared to be the first degree of *sāhasa* (violence).
Regarding clothing, vehicles, food and drink, and household utensils—
by this very same method, the middle amercement is prescribed.

"Malice, the use of poison, weapons, and the like, the violation of another's wife, and whatever else obstructs life—these are declared to be the highest amercement (*uttamasāhasa*). Thus [it is said]. He (Yājñavalkya) himself states the punishment for all three types of violence:
For the first of these, the punishment depends on the specific act and shall not be less than one hundred;
for the middle one, however, it is seen by those learned in the scriptures as being not less than five hundred.
For the highest degree of violence, a fine of at least one thousand [paṇas] is prescribed;
[the punishments may include] execution, confiscation of all property, banishment from the city, and branding.
In the case of the highest violence, the punishment is declared to be the cutting off of that limb.

[451] Thus, Yājñavalkya states the punishment for *sāhasa* (violent crime) consisting of the seizure of another's property: "The fine shall be double the value of that [property]; however, if there is denial, it is fourfold. He who causes the *sāhasa* to be committed shall be made to pay double the fine."
"And he who, having spoken thus, acts as the giver [of the gift], shall incur a fourfold [penalty]. (YDh 2.230–31).
Regarding specific types of *sāhasa* (violent crimes), Yājñavalkya states the punishment:
"One who insults or transgresses against those worthy of honor (*arghya*), and one who strikes a brother's wife."
One who fails to deliver what has been entrusted, and one who breaks into a house situated by the sea.
For those who cause harm to neighbors, guild members, and others,
the settled rule is that their fine shall be fifty paṇas.
One who approaches a widow of his own accord, one who does not run to the aid of someone crying out for help,
one who raises a cry for help without cause, and a Caṇḍāla who touches those of the highest caste— [these are all equal].
One who feeds Śūdras or renunciants at rites for the gods or the ancestors;
one who makes an improper oath; one who performs unsuitable acts of yoga;
and one who obstructs the virility of bulls or small animals.
One who denies common property and one who causes the destruction of a maidservant’s fetus.

One who abandons any of these— father, son, sister, brother, husband, wife, teacher, or officiating priest— provided they have not lost their caste, shall be liable to a fine of one hundred [paṇas]. For causing an abortion by striking with a weapon, the highest amercement is the punishment.
Whether he be superior or inferior, [the same penalty applies] for the killing of a man or a woman.
A woman who is extremely corrupt, one who has killed her husband, one who is not pregnant, or one who destroys a dam—
having bound a stone to her, he shall cause her to be immersed in water.
One who administers poison or sets fire, or who causes the death of her husband, her elders, or her own children,
should have her ears, hands, nose, and lips cut off and then be put to death by cattle.
"Those who set fire to fields, houses, forests, villages, pastures, or threshing floors, as well as one who approaches the wife of a king, shall be burned by a fire of straw. (YDh 2.277–82).
Regarding a violent crime (*sāhasa*) whose perpetrator is unknown, Bṛhaspati states the means for identifying the assailant:
Where a person is seen slain but the killer is not seen,
he should be identified by the king through inference based on prior enmity.
His neighbors, both those living next door and those further away, as well as his friends, enemies, and kinsmen,
should be questioned by the king’s officers using conciliation and other such means.
"He is to be recognized through association with the wicked, by signs, and by hidden characteristics;
thus has been declared the disposition of murderers and thieves.
So too says Yājñavalkya:
Even in the case of one killed while unobserved, his sons, kinsmen,
and women who are devoted to him should be questioned individually regarding the quarrel.
"Or [he may ask] one who desires his wife, property, or livelihood: 'With whom has he gone? Or he should slowly question people near the place of death. (YDh 2.280–81).
However, when the aforementioned means of knowledge are unavailable, Kātyāyana states:
But when a legal matter proceeds without marks [of guilt] and is termed a *sāhasa* (an act of violence), it must be cleared by means of oaths; this rule applies to all types of disputes.
[454] Thus it is said. Vyāsa states a specific rule regarding the killing of a perpetrator of a rash act:
"Having properly identified the slayer, along with his accomplices and kinsmen, the king shall put them to death by various means of execution that cause terror. Thus it is said.
Bṛhaspati also says:
"Those who are open assassins as well as those who kill in secret,
having been identified and their wealth properly confiscated, shall be executed by various means of death."

This refers to the case of those who kill a Brāhmaṇa, such as Kṣatriyas and others. Regarding this, Baudhāyana says: “For Kṣatriyas and others who have killed a Brāhmaṇa, the punishment is death and the confiscation of all property. For those same persons, in the case of killing an equal or an inferior, one should prescribe a corresponding punishment according to their power” (BDh 1.10.18–20). To specify the punishment for each individual among many who have set out with the intent to kill a single person, Kātyāyana says: “If many men, being enraged, should kill a single person, he among them who strikes a vital organ is traditionally considered the killer.”

The meaning is that whoever strikes a vital organ (marmaghātaka) shall indeed receive a punishment corresponding to that killing. Furthermore, a punishment for those other than the actual killer has also been stated by that same author:

"The one who initiates the act, the accomplice, likewise the one who instructs in the method, the one who provides shelter, the giver of weapons, and the giver of food to those who perform forbidden acts."
The instructor of war, the one who incites its destruction,
the one who remains indifferent, the one who speaks of its faults, and the one who approves of it.
"He who is capable and does not forbid [an act], all of them are performers of that deed;

one should impose upon them a punishment according to their capacity and in accordance with the fault. Here, "in accordance" means in accordance with the fault. That same author shows that both [the instigator and the executor] share in the guilt for one who strikes a vital spot (*marmahantr*).
"The initiator and the accomplice share the guilt; [the others] are liable for half of that.

In this manner, it should be inferred that even for those who merely point out the path [to a crime], their culpability is diminished over time. Yājñavalkya also states the punishment for offenses similar to acts of violence:
"A washerman who wears another's garment [without permission] shall be fined three *paṇas*."
"In cases of sale, lease, pledge, or borrowing, ten *paṇas* [shall be the fine].

(YDh 2.238) Regarding "lease" (*avakraya*), Manu states the following rule for the purpose of ensuring that the washerman does not violate his agreement—namely, the agreement made when giving a garment with the understanding: "I will give you this garment for use for such a length of time; you must give me such an amount of money"—in order that the washerman may incur punishment for transgressing that rule:
"A washerman shall wash [clothes] slowly on a smooth board made of *śālmalī* wood. (MDh 8.394)
"One should not take away garments for other garments, nor should one cause them to be worn [as collateral]. (MDh 8.396). Regarding loss through negligence, Nārada states:
"An eighth part of the value is forfeited for a garment that has been washed once."
Twice [the fine] for a foot, thrice for a third part, and half [the value] when it has been washed four times.
"But beyond the point when it is half-decayed, there is a gradual reduction by one-quarter at each stage until it reaches the state of being worn out;
for that which is worn out, there is no fixed rule regarding its decay."

If a garment purchased for eight *paṇas* is lost after being washed once, its value shall be paid minus one *paṇa*. If it was washed twice, two *paṇas* less; if three times, three *paṇas* less; and if four times, four *paṇas*. Beyond that, for each subsequent washing, the remaining value shall be paid according to a reduction of one-quarter until it is worn out. The meaning is that, upon the loss of a worn-out garment, the payment of its value is to be determined at the owner's discretion. He (Yājñavalkya) himself states the punishment for witnesses and others in the case of a dispute between father and son:
"But in a dispute between father and son, the witness shall be fined three *paṇas*;

he who stands between them shall also be fined eight times that amount" (YDh 2.239). The meaning is this: in a quarrel between father and son, he who accepts the role of a witness but does not prevent the quarrel shall be fined three *paṇas*. Furthermore, he who acts as a guarantor for the payment of a wager in their contested lawsuit, or who inflames the quarrel, shall be punished with twenty-four *paṇas*—that is, eight times the three *paṇas*. The same author states the punishment for other similar offenses as well:
One who forges scales, royal edicts, measures, or coins,
and anyone who deals with such forged items, shall be made to pay the highest fine.
He who declares a counterfeit coin to be genuine, or a genuine coin to be counterfeit—
that examiner of coins shall be made to pay the highest fine.
A physician who practices falsely shall be punished with the first amercement for treating animals,
the middle amercement for humans, and the highest amercement for royal officials.
He who imprisons one who should not be imprisoned, or releases one who has been imprisoned,
and he who interferes with legal proceedings, shall be compelled to pay the highest fine.
Whoever should take even one-eighth part by means of a measure or a scale, shall be made to pay a fine of two hundred; this is ordained for both increase and decrease.
One who adulterates medicinal herbs, oils, salts, perfumes, grains, molasses,
and other such commodities with inferior substances shall be fined sixteen paṇas.
For making a false attribution of quality to clay, leather, gems, thread, iron, wood, bark, or cloth,
the fine shall be eight times the value of the saleable item.
For one who brings back from the sea counterfeit merchandise, whether it be genuine goods or artificial items,
as well as for one who deposits or sells such goods, a judicial penalty shall be determined.
For an inferior article, the fine is fifty paṇas; for one of medium quality, it is said to be one hundred;
for one of superior quality, the fine is two hundred paṇas; and as the value increases, the fine increases accordingly.
For artisans and craftsmen who, acting together,
fix a price with difficulty while knowing whether that price ought to decrease or increase, the highest fine shall be imposed.
For merchants who, having banded together, withhold merchandise by fixing an excessive price,
or for those who sell it [at such a price], the prescribed fine is the highest amercement.
Whatever price is established by the king for daily sale,
whether it be a sale or a purchase, the profit derived from that is declared to be the merchant's gain.
A merchant who buys and sells immediately may take five percent on goods from his own country, but ten percent on those from a foreign land.
"Having set aside the expenses arising from the merchandise upon the value of the goods, a price should be established that is favorable to both the buyer and the seller. (YDh 2.240–53)

A *tulā* is a balance scale; a *prastha* and the like are measures of capacity; a *nāṇaka* is a coin marked with a seal, such as a *dramma* or a *niṣka*. One who forges these—by making them otherwise than the standard measures established by the country, whether by reducing or increasing the weight of a *dramma* and so forth, or by making them bear non-standard seals, or by filling them with copper and the like—is to be punished. Likewise, both he who deals with such coins and he who uses them are each to be punished with the highest fine (*uttama-sāhasa*). Furthermore, the examiner of coins who declares what is genuine to be forged, or what is forged to be genuine, is also to be punished with the highest fine. Moreover, a physician who, though ignorant of Āyurveda, practices medicine among animals, humans, or royal servants for the sake of a livelihood while claiming to be a skilled healer, is to be punished with the first, middle, or highest fine respectively. He who imprisons one who is innocent without the king’s command, or releases one who is imprisoned without such command, or dismisses one summoned for a legal proceeding before the case has been concluded, is also to be punished with the highest fine. A merchant who steals an eighth part of his merchandise, such as rice or cotton, by means of false weights or false measures, is to be fined two hundred *paṇas*; however, the increase or decrease of the fine should be calculated according to the increase or decrease of the value of the stolen goods. Medicine refers to medicinal substances; oil refers to ghee and the like; fragrant substances refer to *uśīra* (vetiver) and the like. For one who mixes worthless substances into these for the purpose of sale, the fine is sixteen *paṇas*. Regarding that which is "non-genuine" (*ajāti*)—such as clay or leather in which no high-value species exists—for one who creates the appearance of genuineness by imparting different scents, colors, or tastes to produce a resemblance to a high-value species, the fine is eight times the value of the merchandise, such as the clay or leather, once it has been made to appear similar. The "exchange" (*parivartana*) of a casket or box refers to its transposition. If one shows a casket full of pearls but, through sleight of hand, hands over another full of crystals, or if one manufactures artificial musk and the like and offers it for sale or as a pledge, the following calculation of punishment applies: if the counterfeit musk and such is of low value, meaning its price is less than one *paṇa*, the fine upon its sale is fifty *paṇas*. If its value is one *paṇa*, the fine is one hundred; if its value is two *paṇas*, the fine is two hundred. In this manner, the increase of the fine should be inferred from the increase of the value. Merchants who, acting in concert out of greed for profit, establish a different price—one that causes oppression to artisans and craftsmen, such as washermen and painters—even when the king is present and aware of the rise or fall of prices, are to be fined one thousand *paṇas*. Furthermore, those who seek to buy merchandise arrived from another country at a low price, obstructing it, or sell it at a high price, are subject to the highest fine. Even when the king is present, buying or selling must be conducted at the price determined by him. "Remainder" (*niḥsrava*) means that which remains after what has flowed out; therefore, only that profit which results from the price fixed by the king is lawful for merchants, not that which is arbitrarily determined by themselves.
