Merchants who, acting in concert out of greed for profit, establish a different price—one that causes oppression to artisans and craftsmen, such as washermen and painters—even when the king is present and aware of the rise or fall of prices, are to be fined one thousand *paṇas*. Furthermore,
"Every five nights, or else every fortnight when it has passed, the king should perform the formal offering of the guest-water (argha) in their presence. (MDh 8.402)

On merchandise from one's own country, one should take a five-pana profit on goods worth one hundred panas. However, on foreign merchandise, one should take a ten-pana profit, provided the sale occurs on the very day the purchase price is received. For one who sells at a later time, an increase in profit should be determined according to the passage of time. Regarding merchandise arrived from another country, the king, having calculated the expenses incurred for traveling to and from that foreign land, for receiving the goods, and for duties (*śulka*) and other such points, and having combined these with the cost of the merchandise, should fix the price so as to benefit both the buyer and the seller; such that on merchandise worth one hundred panas, a ten-pana profit is realized. Thus should the price be established by the king.
Thus ends the section on rash acts [462];
now follows the section on sexual intercourse with women.
Bṛhaspati states that it is of three kinds:
"Learn that adultery, which is the root of sin, is of three types:
two are committed through force or fraud, and the third arises from passion."
But that which is done against one's will, as well as that done by one who is intoxicated or insane,
or that which is committed in secret during a state of delirium or by means of force, is not [considered adultery].
When a union is brought about by deceitfully bringing someone to one's house or by giving them intoxicants,
they know that to be "contracted through fraud" (*upādhikṛta*).
"Love born of passion (*anurāga*) is to be known as that which arises through mutual affection, by the dispatching of messengers, or through greed for beauty and wealth.
Thus he spoke; furthermore, he himself stated its threefold nature:
That, moreover, is said to be threefold— initial, intermediate, and supreme—
consisting of a sidelong glance, laughter, and likewise the dispatching of a messenger.
Touching is considered the first ornament of garments and the primary means of acquiring them;
likewise, the sending forth of perfumes, garlands, incense, and new clothes [is prescribed].
They know that conversation in private constitutes the middling form of seduction;
likewise, sharing a single bed or seat, as well as playfulness, kissing, and embracing.
"This is declared by those who know the treatises to be the highest form of *saṃgrahaṇa* (adultery). Regarding the means of identifying a woman's adultery, Yājñavalkya says:
"In the case of adultery, a man is to be apprehended while pulling each other's hair with another's wife."
Or immediately by the signs born of desire, or likewise upon the realization of both.
"Touching the knot of the lower garment, the breasts, the upper covering, the thighs, or the hair; conversing at an improper place or time; and staying in the same place together. (YDh 2.283–84)

Adultery (*saṃgrahaṇa*) is the sexual union of a man and a woman. One engaged therein may be apprehended while sporting with another’s wife by means of hair-to-hair grappling, or through the immediate signs of fresh marks produced by passion—such as wounds inflicted by fingernails or teeth—or by the mutual confession of both parties. Furthermore, one who acts as if full of desire when touching the knot of another’s garment, the region of her breasts, her upper body, her hips, or her hair; or one who engages in conversation with another’s wife in a secluded place, or even in a crowded area thick with darkness at an improper time; or one who stays together with another’s wife on a single bed or similar seat—he too is to be apprehended. Manu also says:

If a man touches a woman in an improper place, or if he, being touched by her, consents to it— when there is mutual consent, all such acts are recorded in the legal tradition as *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual misconduct).
Whether out of pride, delusion, or self-praise, if he should speak of it himself...
"I previously enjoyed her"—this is recorded as *saṃgrahaṇa* (sexual intercourse).
Regarding the punishment for this, Yājñavalkya says:
"In the case of one of equal caste, the highest fine; but in the case of approaching [a woman] in the direct order of castes (*ānulomya*), the middle fine."

"In the case of the reverse order (*prātilomya*), there shall be death for the man and the cutting off of the ears and so forth for the woman" (YDh 2.286). For all four castes, when one forcibly approaches the protected wife of another of the same caste, the fine is one thousand and eighty *paṇas*. However, when one approaches the protected wife of another who is of a lower caste in the natural order (*ānulomya*), the fine is the middle amercement (*madhyama-sāhasa*). Furthermore, regarding the case where one approaches a woman of his own caste who is unprotected, or one who is protected, in the natural order, a specific rule has been stated by Manu:
"A Brāhmaṇa approaching a protected Brāhmaṇa woman by force shall be fined one thousand [paṇas]."
He who has sexual intercourse with a willing woman shall be fined five hundred [paṇas].
"A Brāhmaṇa should be made to pay a fine of one thousand [paṇas] when approaching those [women] who are protected;
however, for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya approaching a Śūdra woman, the fine shall indeed be one thousand. (MDh 8.378, 383).
This refers to cases other than those involving the wives of teachers or friends, because different penalties are prescribed therein. To that effect, Nārada says:
Mother, mother’s sister, mother-in-law, maternal uncle’s wife,
father’s sister, paternal uncle’s wife, friend’s wife, female disciple, sister, her friend, and daughter-in-law.
A daughter, a teacher’s wife, one of the same lineage, one who has sought refuge,
a queen, a female renunciant, a nurse, a virtuous woman, and one of the highest caste.
"Going to any one of these [wives] is called violating the Guru's bed;
for him, the cutting off of the penis is ordained as the punishment, and no other.

Thus, in the case of approaching a superior woman through inverse order (*pratilomyena*), there is execution for a Kṣatriya and others. This refers to the case of a protected woman (*guptā*); otherwise, there is a monetary fine. And so says Manu:
But both of them, having violated a guarded Brahmin woman,
should be punished like Shudras or burned in a fire of straw mats.
"If a Vaiśya or a Kṣatriya should have intercourse with an unprotected Brāhmaṇa woman, he should fine the Vaiśya five hundred [paṇas] and the Kṣatriya one thousand. (MDh 8.377, 376).

For a Śūdra who has intercourse with an unprotected woman of a higher caste, there shall be the cutting off of the penis and the confiscation of all property; however, for intercourse with a protected woman, there shall be execution and the seizure of all property. And so says that same author:

[466] "A Śūdra who dwells with a member of the twice-born caste—whether that person is protected or unprotected—is deprived of one limb and all his property if she was unprotected, and is deprived of everything if she was protected. Thus says Manu (MDh 8.374). On this very point, Bṛhaspati also says:
"But he who desires her by force, one shall seize all his wealth;
having cut off his penis and testicles, one shall cause him to be paraded on a donkey. Thus it is said.

With the phrase "of a Śūdra" understood as a recurring reference, Gautama states: "In the case of approaching an Ārya woman, there shall be the excision of the organ and the confiscation of all property" (GDh 12.2). Furthermore, in the case of an Ārya woman approaching a man of lower caste, there shall be the cutting off of her nose and other features. This instruction regarding execution and the like applies specifically to the king, because he alone possesses the authority for protection, and not to every twice-born person; for there is a prohibition against taking up weapons, stating: "A Brāhmaṇa shall not take up a weapon even for the sake of testing it" (ĀpDh 1.10.29.6). However, when there is a fear of delay in reporting the matter to the king, then the execution and other such punishments certainly apply even to every twice-born person.
The twice-born may take up arms when their duty is obstructed;
there is no fault whatsoever for the slayer in killing an assailant.
"Whether it be in public or in private, it is wrath that encounters that wrath. (MDh 8.348, 351).

Because of this permission to take up arms, if a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya have sexual intercourse with each other's wives, the fines shall be one thousand and five hundred paṇas respectively. Regarding this, Manu says:
"If a Vaiśya approaches a guarded Kṣatriya woman, or a Kṣatriya approaches a guarded Vaiśya woman..."
"Both of them deserve punishment for [intercourse with] an unprotected Brāhmaṇa woman. (MDh 8.382).
Yājñavalkya states the punishment for approaching a common woman:
"In the case of enslaved women who are confined, and likewise those who are independent..."
"A man shall also be made to pay a fine of fifty paṇas for approaching women who are [sexually] accessible. (YDh 2.290)

Women of the castes whose characteristics have been described are *dāsīs* (female slaves). They are called *avaruddhās* (confined) when, for the sake of preventing the neglect of service, they are restricted by their master to remain only within the house, being thus barred from enjoyment with other men. They are called *bhujiṣyās* (servants) because they are appropriated by a specific man. When these women are *dāsīs*, *avaruddhās*, or *bhujiṣyās*, or—by virtue of the word "and" (*ca*)—when they are courtesans (*veśyās*), wanton women (*svairiṇīs*), or common women (*sādhāraṇastrīs*) who are servants, one who approaches them—even though they are accessible to all men because of their common status—is to be fined fifty *paṇas*. This is because, due to being appropriated by another, they are equivalent to the wives of others. With this very intent, Nārada also says: [The verse follows...]

A woman who is self-willed, a non-Brāhmaṇa woman, a courtesan, a female slave, and one who has left her husband— all these women may be approached in the direct order of castes, but never in the inverse order.
"But in the case of these very female slaves, there would be a fault similar to that regarding the wives of others;
for even though they may be approachable, one should not have intercourse with them, since they are the property of another.
A *niṣkāsinī* is a female slave kept by her master. Regarding sexual intercourse with a female slave who is not so kept (*anavaruddhā*), Yājñavalkya states:
"A fine of ten *paṇas* is prescribed for one who approaches a female slave by force;

if she is unwilling and there are many [men], the fine is twenty-four [paṇas] for each. (YDh 2.291). For those who approach by force without the payment of a fee (*śulka*) women who live by sexual intercourse, such as female slaves, unchaste women (*svairiṇī*), and others, the fine is ten *paṇas*. For many men approaching a single woman against her will, the fine is twenty-four *paṇas* for each individual. Regarding the abduction of a maiden, Yājñavalkya states the following concerning the fine:

[469] One who abducts an adorned maiden should pay the highest fine; otherwise, the lowest. In the case of women of the same caste, he should pay a fine; but for abduction in the reverse order of castes, death is ordained by tradition.

"But there is no fault in [abducting] those who are willing and of a compatible [class]; otherwise, there is punishment. (YDh 2.287–88) One who abducts a maiden who is adorned and ready for marriage shall be punished with the highest fine (*uttamasāhasa*). One who abducts a maiden of the same caste (*savarṇā*) who is not so inclined shall be punished with the first fine (*prathamasāhasa*). For one who abducts a maiden born of a superior caste, such as a Kṣatriya and others, there is indeed death. One who abducts a willing maiden according to the natural order of castes (*ānulomyena*) does not incur punishment. One who abducts an unwilling maiden shall be punished with the first fine. Regarding the defilement of a maiden, the same author states the following punishment:
In the case of defiling [a woman], the cutting off of the hand is ordained; for violating a woman of the highest caste, death is prescribed.
For defiling a woman, one should pay a fine of one hundred [paṇas]; but for making a false accusation, two hundred.
"Having sexual intercourse with cattle, one shall be made to pay a hundred [paṇas]; for a low-caste woman or a cow, the middle amercement. (YDh 2.288–89)

If a man violates an unwilling maiden by force, such as by inflicting nail-marks and the like, his hand shall be cut off; if he violates one of high status, he shall be executed. If someone defames a maiden by proclaiming her existing defects, such as epilepsy or consumption, saying "she is not a virgin," he shall be made to pay a fine of one hundred [paṇas]. However, for false accusation—specifically, for defaming her by revealing non-existent defects—he shall be made to pay two hundred. For sexual intercourse with animals other than cows, he shall be made to pay one hundred paṇas. Likewise, the meaning is that one who has intercourse with a woman of lower caste, an Antyāvasāyinī, or a cow, shall be punished with the middle amercement. Furthermore, when he defiles her by causing a wound in the vulva through the insertion of a finger, Manu states a specific rule: [Manu 8.365–367] "If a man defiles a maiden of equal status with blood, he shall be fined five hundred [paṇas]; if she was unwilling, he shall be punished with the highest amercement. But if she was willing, he shall not suffer corporal punishment; rather, he shall be fined two hundred and shall marry her according to the prescribed rite. If a man of higher caste defiles a maiden of lower caste, he shall be fined one hundred and shall marry her after paying her father the bride-price."* *Note: The original text provided does not contain the full verses of Manu, but the summary reflects their general sense regarding the fines and marriage provisions.*
But that man who, out of arrogance, violates a maiden by force,
his two fingers shall be immediately cut off, and he deserves a fine of six hundred [paṇas].
One who defiles a willing woman is equal [to one who defiles an unwilling one] and does not deserve the cutting off of his fingers;
however, he should be made to pay a fine of two hundred [paṇas] to prevent a repetition of the offense.
If a maiden should defile another maiden, she shall be fined two hundred panas;
she must also pay double the bride-price and receive ten lashes with a cane.
"But a woman who violates a maiden deserves immediate shaving of the head, or else the cutting off of two fingers, as well as being led away on a donkey.

(MDh 8.367–70) Furthermore, when one approaches a maiden of a superior caste who is full of passion but unwilling, then there is corporal punishment—execution—for that Kṣatriya or other offender. When he approaches a maiden of his own caste who is willing, then he shall give a pair of cattle as a fee (*śulka*) to her father; if the father does not wish it, he shall give it to the king as a fine. But for one who approaches a maiden of his own caste who is unwilling, there is indeed execution. Thus says Manu:
But a man of lower caste who has intercourse with a woman of the highest caste deserves death;
one who has intercourse with a woman of equal caste should pay a fine, provided her father desires it.
"He who violates an unwilling maiden deserves immediate execution;
but a man who violates one who is willing, being of equal status, shall not suffer execution. (MDh 8.366, 364).
He [Manu] himself states the punishment for sexual intercourse with a Caṇḍālī and others:
But for approaching a woman of the lowest caste, one should brand him with the mark of a eunuch and banish him;
likewise, a Śūdra who approaches an Ārya woman should be branded, while for an Ārya who approaches a woman of the lowest caste, there shall be death.

"For one who approaches a woman in a non-vaginal passage, or even for one who urinates upon a man, as well as for those who approach female renunciants, the fine is twenty-four [paṇas]. (YDh 2.294, 293)

The *antyā* is a *caṇḍālī*. According to the statement of Manu, "A thousand for one who approaches a woman of the lowest caste" (*MDh* 8.385), a member of the three higher castes who approaches her without being inclined toward penance should be fined one thousand [paṇas], branded with the mark of a vulva by means of an ignoble metal, and banished from his own kingdom. A Śūdra, however, approaching a *caṇḍālī*, is merely to be branded. If the reading is *antyaja*, he becomes a *caṇḍāla* himself. But for a *caṇḍāla* who approaches a woman of a superior caste, there is indeed death. For a man who approaches a woman in the mouth or other such places, or urinates in the mouth of a man, or approaches a female ascetic (*pravrajitā*), the fine is twenty-four paṇas. Bṛhaspati states the punishment for adultery through deception: [End of provided text]
"He who causes [the offense] through deception shall receive a fine that seizes all his property;
having been branded with the mark of a female organ, he shall then be banished from the city.
Thus ends the section on sexual intercourse with women (*strī-saṃgrahaṇa*).
Now, regarding the title of the legal dispute known as *strīpuṃsayoga* (the union of woman and man), Nārada states its nature:
"That wherein the rites of marriage and so forth for women and men are proclaimed."
"That is called the title of law known as *strīpuṃsayoga* (the union of woman and man).
Regarding the protection of women, Manu says:
"Women must be kept in a state of dependence by their own men day and night."
And those who are attached to sense objects must indeed be established under one's own control.
Women must be guarded especially against even the slightest of attachments;
for if they are not protected, they will bring grief upon two families.
For seeing this supreme dharma common to all castes,
husbands— even those who are weak— strive to protect their wives.
For by protecting his wife with diligence, he indeed protects his offspring, his conduct, his lineage, himself, and his own dharma.
No one is able to protect women by force;
however, they can be protected through the application of these various means.

"He should employ her in the collection of wealth and in its expenditure, as well as in cleanliness, religious duty, the cooking of food, and the supervision of household utensils. (MDh 9.2, 5–7, 10–11)

Women must always be kept dependent by their own men, namely their husbands; when attached to objects such as singing and the like, they should be turned away from them. If left unprotected, however, through their misconduct they would cause grief to both the husband’s and the father’s families. Therefore, for the sake of the prosperity of both families, they must be guarded. Even though it may be impossible to guard them by forceful confinement, the meaning is that one should guard them by employing them in tasks such as the management of wealth and by not giving them the opportunity to think of other men. Bṛhaspati also says:
"A woman must be kept away from even the slightest opportunities for misconduct by her own kinsmen;
she must be protected day and night by her mother-in-law and other elder women.
Thus spoke Nārada regarding one who abandons a wife who is free from fault.

"One who abandons a wife who is compliant, not foul-mouthed, skillful, virtuous, and a mother of children, shall be punished by the king with a heavy fine. Regarding the case where she cannot be restrained by punishment, Yājñavalkya says:

"Abandoning a wife who is obedient, skillful, the mother of sons, and sweet-spoken, he should be made to pay a third part [of his property]; one without wealth must provide maintenance for his wife. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.76).
Nārada states that one may abandon a wife after having recognized her faults.
"There is no offense for a man and a woman who are mutually opposed to abandon one another; however, this is not the case for a married woman, except in the event of her adultery.

This means that there is no fault in a man and a woman of low caste who lack the sacrament of marriage abandoning each other due to mutual opposition. But for a woman consecrated by the rite of marriage, abandonment occurs only through adultery, not merely through opposition. And this refers specifically to the case of a woman who commits adultery of her own accord.

[475] "But for that woman who goes according to her own will, abandonment is ordained," because of this traditional teaching of Yama. Women who have gone to a disciple and so forth must also be abandoned. And likewise Vasiṣṭha says:
"Four, however, are to be abandoned: one who has gone to a disciple, and likewise one who has gone to a guru."
"But she who destroys [the household] especially, as does one who has approached a degraded man. (VaDh 21.19)

Hārīta also says: “One should avoid a woman who causes abortion, one of inferior caste, one who goes to her disciple or son, one addicted to the vice of drinking, and one who sells wealth or grain” (HārSm 13.21). Avoidance here means the abandonment of social and ritual interaction. Thus Vasiṣṭha states: “In sexual intercourse, in visiting sacred fords, and in religious duties, she is excluded” (VaDh 21.9). *Vyavāya* means sexual union. By the term “visiting sacred fords,” Smārta rites are indicated; by the word “dharma,” Śrauta rites; and by the word “and” (*ca*), conversation and so forth are included. However, regarding those who are ill and the like, Devala states that only the cessation of sexual enjoyment is required.

One may abandon at sacred fords a wife who is diseased, who bears only daughters, who is barren, insane, or whose menses have ceased, provided she is not otherwise corrupt; but one may never abandon her on account of her religious duties.

[476] Thus. "From the sacred ford" means from sexual enjoyment. And so Nārada says: "One should not, out of desire, take pleasure in a barren woman, one who gives birth only to daughters, one who is censurable, or one who is always hostile; by acting in this manner, one incurs no fault."
A wife who is habitually engaged in harmful acts, likewise one who speaks unpleasantly,
and one who eats before her husband— such a woman he should quickly expel from the home.
"A woman who has lost all her wealth, who causes the destruction of a fetus,
or who desires the death of her husband— such a woman should be banished from the city. Thus says Baudhāyana as well.

"One should abandon a wife who bears no offspring in the tenth year, one whose offspring are all female in the twelfth year, one whose offspring die in the fifteenth year, but one who speaks unpleasantly immediately. (BDh 2.2.4.6).
The word "union" (*saṃyoga*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].
[477] A wife who, out of malice toward her husband, causes him to miss his fertile season, shall be proclaimed in the midst of the village as a destroyer of the embryo and banished from the house.
A woman who fails to serve, an unchaste woman, or one who harms her husband [shall likewise be punished].
"Wise men quickly abandon a woman who speaks unpleasantly.
And this abandonment should be carried out as a substitute for killing; thus says Yama:
"Vivasvat declared the abandonment of a woman who acts wantonly."
"One should avoid killing or disfigurement; one should avoid the killing of women.

One must not commit the murder of a woman, nor the cutting off of her ears, nose, or other limbs. This means that a husband, when faced with the possibility of killing his wife, should instead avoid her [by renouncing her]; he must not perform the amputation of her ears, nose, and so forth. Other duties pertaining to women and men have been elaborated upon in the Chapter on Conduct (*Ācārādhyāya*) and thus are not detailed here.
Thus ends the section on the seduction of women.
Now, the legal title known as the Partition of Inheritance is described; its definition was stated by Nārada:
Where the partition of paternal property is carried out by the sons,
that is declared by the learned to be the legal title of "Inheritance" (dāyabhāga).

[478] Thus: what is called *dāya* (inheritance) is that wealth which becomes the property of another solely through its connection with the owner; that is so described. It is of two kinds: unobstructed (*apratibandha*) and obstructed (*sapratibandha*). Paternal or grandpaternal wealth is unobstructed inheritance; however, the wealth of sons and others is obstructed inheritance for the father and others. The division of that is called *dāyavibhāga* (partition of inheritance). For this very reason, the Lord of Yoga (Yājñavalkya) states that by the word *dāya*, only the property coming through the father or through the mother is meant. And the author of the *Saṃgraha* says:

"Whatever property has come down through the father and whatever has come down through the mother is designated by the term *dāya* (inheritance); its partition is now being described. Thus [it is said].
Manu states the time for partition:
After the father and the mother have passed away, the brothers, having assembled, shall divide the paternal inheritance equally; for they have no power over it while the two are alive. (MDh 9.104)

[479] Thus: "After the father" refers to the time for the partition of the father's property; "after the mother" refers to the time for the partition of the mother's property. From this, the following is stated: after the father, even while the mother is living, the partition of the father's property must be performed; likewise, after the mother, even while the father is living, the partition of the mother's property must indeed be performed, because there is no utility in waiting for the time after both have passed when the partition of the property of either one is at hand. This has been stated by the author of the *Saṃgraha*: "Regarding the partition of the father's wealth, even while the mother is living..."
Because she lacks independence, she has no ownership [of property] without her husband.
"Likewise, even the division of the mother's property while the father is alive [is not permitted],
because, as long as there are offspring, the husband is not the master of the woman's wealth."

This is the meaning: upon the death of the husband, because the father’s wife lacks independent ownership over the husband’s wealth due to his passing, and because—even when children exist—the husband is not the owner of the wife’s wealth even upon her death, it is therefore proper that there be a division of the wealth of either one while the other still lives. By this, it is implied that sons have no independence regarding the division of those respective properties while [the parents] are alive. And so Śaṅkha says: “Sons shall not divide the inheritance while the father is alive; even if they should acquire property later, the sons are indeed unworthy [to do so], because of their lack of independence in matters of wealth and dharma. This is its meaning: although sons attain ownership in the father’s wealth immediately after birth, nevertheless, while the father is alive, they shall not divide that wealth; for, due to their lack of independence in dharma and artha, they are unfit to effect a partition. Lack of independence in artha means a lack of independence in taking or giving that [wealth]. Hārīta states: “While the father is alive, sons have no independence in the taking, giving, or pledging of wealth” (HārSm 17.21). Taking wealth means the enjoyment of wealth; giving means expenditure; pledging means the dismissal of servants and others for the sake of instruction. Lack of independence in dharma means the inability to engage independently in separate sacrifices, *iṣṭāpūrta*, and so forth. As for what was stated by Devala:
"When the father has passed away, the sons shall divide the father's wealth;
for they would have no ownership while the father remains free from defect.
This [text] also aims to establish their lack of independence, because the sons' ownership of the paternal wealth is established by worldly consensus through the mere fact of birth.

An objection: How can ownership (*svatva*), which is to be understood solely through the scriptures (*śāstra*), be established by worldly consensus? Furthermore, its scriptural establishment is understood from the statement of Gautama: “One becomes an owner through inheritance, purchase, partition, seizure, and discovery. For a Brāhmaṇa, what is additionally obtained is [exclusive]; for a Kṣatriya, what is conquered; for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra, what is earned (*nirviṣṭa*)” (GDh 10.39–42). Inheritance (*riktha*) is an unobstructed gift; a partition (*saṃvibhāga*) is an obstructed gift. Seizure (*parigraha*) is the appropriation of water, grass, wood, and so forth, which previously belonged to no one. Discovery (*adhigama*) is the finding of treasure-troves and the like. When these causes are present, one becomes the owner. For a Brāhmaṇa, that which is obtained through receiving gifts and so forth is “additional,” meaning it is not common to others. For a Kṣatriya, that which is obtained through victory, punishment, and so forth is not common to others. For a Vaiśya, that which is obtained through agriculture, cattle-rearing, and so forth—namely, what is earned—is not common to others. For a Śūdra, that which is obtained in the form of wages through service to the twice-born and so forth is not common to others. Likewise, for those born of *anuloma* and *pratiloma* unions, that which is obtained through their respective prescribed duties such as horse-riding or charioteering is “additional”; this is the meaning. On this very point, the author of the *Saṃgraha* states the underlying logic:

"Whatever is in someone's hand belongs to him alone; for what is not the property of another, which is held in the hands of others, is not treated as stolen by those [who take it]? For if ownership were established merely by seeing something belonging to another in the hand of someone else, then that person would become its owner. Therefore, ownership (*svatva*) is to be understood solely through the scriptures. Furthermore, if whoever is seen to have a certain object in their possession were its owner, then one could not say, "This was stolen by him," because he who saw it in his possession would be its owner. If ownership were merely a worldly matter, [the legal system would collapse].
[482] "The Brahmin who seeks wealth from the hand of one who takes what is not given, even by means of officiating at sacrifices or teaching, is just like a thief. (MDh 8.340).

If ownership were established by anything other than the scriptures, it would be illogical to prescribe a punishment for one who acquires property from a thief through officiating at sacrifices and the like. Therefore, ownership is to be understood solely through the scriptures.

Do not say this: ownership (*svatva*) is indeed worldly, because it is a means for accomplishing worldly purposes (*laukika-artha-kriyā*), like rice and other grains. If it is argued that the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because even Vedic things such as the *āhavanīya* fire possess the capacity to accomplish worldly tasks such as cooking—[we reply: no.

No; for there is a disparity, since those [sacrificial fires] do not serve as means for the feet and so forth in the form of the *āhavanīya* fire and the like, but rather in the form of ordinary fire and the like. Furthermore, because even common people (*pāmara*) are observed to engage in transactions involving ownership, it is understood that ownership is a worldly (*laukika*) matter. As for the statement from Gautama: "The owner [is established] through inheritance, purchase, and partition" (GDh 10.39), etc., which was said to be untenable—[that objection is refuted by the above].

That is not so. Since it is established that ownership (*svatva*) arises from worldly means such as acceptance (*pratigraha*), the scripture serves the purpose of restricting those means for Brāhmaṇas and others. As for what was said—that one should not say "the property of another was taken away by me"—that is incorrect, because a doubt regarding ownership can indeed arise from a doubt concerning the purchase or other transactions that constitute the cause of ownership. Furthermore, as for the statement, "He who [takes from] one who takes what is not given" [YDh 2.165], the objection that it is illogical to prescribe a punishment for one who acquires wealth through officiating at sacrifices and so forth from a person who takes what is not given, is also incorrect. This is because ownership is worldly in nature, being restricted to specific means such as acceptance; therefore, the prescription of punishment for one who acquires wealth by transgressing those restrictions is entirely appropriate. The same applies to the injunction for penance: "They are purified by its renunciation. Thus, since ownership is worldly, wealth acquired through improper acceptance and the like becomes the property of the son and others by way of inheritance (*dāya*); they do not incur the fault [of their father].

For it is stated in the Smṛti of Manu: "There are seven righteous means of acquiring wealth: inheritance, gain, purchase, victory, investment, the application of labor, and the acceptance of gifts from the virtuous" (MDh 10.115).

This must be considered here: does ownership arise from partition, or is there partition of what is already one’s own? On this point, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: If ownership arises from partition, then since property is common to all sons by the very fact of their birth, the injunction regarding the father’s entitlement to perform rites such as the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration), which require material wealth, would not apply. Furthermore, that which is given to a wife by her husband out of affection remains hers even after he has died.

"She may eat or give away as she pleases, with the exception of immovable property. Thus, even the statement regarding a gift out of affection would be inconsistent. Furthermore: "The father is the master of all gems, pearls, corals, and so forth."
But for all immovable property, there is neither a father nor a grandfather [as a legal owner].
By the favor of the father, garments and ornaments are enjoyed;
however, immovable property should not be enjoyed even when there is paternal favor.
Thus, that refers to immovable property acquired by the grandfather; therefore, ownership arises either from the destruction of the owner or from partition, and not merely from birth.

The established conclusion (*rāddhānta*), however, is as follows: ownership by birth alone is well-known in the world. Furthermore, the term "partition" (*vibhāga*) is commonly used in the world with reference to wealth belonging to multiple owners; it does not refer to the wealth of another person, nor to property that has been abandoned. Moreover, from the statement of Gautama, "By virtue of birth alone, one acquires ownership of property—so say the Teachers," it is understood that ownership arises through birth itself. As for the claim that the statement beginning with "gems, pearls, and coral" refers to immovable property acquired by a grandfather, that is incorrect. Because of the statement, "Neither the father nor the grandfather [may give it away]," this injunction—that even the wealth earned by a grandfather must not be given away while his son and grandson are living—implies that ownership arises through birth. Furthermore, the claim that in matters to be accomplished through wealth, such as the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*), the father lacks authority, is also incorrect, because authority is understood precisely from the scriptural text itself. And as for the claim that if ownership arose solely through birth, the statement of Viṣṇu—"What is given by a husband who is pleased," etc.—would be untenable, that too is incorrect; for even though the property is common to all, the father’s authority to give it as a gift of affection is established by the text itself. However, in the case of immovable property and the like, even if it was self-acquired, there is indeed dependence upon the sons and others.
Neither the gift nor the sale of immovable property, nor even of bipeds, may be made— even if acquired by oneself— without having assembled all the sons.
Those who have been born, those yet unborn, and those dwelling in the womb— all of them desire a livelihood, but not through giving or selling.

Because of such statements as these. However, in times of distress and the like, there is indeed independence [of action]: "Even a single person may perform giving, mortgaging, or selling of immovable property in a time of distress for the sake of the family, and especially for the sake of dharma."
Because of this traditional authority (*smaraṇa*), it is well said that ownership arises by birth alone. Let us return to the subject at hand. Yājñavalkya also states another time for partition:
"If the father should effect a partition, he may divide the sons according to his will;
[he may give] the eldest an excellent share, or all may be equal sharers" (YDh 2.114).

When the father desires to make a partition, he may then divide the sons from himself according to his will. The manner of division according to will is expressed by the words "or the eldest with an excellent share. An "excellent share" refers to a preferential share (*uddhāra*); the method for such a preferential share is shown in another *smṛti*:

[486] “The eldest shall receive a twentieth part as his preferential share (*uddhāra*) from all the property, as well as whatever is best; half of that shall belong to the middlemost, and a fourth to the youngest. (MDh 9.112). Alternatively: all sons, beginning with the eldest, should be made sharers of equal portions. Furthermore, an unequal division applies only to property acquired by an individual himself. However, in the case of property inherited through succession, there should be an equal share for all, because they possess equal ownership; for an unequal division by the father’s mere wish is improper. Nārada also speaks of another occasion [for such a division].
After this, the sons shall divide the father’s wealth equally,
once the mother’s menses have ceased and her daughters have been given away in marriage.
Or even when the father has ceased from dalliance and his desire has subsided.

[487] Thus says Śaṅkha: "The division of the inheritance takes place even against the father's will when he is aged, mentally deranged, or afflicted by a chronic illness. The meaning of this is as follows: when the father—though unwilling to divide the estate—is excessively old, mentally deranged (that is, not in his natural state), or afflicted by a chronic illness (meaning seized by an incurable disease), the division occurs solely by the will of the sons. The mention of a "chronic illness" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for one who is excessively angry and so forth. For this very reason, Nārada says: "One who is diseased, one who is angry, and one whose mind is attached to sensual objects..."
"And one who acts otherwise than the scripture does not have authority over the partition. Regarding the specific rule for making equal divisions by the father, Yājñavalkya says:
"If he should make equal shares, the wives must be made sharers of equal portions."
"Those women to whom no woman’s property (*strīdhana*) has been given by their husband or by their father-in-law... (YDh 2.115).

If the father, of his own free will, makes his sons equal sharers, then the wives who have not been given woman’s property must also be made sharers of portions equal to those of the sons. But when woman’s property has been given, according to the rule, "But when it is given, one should assign half," (YDh 2.148), they become entitled to half a share of the sons' portion. Prajāpati states that after the father's death, a partition should be made for the sake of increasing merit (*dharma*).
"Thus they may live together or separately out of a desire for dharma; dharma increases through separation; therefore, separation is consistent with dharma. (MDh 9.111). Bṛhaspati also says:
"For those living together with a single cooking fire, the worship of the ancestors, the gods, and the twice-born shall be one;
for those who are divided, that same worship shall be performed in every individual household.
Thus [it is said]. Yājñavalkya states the rule regarding the method of division after the death of the parents:
[489] "After the death of their parents, the sons shall divide the inheritance and the debt equally.

(YDh 2.117) Now, one might object: even regarding division after the death of the parents, an unequal division has been shown by Manu; for, having begun with the words, "After the death of the father and the mother" (MDh 9.104), he states:
"The eldest alone shall take the paternal wealth in its entirety..."
The remaining [sons] should depend upon him just as they would upon their father.
"The eldest shall receive a twentieth part as an additional share (*uddhāra*) and whatever is the best among all the goods;
half of that shall belong to the middle son, and a fourth to the youngest.
Likewise:
If the portion for extraction has not been extracted from them, this distribution of shares shall apply:
the eldest son shall take one share in excess, and the younger brother half as much more than that.
"The younger brothers shall each receive their respective shares; such is the established rule of Dharma. (MDh 9.105, 112, 116–27)

Gautama also states: "A twentieth part of the eldest’s share consists of a pair [of animals], a chariot yoked with two animals from both sides, and a bull; for the middle son, a one-eyed, lame, hornless, or tailless animal, provided there are several; for the youngest, a sheep, grain, iron, a house, a yoke for a cart, and one of each kind of four-footed animal; all other property shall be divided equally. (GDh 28.5–8). This is the meaning: from the entire paternal estate, a twentieth part belongs to the eldest. A "pair" refers to a well-known pair of cattle. "Yoked on both sides" refers to horses, mules, and donkeys; a chariot yoked with either of these as available. "Lame" means old. "Hornless" means lacking horns. "Tailless" means one whose tail has been cut off. Since no specific distinction is made regarding cows, horses, and so forth, a choice of one or the other from among them should be made as the preferential share (*uddhāra*) for the middle son. For the youngest, however, the preferential share consists of grain such as rice, iron, a cart-yoke, and one of each type of four-footed animal, such as cows and the like, taken individually and in order. Bṛhaspati also says:
"One who is senior by reason of birth, learning, or virtues shall receive two shares of the inheritance. Thus [says Manu]. Kātyāyana also says:
"In whatever manner the wealth obtained through partition may serve the purpose of sacrifice..."
In such a manner should the experts ensure the dignity of the portions.

[491] Thus. Even regarding the division during one's lifetime, an unequal division has been stated by Nārada: "Or the father himself, established in old age, may divide his sons, giving the eldest a superior share, according as his mind may so desire."

But for those who have been divided by the father himself with shares of wealth that are equal, deficient, or excessive, that very same rule shall apply; for the father is the master of all. When dividing [the estate] among himself, the father shall receive two shares.

[492] Thus says Bṛhaspati as well: "The shares which have been assigned by the father, whether equal, deficient, or excessive, must be maintained exactly as they were; otherwise, those sons would be subject to correction."
Therefore, since there is an unequal division both in the case of a living father and in the case of one who is deceased, how can it be enjoined that "sons shall divide [the estate] equally"?

Not so. It is true that, according to the scriptures, an unequal division exists; nevertheless, because it is loathed by the world, it is not practiced—just like the immolation of the *anubandhyā* cow and other such acts. And it has been said by the author of the *Saṃgraha*:
"Just as this practice of *niyoga* [is forbidden], or even the slaughter of the *anubandhyā* cow."
Likewise, even the distribution of the Uddāras does not exist at present.

[493] Thus says Āpastamba as well: having first set forth his own view, “One who is alive shall divide the inheritance among his sons equally” (ĀpDh 2.6.14.1), he then introduces the view of certain authorities (eke) regarding the eldest son’s taking of the entire estate: “The eldest is the heir” (ĀpDh 2.6.14.6). He further demonstrates the method of preferential allotment (*uddhāra-vibhāga*) according to the same authorities: “In a specific region, gold, black cows, and black land belong to the eldest; the chariot, the father’s personal effects, and the household utensils [belong to him]; the ornaments and the wife’s paternal property [belong to her], so say some” (ĀpDh 2.6.14.7–9). However, he rejects this with the statement: “That is prohibited by the scriptures” (ĀpDh 2.6.14.10). He himself demonstrates that scriptural prohibition: “It is heard in the Veda without qualification that ‘Manu divided the inheritance among his sons’” (ĀpDh 2.6.14.11). [494] Therefore, although unequal division is established by certain texts, it should not be practiced because it contradicts common worldly practice and contradicts the Veda. Thus, the rule that one should divide it “equally” alone is consistent.

Yājñavalkya states that because he is himself capable of acquiring wealth, the partition of the paternal estate must be carried out by giving him some small portion even against his will, in order to prevent his sons and others from desiring to take the inheritance: "For one who is capable but does not desire [it], a separate allotment should be made after giving him something" (YDh 2.116). Furthermore, the partition of the mother's property among sons should be understood to apply only in the absence of daughters; and so says that same author:
"The daughters of the mother [inherit] the remainder; after them, the lineage [inherits] from the debt. (YDh 2.117)

The daughters shall divide the mother’s property remaining after the discharge of debts incurred by the mother. From this, it is understood by implication that if the mother’s property is equal to or less than the debts she contracted, the sons alone shall divide it, even when daughters are present. Regarding this, Gautama has shown a distinction: “The woman’s property belongs to the unmarried and the unsettled daughters” (GDh 28.24). This means that when there is a combination of married and unmarried daughters, the mother’s property goes to the unmarried ones alone; and even among the married, when there is a combination of wealthy and indigent daughters, it goes to the indigent ones alone. Yājñavalkya states a specific rule regarding the division of the grandfather’s property among grandsons:
"But for those who have many fathers, the allotment of shares is according to the father" (YDh 2.120).

This means that when brothers who are undivided from their father die after having begotten sons—where one has two sons, another three, and another four—the grandsons obtain, in the paternal estate, one share each; even though by birth alone their ownership is no different from that of their fathers, nevertheless, two [grandsons] receive one share of their father's portion, three [grandsons] receive one, and four [grandsons] also receive one. Having this very point in mind, Bṛhaspati also says:
"His sons, whether equal or unequal [in number], are declared to be the takers of the father's share.

This means that the sons of those whose fathers have died—whether they be equal (the same number) or unequal (fewer or more in number)—each receive their own respective paternal share. When, between two brothers who were undivided, one brother has died and his son has not yet received a share even from the grandfather, and the grandfather himself is no longer living, then Kātyāyana says: "When a younger brother has died while undivided, his son is the heir to the inheritance."
One should earn one's livelihood by means other than what has been inherited from one's grandfather.
He shall receive his paternal share from his uncle or from that uncle's son;
for according to the law, that very share belongs equally to all the brothers.
"Or his son may obtain it; thereafter there shall be cessation.

The meaning of "or his son may obtain it" is this: even the son of that grandson—who is the owner of the divisible property—may obtain his father’s share in the absence of the father; beyond that, there is a cessation of the division of the great-grandfather’s wealth within that lineage. And so says Devala:
"Among kinsmen who are undivided or divided, living together..."
The established rule is that there may be a further division of inheritance up to the fourth generation.
"Until then, the lineages shall be sapinda; beyond that, there is a division of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa).
Regarding the inquiry as to how the division of the grandfather’s wealth occurs for one whose father is still living—namely, with whom [the son] shares it—Bṛhaspati says:
"In property acquired by the grandfather, whether movable or immovable..."
"For equality of ownership between father and son has indeed been declared.
Yājñavalkya also says:
"Land acquired by the grandfather, or a fixed tenure (*nibandha*), or even property..."
"In that case, there would be equal ownership for both the father and the son. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.121)

* Bhū* refers to fields of rice and the like. *Nibandha* is defined as follows: for one bundle of leaves there are so many leaves, and likewise for one bundle of betel nuts there are so many betel nuts, and so forth. *Dravya* refers to gold, silver, and the like, which have been acquired by the father through gifts, victory, or other means; in such cases, the ownership of both father and son is well-known in the world, and thus a partition exists. Since the ownership is similar—that is, equal—therefore, partition does not occur solely by the father’s wish, nor does the father receive two shares. Consequently, the rule that "the allotment of shares is according to the father" is a mere textual convention (*vācanika*), even though ownership is equal. Therefore:

"The father, dividing [the estate], may adopt the twenty-second [share for himself]"—such passages establish that an unequal division was prescribed for other *yugas*, or they refer to property acquired by the father himself. However, regarding ancestral (*paitāmaha*) wealth, there is nowhere an unequal division. Likewise, it is understood that when ancestral property is being given away or sold by an undivided father, the grandson also possesses the right to object. Furthermore, even regarding property acquired by the grandfather, in some cases a division occurs according to the father's wish alone, as if it were his own self-acquired property; thus says Manu:

"But whatever paternal property a father may acquire that was previously unobtained, he need not share that with his sons if he so desires, for it is self-acquired. (MDh 9.209) This means that if a father recovers ancestral property that had been seized by someone, he need not divide it with his sons against his will, as if it were his own acquisition. Thus, it is stated that regarding property acquired by the grandfather, there is no division according to the father's own will. Bṛhaspati also says:

"That which was seized from the grandfather, that which was acquired by the father through his own power, and that which was obtained through learning, valor, and so forth— in these cases, the ownership of the father is declared. Thus says Kātyāyana as well.
"Property recovered by one's own effort and whatever may have been acquired by oneself—all this, the father shall not be compelled by his sons to divide.

This means that whatever was seized by others and recovered by one's own effort, whatever ancestral property was lost and recovered by one's own effort, and whatever was earned by oneself through learning, valor, and so forth—all that the father need not give to the sons at the time of partition; such is the meaning. Yājñavalkya states the method for calculating the share of a son born after the time of partition:

[499] "A son born after the partition of the estate from a wife of equal caste is entitled to a share. (YDh 2.122). This is the meaning: a son born from a wife of equal caste (*savarṇā*) after the sons have been divided inherits a portion of the parents' property; thus he is called "one entitled to a share" (*vibhāgabhāk*). Furthermore, regarding the mother's share, since it has been stated that "in her absence, the inheritance goes to the offspring" (*tābhya ṛte 'nvayaḥ*, YDh 2.117), this applies when there is no daughter. However, one born from a wife of unequal caste (*asavarṇā*) receives only his own share from the paternal estate, but the entire maternal share. For this very reason, Manu says:
"But the wealth that arises after the partition belongs only to the father. (MDh 9.216) "Belonging to the parents" means *pitryam*;
those born before the partition have no authority over the share of the parents, whereas those born after the partition [have authority] over the brothers' share.

Thus it is stated in the Smṛti. One born before the partition of the estate between the mother and father is not an owner, because he was previously divided from the father. And the meaning is that one born after partition is not an owner of the brother’s wealth. However, property acquired by the father himself after the time of partition belongs solely to the one born after that partition. And so Manu says:

"Whatever has been acquired by the father himself after being divided from his sons—all that is declared to belong to the one born after partition; the earlier-born sons are held to have no ownership."
Manu states that for those who were previously divided but later reunited with their father, there is a subsequent partition with the son born after that time of reunion:
"Or he should divide with those who may have been reunited with him" (MDh 9.216).
Yājñavalkya states the rule for the allotment of shares to a son born after the partition of the estate while the father was still living:
"Or his share may be determined from what is visible, after deducting income and expenses" (YDh 2.122).

This means that when the father has died and the brothers are in the process of partition, if the mother is pregnant with an unmanifested fetus, the share for the child born after the brothers' partition must be given; having set aside a portion equal to his own share from the wealth already taken by the brothers—which is "visible," meaning its quantity has been ascertained through the increase or decrease resulting from income and expenses, and from which income and expenses have been deducted.

This should also be understood to apply to the wife of a deceased brother who was not clearly pregnant at the time of partition; even for a son born after the partition, the same rule holds. However, if she was clearly pregnant, the partition must be performed only after waiting for her delivery, because of the traditional teaching of Vasiṣṭha: "Now, regarding the partition of inheritance among brothers, those women who are childless [shall have their shares withheld] until the birth of a son" (VaDh 17.40–41). Yājñavalkya states that when property is given by the parents to those who have already been partitioned, there is no right for the son born after partition (*vibhaktaja*) to prohibit such a gift, nor should what has been given by him be reclaimed.
"Whatever has been given by both parents to anyone shall belong to that person alone. (YDh 2.123).
Regarding the allotment of a share for the mother in a partition made while she is still living, Yājñavalkya says:
"When those who divide [the estate] after the father's death, the mother also shall take an equal share. (YDh 2.123).

And this should be understood to apply when the woman’s property (*strīdhana*) has not been given; however, if it has been given, she receives only half, according to the traditional law (*smṛti*): "But if it has been given, she takes a half-share" (YDh 2.148). For this very reason, another *smṛti* states: "If a mother possesses no separate property, she shall take an equal share at the partition by the sons. The meaning is that a mother who lacks her own separate property—that is, one who is devoid of individual *strīdhana*—shall take a share equal to that of the sons when the partition is being made. The mention of the term "mother" is intended to include stepmothers and others by way of illustration. Thus says Vyāsa:
"But the wives of the father who have no sons are declared to receive equal shares;
and all those paternal grandmothers are declared to be equal to mothers.
As for what has been stated by some—that "the mother also takes an equal share" means that the mother takes only so much wealth as is necessary for her maintenance—[that is incorrect].
That is not so, because it would follow that the words "part" (*aṃśa*) and "equal" (*sama*) would be meaningless.

If it were argued that [the rule] applies when there is much wealth, taking what is necessary for subsistence, whereas when there is little wealth, the sons take equal shares—that too is not correct, because it would result in an inconsistency of injunctions (*vidhivaiṣamya*). Vyāsa states the method of partition for those of the same caste (*savarṇa*) born of different mothers who are equal in number:
"Those sons who are born of one [father] but have mothers of the same caste and number,
for them the share of the mother is recommended.
Thus says Bṛhaspati as well.
"If many [sons] are born of one [mother] and are equal in the number of their birth-order,
they shall divide their own property according to the mother's share, in accordance with the law.
Regarding the division of those who are of unequal numbers, he says the same:
"The division among those [sons] who possess the same caste, gender, and number is recommended.
Thus [it is said]. Yājñavalkya states the method of division for sons of different castes:
"The sons born of a Brāhmaṇa [father] shall have shares of four, three, two, and one, according to their respective castes."
Those born of the Kṣatriya caste receive three, two, or one shares, while those born of the Vaiśya caste receive two or one shares. (YDh 2.125)

[504] Thus: Sons born to Brāhmaṇas from women of the various castes—specifically those born to a Brāhmaṇa from women of the Brāhmaṇa and other castes—are the Brāhmaṇa, the Mūrdhāvasikta, the Ambaṣṭha, and the Niṣāda. Respective shares for each of these shall be four, three, two, and one parts. Those born to a Kṣatriya from women of the Kṣatriya and other castes—the Kṣatriya, the Māhiṣya, and the Ugra—receive three, two, and one parts respectively. From a Vaiśya, sons born to a Vaiśya and a Śūdra woman are the Vaiśya and the Karaṇa, who receive two and one parts respectively. Since a Śūdra has only one wife, there is no son of a different caste; therefore, for his sons, there is only the single division previously mentioned. Manu also says:
If a Brāhmaṇa has four wives in the direct order [of castes],
this is the rule recorded for the partition when sons have been born to them.
[505] From the inheritance, the son of a Brāhmaṇa shall take three parts; the son of a Kṣatriya woman, two parts;
the son born of a Vaiśya woman, one and a half parts; and the son of a Śūdra woman shall take one part.
Or, having divided the entire collection of inherited property into ten parts,
one who knows the Dharma should make a righteous partition according to this rule.
"A Brahmin son shall take four shares; the son of a Kṣatriya woman, three shares;

the son of a Vaiśya woman shall take two shares; and the son of a Śūdra woman shall take one share. (MDh 9.149, 151–53). And this refers specifically to land obtained through gift (*pratigraha*), excluding [land acquired by] conquest. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says:
"Land acquired through acceptance as a gift (pratigraha) must not be given to the son of a Kṣatriya or others;
even if their father should give it, upon his death, the son of the Brāhmaṇa wife shall take it.

By the force of this qualification "through acceptance," land obtained by purchase and other means certainly belongs even to the sons of Kṣatriyas and others, and this is also because of the specific prohibition regarding the son of a Śūdra wife.
"One born to a Śūdra woman by men of the twice-born castes does not deserve a share of the land. As for the statement of Manu:
"The son of a Śūdra woman by Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya is not an heir to the estate."

"Whatever his father might give him, that alone shall be his wealth" (MDh 9.155). This is not contradictory, as it refers to a situation where there is property given out of affection (*prītidatta*). Devala states the manner of inheriting the estate for a single son born in the direct order of castes (*ānulomya*): "But a single son born in the direct order shall be the recipient of the entire property."
And this refers to cases other than the Niṣāda. For this very reason, it was stated by that same author:
"But if there is a Niṣāda who is the only son, he shall take the third share of the Brāhmaṇa's property;
however, two [others], namely a sapinda or a sakulya, shall take the property intended for the svadhā offering."
As for the statement of Manu:
"Whether he has a virtuous son or even if he be sonless, one should not, according to the law, give more than a tenth part to the son of a Śūdra woman. (MDh 9.154)

This refers to the case of a son born to a Śūdra woman by a Śūdra who is unwilling to serve [his father]. A single son born to a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya by a Śūdra woman shall take only half [of the estate], and not a third share like a Niṣāda. Thus says Viṣṇu: “Among the twice-born, a Śūdra son alone takes half; the disposition of the inheritance for one who has no other sons applies to that half-share. (ViDh 18.32–33). The meaning is that the other half belongs to a near sapinda relative. Regarding partition during the father's lifetime, Vyāsa states that if some brothers or sisters have not yet been initiated, their initiation must be performed by those brothers who have already been initiated.

"But those among them who have not been consecrated should be consecrated by their elder brothers from that very paternal wealth, as well as the unmarried daughters, according to the prescribed rule" (YDh 2.124).
Regarding the consecration of a sister, however, Yājñavalkya states a specific rule:
"However, those who have not been consecrated should be consecrated by the brothers who have already been consecrated;
and the sisters, having given a fourth part from their own shares," so it is said (YDh 2.124).

When brothers divide the estate after their father’s death, they must perform the *saṃskāra* rites for any brothers who have not yet been consecrated by means of the collective property. Likewise, unmarried sisters must be consecrated by giving them from their own shares a fourth part (*turīya*)—that is, one-fourth—of the share belonging to a son of the same caste as the maiden. From this it is understood that daughters also participate in the inheritance after the father’s death; for this very reason, Manu says:
"The brothers shall each separately give to the maidens their own respective shares."
"From their own respective shares, those who are unwilling to give shall be outcasts; they must pay a fourth part from each of their own portions.

(MDh 9.118) Brothers, such as Brāhmaṇas and others, should give a fourth part from each of their own shares—that is, from their respective portions—to sisters belonging to the Brāhmaṇa and other classes, according to the shares prescribed for their own caste.

This is what is meant: if someone has only a Brāhmaṇa wife, and one son and one daughter, then the paternal property shall be divided into two parts; one of those parts shall be divided into four, and a fourth part shall be given to the daughter, while the son takes the remainder. If there are two sons and one daughter, then the father's wealth shall be divided into three parts; one of those parts shall be divided into four, and a fourth part shall be given to the daughter, while the remaining portion shall be divided between the two sons and they shall take it. But if there is one son and two daughters, then the paternal wealth shall be divided into three parts; one of those parts shall be divided into four, and two parts shall be given to the two daughters, while the son takes all that remains. This same principle should be applied to brothers and sisters of the same caste, whether they are equal or unequal in number.

When there is one son of a Brāhmaṇī woman and one daughter of a Kṣatriya woman, the paternal property shall be divided into seven parts; having divided three shares belonging to the Kṣatriya son into four parts and giving one-fourth of those to the Kṣatriya daughter, the remaining portion is taken by the son of the Brāhmaṇī woman. When there are two sons of a Brāhmaṇī woman and one daughter of a Kṣatriya woman, the paternal wealth shall be divided into eleven parts; having divided three of those shares into four parts and giving one-fourth of those to the Kṣatriya daughter, the two sons of the Brāhmaṇī woman shall divide and take the remainder.

Thus, Medhātithi explains that this rule applies everywhere in cases of inequality of birth and inequality in number among brothers and sisters. This very view is also intended by the sage Vijñāneśvara. Bhāruci, however, maintains that by the term "fourth part," the wealth necessary solely for the sacrament of marriage is meant; therefore, he considers that there is no entitlement to inheritance for unmarried daughters. This is also the intention of the author of the *Candrikā*, who says: "Precisely because the taking of a share is not for the purpose of inheritance, but rather for the purpose of the sacrament of marriage. For this very reason, it was stated by Devala.

"And daughters should be given their father's property, the wealth intended for marriage. (511) Regarding this, whatever is consistent with reason should be accepted. In the case of a partition during the father's lifetime, the daughter receives exactly what the father gives her, since no specific distinction is heard in the texts. In the absence of paternal wealth, Nārada says:
"Or, if paternal property does not exist, having extracted [an amount] from his own share..."
"The purificatory rites (saṃskāras) that must necessarily be performed—here, a restriction is intended. Thus [it is said].

The sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*) for brothers and sisters, beginning with the birth-rite (*jātakarman*), must be performed by brothers who have already been consecrated, even in the absence of paternal wealth, because they are obligatory. Regarding the fact that a maiden receives her own worn ornaments and so forth at the time of the partition of the paternal estate, Śaṅkha says: "When the inheritance is being divided, the maiden indeed receives her personal ornaments, as well as wedding gifts and woman’s property (*strīdhana*). Yājñavalkya states the nature of the primary and secondary sons and the order in which they receive the inheritance.

The legitimate son (aurasa) is one born of a lawful wife; equal to him is the son of an appointed daughter (putrikāsuta). The son of the soil (kṣetraja) is one begotten by a kinsman of the same lineage (sagotra) or by another.
A son born secretly in the house is known as a *gūḍhaja* (secretly born);
one born of an unmarried girl is considered a *kānīna*, the son of his maternal grandfather.
One born of a woman who has been either unwounded or wounded is known as a *paunarbhava*.
He whom a mother or a father gives away becomes a *dattaka* son.
One who is purchased by the two [parents] is a "purchased" son; one who is sold is a "sold" son; one who is made so by himself is an "artificial" (kṛtrima) son;
one who has given himself is a "self-given" (svayandatta) son; and one conceived in the womb and taken up while pregnant is a "son received with the bride" (sahoḍhaja).

"He who is taken after being abandoned shall be an *apagiddha* son; he offers the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) and takes the share among these, each subsequent one in the absence of the preceding. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.128–32) [514].

The meaning is that among these twelve sons, in the absence of each preceding one, each subsequent one is the offerer of the *piṇḍa*—that is, the performer of the *śrāddha*—and the taker of the share—that is, the taker of the wealth. Regarding the case where a legitimate son (*aurasa*) and a daughter appointed as a son (*putrikā*) coexist, since the legitimate son alone would normally be entitled to take the wealth, Manu states an exception:
"But if a son is born after a daughter has been appointed as a *putrikā*, the division of the estate shall be equal; for there is no right of primogeniture for a woman. (MDh 9.134).

Vasiṣṭha also states an exception in one instance: "If an *aurasa* son is born after that [appointed daughter] has been accepted, the *dattaka* son shall be entitled to a fourth share. (VaDh 15.9). Kātyāyana also says:

"But when a legitimate son (aurasa) has been born, the sons—whether of the same caste (savarṇa) or of a different caste (asavarṇa)—are entitled to a fourth part, provided they receive food and clothing. Here, "of the same caste" refers to the *kṣetraja*, *dattaka*, and others; even when a legitimate son exists, they are entitled to a fourth part. "Of a different caste" refers to the *kānīna*, *gūḍhotpanna*, *sahoḍha*, and *paunarbhava* sons; when a legitimate son exists, they do not receive a fourth part, but rather obtain only food and clothing—this is the meaning. As for that which was stated by Viṣṇu:

"But those born of an unmarried girl (*kānīna*), those born in secret (*gūḍhotpanna*), those born of a woman pregnant at marriage (*sahoḍhaja*), and the son of a remarried woman (*paunarbhava*)—these are not praiseworthy; they do not share in the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) or the portion of the inheritance.
This [text] is intended solely to prohibit the fourth share when a legitimate son (*aurasa*) exists. And as for that which was stated by Manu:

"The biological son alone is the master of the paternal wealth; however, for the sake of compassion toward the others, he should provide them with a livelihood"—this statement is intended solely as praise for the biological son, and not as a prohibition against his receiving a fourth share. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of rendering the statements of Vasiṣṭha and Kātyāyana—which establish that he is entitled to a fourth share—meaningless. Furthermore, as has been stated by that very same author:
"But when dividing the paternal inheritance, the legitimate son (aurasa) should give a sixth share of the father's wealth to the son begotten on the wife (kṣetraja), or even a fifth. (MDh 9.164)

In this regard, the established rule is as follows: if [the other sons] possess extreme merit, the son of the appointed daughter (*kānīna*) receives a fourth part; if they are both hostile and devoid of merit, he receives a sixth part; and if they are merely hostile or merely devoid of merit, he receives a fifth part. As for that which was stated by Hārīta: “[When about to divide the estate], one should give a twenty-first part to the *kānīna*, a twentieth to the son of a remarried woman (*paunarbhava*), a nineteenth to the son of two fathers (*dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa*), an eighteenth part to the son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*), a seventeenth part to the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*), and the remainder to the legitimate son of the body (*aurasa*]”—this refers to the case of sons who are of a different caste or lack merit. As for that which was stated by Manu...
The legitimate son of the body, the son begotten on the wife, the adopted son, the made son, the son secretly born, and the cast-off son— these six are both heirs and kinsmen.

The son of an unmarried woman, the son received with a bride, the purchased son, the son of a remarried woman, the self-given son, and the Śūdra-born son—these six are kinsmen who do not inherit. (MDh 9.159–60)

Having thus stated the two groups of six, it was declared that the first group of six constitutes *dāyāda-bāndhavas* (heirs and kinsmen), while the latter group of six constitutes *adāyāda-bāndhavas* (non-heirs but kinsmen). This should be explained as follows: when there is *sapiṇḍa* relationship with one's own father, and in the absence of any other nearer heirs who take the inheritance, those in the first group of six inherit that property, whereas for the latter group of six, that does not exist. Furthermore, their status as *bāndhavas*—meaning they perform duties such as the offering of water (*udaka*)—is equal for both groups of six by virtue of having the same *gotra* or being *sapiṇḍas*. However, the taking of the paternal wealth belongs to all of them indeed, provided each preceding person is absent.

"Neither brothers nor fathers, but sons are the heirs of the father" (MDh 9.185). Since Manu has thus established that all substitutes for a son—excluding the *aurasa* (legitimate son)—are entitled to inherit the estate, the *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa* (son of two fathers) shares the inheritance of his progenitor as well. Accordingly, Yājñavalkya states:
"A son begotten by appointment (*niyoga*) upon the wife of another by one who is childless..."
"He is, according to the law, the heir and the giver of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) to both.

(Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.127) When one such as a brother-in-law (*devara*), being authorized by his teacher or others, himself childless, engages in the field of a childless man for the sake of obtaining a son for himself and another, the son he procreates belongs to two fathers and is *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa*; he is the heir and the giver of the funeral cake to both. However, when one who already has sons produces a son in the field of another solely for the sake of another's son, that son born belongs only to the owner of the field (*kṣetrin*), not to the owner of the seed (*bījin*). As it has been stated by Manu:
When a field is given for the sake of seed because of an agreement on the labor,
both the owner of the seed and the owner of the field are seen here as sharers of the crop.

But when the fruit is not intended by either the owner of the field or the sower of the seed, the benefit belongs clearly to the owners of the field; the womb is more powerful than the seed. (MDh 9.53, 52)

[519] Thus. This is its meaning: Having made an agreement that "the offspring born here shall belong to both," when a field is given by the owner to the sower for the purpose of sowing seed, the offspring born in that field has both the sower and the owner of the field as its owners. However, when an offspring is produced in another's field by the sower without having made an agreement that "the offspring born there shall belong to us both," that offspring belongs to the owner of the field alone, not to the sower; for the womb is more powerful than the seed, as is observed in the case of cows, horses, and so forth—this is the meaning. Furthermore, the appointment (*niyoga*) of a preceptor and others applies only to the case of a girl betrothed in word (*vāgdattā*), because any other form of *niyoga* has been prohibited by Manu.
When the lineage is on the verge of extinction, a woman who has been duly authorized by her husband or by a sapinda relative may obtain the desired offspring.

"But one appointed to a widow, anointed with clarified butter and restrained in speech, shall procreate only one son at night, and never a second. Once a son has been produced through such appointment, she remains a widow as before. (MDh 9.59–60)
Having thus proposed the practice of *niyoga*, Manu himself prohibits it:
"A widow must not be appointed to another man by members of the twice-born classes;
for those who appoint her to another would destroy the eternal Dharma."
Nowhere in the mantras pertaining to marriage is the practice of *niyoga* (appointment) mentioned;
nor, furthermore, is the remarriage of a widow prescribed in the rules for wedding ceremonies.
Indeed, this practice, which is a law fit for beasts, was censured by learned twice-born men even when it was prescribed for human beings while Vena was ruling the kingdom.
[520] In former times, that foremost of royal sages, while ruling over the entire earth,
brought about the intermixture of the social orders, his mind being struck down by lust.
"From that time forward, the virtuous censure anyone who, out of delusion, appoints a woman whose husband has died to produce offspring through *niyoga*. (MDh 9.64–68) [521] Thus it is said.

[Objection: But surely, let there be an option here, since both injunction and prohibition are observed; therefore, it is untenable that the *niyoga* (levirate union) has as its object a woman already betrothed (*vāgdattā*) and so forth. [Reply:
No, because Manu himself establishes that *niyoga* has such women as its object:
"If the husband of a maiden should die after the betrothal has been made true..."
Her husband's younger brother shall take her for himself according to this procedure.

"Having approached her according to the prescribed rule—she who is clad in white garments and pure in her vows—the husband and wife should enjoy each other once during each fertile period until conception. (MDh 9.69–69).
For those such as the *dattaka* (adopted son) and others, there is no entitlement to the inheritance based on the seed (*bīja*). And so says Manu:

[522] “The adopted son (dattima) shall not share in the lineage (gotra) or the inheritance (ṛktha) of his biological father; the funeral cake (piṇḍa) follows the lineage and inheritance, and the ancestral offering (svadhā) ceases for one who gives him away. (MDh 9.142).

The mention of the "adopted son" (dattima) is intended to include the "bought son" (krīta) by implication. Statements establishing that other secondary sons (gauṇaputra) are entitled to inherit pertain to other ages (yugāntara), because in the Kali age, their formal adoption as sons is prohibited by another Smṛti text.
The adoption of sons other than the *datta* and *aurasa*,
the procreation of offspring by a brother-in-law (*devara*), and the undertaking of the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) stage of life [are forbidden].
"In the Kali age, however, the wise declare these duties to be abandoned.
