Regarding the specific rules for the distribution of a Śūdra's wealth, Yājñavalkya says:
"Even one born of a Śūdra’s slave woman shall, if born of desire, be a sharer of the inheritance."
When the father has died, the brothers shall make him a recipient of half a share.
One who has no brother shall take the entire estate, except for the son of the daughters.

[523] Thus: he receives a share by the will of the father. If the father has died and there are brothers who have sons from wives of equal status, then they shall make the son of the slave-girl a recipient of half a share from their own respective portions. If, however, there are no daughters from wives of equal status, nor their sons, then the son of the slave-girl receives that wealth; if such [heirs] exist, he receives only half. But a son born to the twice-born from a slave-girl does not receive a share even by the will of the father, nor half, much less the whole; for there is the specific qualification [in the law]: "even one born to a Śūdra from a slave-girl. The intention is that if he is well-behaved, he receives merely enough for his subsistence. Yājñavalkya states the order of succession for the inheritance of one who dies without a son:
The wife, the daughters, the parents, the brothers, as well as their son,
a kinsman of the same lineage, a relative, a pupil, and fellow students.
"In the absence of these, each subsequent one among the preceding becomes the heir to the wealth.
This rule applies to all castes regarding one who has died without a son. (YDh 2.135–36)

One who has no twelve kinds of sons, beginning with the *aurasa* (legitimate son born of one’s own body), is "sonless. Upon his death, his wealth is taken by the wife and the others, each succeeding one taking it in the absence of each preceding one. This sequence for the inheritance of property is to be understood as applying to all [sons], from the *mūrdhāvasikta* and others born in the direct order (*anuloma*), as well as to the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa. The "wife" (*patnī*) is a woman consecrated by the marriage rites and other ceremonies; she takes her husband's wealth first. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says: "While kinsmen—fathers, brothers, and blood relations—are present..."
"The wife of one who has died without a son shall be the taker of his wealth.
Regarding this, Vṛddha-Manu states a specific rule:
"A sonless widow, preserving the bed of her husband and remaining steadfast in her vows..."

"The wife alone shall give that funeral cake (piṇḍa) and receive the entire share. By "entire share" is meant the whole property consisting of both movable and immovable assets. Thus, this is the order of succession for the inheritance of one who dies without any of the twelve kinds of sons: the wife takes the wealth of the deceased who is devoid of these twelve types of sons. And so says Prajāpati: "Movable property, immovable property, gold, base metals, grain, and clothing..."
Having taken [the materials], one should cause the śrāddha for the month, the year, and so forth to be offered.

"One should honor paternal uncles, preceptors, daughters' sons, the husband's father, the mother's father, maternal uncles, as well as elders and guests, with offerings to the ancestors (kavya) and works of public utility (pūrta).
In their absence, daughters—both those of the same caste and those of a different caste—shall take [the property] according to their respective shares. And so says Bṛhaspati:
A wife is considered the husband’s heir to his wealth; without her, there is no daughter. From every limb of man, a daughter is born just like a son.
"A virtuous woman, similar [in quality] and wedded to one similar [to herself], is devoted to service;
therefore, how could another man take the paternal wealth?
Thus [it is said]. Regarding the case where a married daughter and an unmarried daughter are present together, Kātyāyana says:
A wife who is unfaithful to her husband shall not be the heir to his wealth;
in her absence, however, it shall be the daughter, provided she be unmarried.

[525] Thus it is said. Even among married daughters, when there is a combination of both those who are established and those who are not established, only the one who is not established receives [the inheritance]. To this effect says Gautama: "The property of a woman belongs to her daughters who are unmarried and those who are not established" (GDh 28.24). Nor should it be thought that this statement of Gautama refers exclusively to the mother's wealth, for it applies equally to the father's wealth as well. In the absence of a daughter, the daughter’s son (dauhitra) is the heir to the wealth. And so says Viṣṇu: "In the absence of a line of sons and grandsons, the daughter’s sons shall obtain the wealth."
"But for the ancestors, the daughter's son is considered equal to the grandson in the offering of *svadhā*. So also Manu:
"Whether she has been formally appointed (*akṛtā*) or not, the son whom she bears from a husband of equal status..."
The maternal grandfather is the grandson’s [heir]; he shall offer the funeral cake and take the wealth. (MDh 9.136)

[526] Thus it is said. Nor should it be thought that the mention of "the parents" immediately after "the daughters" is untenable, because the son of the daughter (*dauhitra*) ought to be mentioned as the heir to the wealth. For by the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and the daughters," there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*); thus, in the absence of a son of the daughter, the parents are the heirs to the wealth. Although no specific order for the parents' succession to the wealth is heard here, some say that since the word "mother" (*mātṛ*) is placed first in the analytical compound (*vigrahavākya*) of "parents" (*pitarau*), and due to the greater proximity [of the mother], it is proper that the mother alone should take the wealth first. Others, however, maintain that the wealth of one who dies without a son goes first to the wife, in her absence to the daughter, in her absence to the father, and in his absence to the mother, based on the statement of Vṛddha-Viṣṇu: "The wealth of one who dies without a son goes to the wife; in her absence, it goes to the daughter; in her absence, it goes to the father; in his absence, it goes to the mother."
Now, for one who has no son, a wife of noble birth or even daughters [are entitled];
in their absence, the father, the mother, the brother, and the son are declared [to be the heirs].

And from the statement of Kātyāyana: “They say that the father alone is the first to take the wealth; what is stated in this regard should be accepted. In the absence of the parents, the brothers are the sharers of the wealth. Likewise, Manu says:
“The father shall take the inheritance of one who has no son, and so too the brothers” (MDh 9.185).
Among the brothers as well, uterine brothers are the first to share the wealth because of their proximity. For this very reason, Manu says:
"The wealth of each shall belong to the nearest sapinda relative of that person. (MDh 9.187)

In the absence of brothers, it should be understood as before that the sons of the brothers [succeed]. Even when brothers and the sons of brothers coexist, there is no connection to the wealth for the sons of the brothers, because the entitlement of the sons of the brothers is heard [in the texts] only upon the absence of the brothers. However, when a brother dies childless and the connection to his wealth has arisen for his [other] brothers without distinction, if some brother should die even before the division of the brothers' wealth and his sons exist, then since those sons would have obtained an entitlement through their father, a division between them and the brothers is appropriate. In the absence of the sons of the brothers, the *gotraja* (members of the same lineage) take the wealth. The *gotrajas* consist of the paternal grandmother, the *sapindas*, and the *samānodakas*; therefore, first the paternal grandmother takes the wealth. As for that which...

"Even when the mother has passed away, the father’s mother shall take the wealth" (MDh 9.217). This statement establishes that after the mother, the paternal grandmother is entitled to take the inheritance. Regarding the property of one who has died without offspring: it first goes to the wife; in her absence, to the mother; in her absence, to the brother's son; in his absence, to a *sakulya*; in his absence, to a relative (*bandhu*); in his absence, to a fellow student (*sahādhyāyin*); in his absence, the property—excluding that of a Brāhmaṇa—goes to the King; however, the property of a Brāhmaṇa should be taken by a Brāhmaṇa alone. And so it is said:
[528] Now, for one who has no son, a wife of noble birth or even daughters are mentioned;
in their absence, the father, the mother, the brother, and the sons are declared [to be the heirs].

And so forth; because this contradicts the plural number used to indicate the sequence [of heirs], it is understood that the grandmother’s claim to the property merely establishes her connection to the inheritance, rather than intending to establish a specific order of succession. In the absence of the paternal grandmother, the grandfather, the paternal uncles, and their sons take the property in that order. In the absence of the lineage of the grandfather, the paternal great-grandmother, the sons of the paternal great-grandfather, and their sons—extending thus to the seventh degree—those belonging to the same *gotra* (*gotrajāḥ*) take the property. In the absence of the *sapiṇḍas*, those entitled to the water-offering (*samānodakas*) take the property. The *samānodakas* consist of seven generations beyond the *sapiṇḍas*, or until the names and births of the ancestors can no longer be known. As it has been stated by Bṛhan-Manu:
The sapinda relationship ceases with the seventh person;
however, the status of being a samānodaka (distant kinsman) ceases with the fourteenth.
"Because of the non-remembrance of their birth, some say that [the maternal lineage] is the supreme *gotra*.
In the absence of those born of the same *gotra*, the kinsmen (*bāndhava*) take the property; and three types of kinsmen have been shown by Baudhāyana:
the sons of one's father's sister, and the sons of one's mother's sister.
One's own maternal uncles' sons should also be understood as one's own kinsmen.
The sons of one's father’s paternal aunt, the sons of one's father’s maternal aunt,
and the sons of one's father’s maternal uncle are to be known as paternal kinsmen (pitṛbāndhava).
The sons of one's mother's paternal aunt, and the sons of one's mother's maternal aunt.
The sons of one's mother's maternal uncle are to be known as the mother's kinsmen (mātṛbāndhava).
[529] Thus it is said. Even among kinsmen, he who is the nearest relative takes first. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati states:

"Where there are many cognate kinsmen (jñātayaḥ), as well as members of the same lineage (sakulyāḥ) and relatives (bāndhavāḥ), he who is the nearest among them shall take the wealth of one who has no offspring. Thus it is said.
In the absence of kinsmen, the teacher [inherits]; in the absence of a teacher, the pupil. Regarding this, Manu says:
"For whoever is next after the sapinda, his shall be the wealth;
beyond him, it shall go to a sakulya, the teacher, or even the pupil" (MDh 9.187).

Āpastamba also says: "In the absence of *sapiṇḍas*, the teacher; in the absence of the teacher, the pupil" (ĀpDh 1.6.14.3). In the absence of a pupil, a fellow student (*sabrahmacārī*); in his absence, any learned *śrotriya* takes it. Regarding this, Gautama says: "Learned *śrotriyas* shall divide the inheritance of a childless Brāhmaṇa" (GDh 28.41). In his absence, a Brāhmaṇa [takes it]. Regarding this, Manu says:
"But in the absence of all [the aforementioned], Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the three Vedas, pure and self-controlled, shall share the inheritance; thus the Dharma is not lost" (MDh 9.188).

[530] Thus, the property of a Brāhmaṇa never goes to the king; however, the property of Kṣatriyas and others goes to the king only in the absence of all heirs down to a fellow religious student (*sabrahmacārin*). As stated by Manu: "The property of a Brāhmaṇa must always be taken as non-confiscable by the king; this is the settled rule. But in the case of the other castes, the king may take the property when there is a total absence [of heirs]. (MDh 9.189)
Nārada also says: "If there is no heir whatsoever for the property of a Brāhmaṇa and that property is lost, it must be given to a Brāhmaṇa; otherwise, the king would be a sinner."
The compiler also [states]:
"Even when the father is no longer present, the wealth belongs to his paternal lineage;
when that is no longer present, it belongs to his grandfather’s lineage."
But even in the absence of that [daughter], the *sapiṇḍas* of the great-grandfather’s lineage,
starting from the next generation upward, are likewise the heirs to the estate.

In their absence, the *asapiṇḍa* relatives shall perform it, or the teacher, or even the pupil; likewise the fellow-student (*sabrahmacārī*) or a learned Brahmin (*sadvipra*); in the absence of each preceding one, each subsequent one shall do so.
"In the absence of a single heir (ekodaka) for a Śūdra, the king shall take the wealth;
likewise in the absence of a teacher, or of a Kṣatriya or Vaiśya.

Now, one might object: it is untenable that the wife takes the wealth of one who has no offspring as the very first [heir], because even when a wife exists, Nārada has stated that the brothers take the wealth or that the wives receive only maintenance.
[531] If among brothers one should die childless or should renounce the world,
the remaining brothers shall divide his property, excluding the woman's separate property (strīdhana).
"And they should provide for her maintenance until the end of her livelihood; if they preserve the bed of their husband, they should take that [property] from the others. (NSm 13.25–26)

That is not so; for, having introduced the topic with the statement, "But that which is the share of those who are reunited," the text proceeds to cite the passage beginning with, "If a brother should die childless," and so forth. From this, it is understood that by this declaration, mere maintenance is ordained for the childless wives of reunited brothers, while the inheritance of their property is established for the reunited brothers themselves. Alternatively, the passage beginning with, "If a brother should die childless," is intended as referring to those who are reunited, according to the principle:
"But that which is the share of those who are reunited, that is desired for them alone."

Because of the consequence of redundancy with the statement: "Even one who has no offspring is entitled to a share; among those without seed, the other [the husband] shall take it" (NSm 13.24). Alternatively, let the [Yājñavalkya] statement concern the case of undivided property, while the statement of Yājñavalkya intends to mean that the wife alone first takes the wealth of a husband who was divided and not reunited; thus there is no contradiction. As for that which was stated by Manu:
"The father shall take the inheritance of one who has no son, or the brothers themselves" (MDh 9.185).
Thus, as for that which was also stated by Kātyāyana:
"When [the father] has died after being divided, in the absence of sons, the father shall take the property;
or the brother, or the mother, or the mother of that [father], in due order."

Thus—the statement of Manu does not aim at establishing a specific sequence, because an option is heard in the words "or indeed the brothers"; however, the statement of Kātyāyana aims at establishing that when the wife is unchaste, the father or others shall take the wealth of the childless [husband]: "The wife who is unchaste shall be the taker of the husband's wealth;
she who is engaged in misconduct, shameless, or a destroyer of wealth [is excluded]."
And a woman who is devoted to adultery does not deserve wealth.

Because it has been stated by that very [author] thus: the meaning is that she is not entitled to the portion of land or the wealth provided for her maintenance. Dhāreśvara, however, states an alternative arrangement for the scope of such a collection of texts as "the wife takes the wealth of one who dies childless," and so forth: the wife who desires *niyoga* (levirate) takes the wealth of her husband who died childless and was previously partitioned. And so Manu says: "He who maintains the wealth or even the widow of his deceased brother shall, having procreated offspring for that brother, hand over that very wealth to him."
"If a younger brother should father a son upon the wife of the elder, the division of the estate there shall be equal; such is the established law. (MDh 9.146, 120)

When a brother has died after the property has been partitioned, the wife’s connection to the wealth occurs only through her offspring, and not otherwise; the intention is that this is likewise the case when the property was not partitioned. Gautama also states (GDh 28.21–22): “Those related by the offering of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*), by *gotra*, or by *ṛṣi* shall divide the inheritance, as shall the wife of one who has no offspring, provided she desires to obtain seed. This is the meaning: those related by the offering of the funeral cake, by *gotra*, or by *ṛṣi* shall divide the inheritance of one who has no offspring, or the wife, if she desires to obtain seed. The author of the *Saṃgraha* also says:
"When the brothers have divided [the estate], or even when they have reunited, or when they are deceased,

the wife who remains under the authority of her husband's instruction shall obtain the property. This is untenable, because the practice of *niyoga* (levirate) is not mentioned in the rule "The wife, the daughters," and so forth.
If it is argued that it is logical to postulate an injunction (niyoga), even though it is not explicitly heard [in the text], on the strength of the words of Gautama and others;

That is not so, because the statements of Gautama and others have a different meaning. To explain: regarding that statement of Gautama, “Those related by the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), by lineage (*gotra*), or by *ṛṣi* shall divide the inheritance; and the wife of one who has no offspring shall take it, or she may seek to obtain seed,” this is its meaning: if she seeks to obtain seed, then the wife takes the wealth of the childless man. However, otherwise, the wealth of one who has no offspring shall be taken by those related by the offering of rice-balls, by lineage, or by *ṛṣi*; or the wife shall take it—provided that the wife either seeks to obtain seed or remains self-restrained (*saṃyatā*). This is because the word “or” (*vā*) expresses an alternative position and is not used in the sense of a conditional “if. Furthermore, as for the statement of Manu beginning with “he who would maintain the wealth,” that too declares the connection to the wealth of the *kṣetraja* son alone, and not of the wife. Even the statement of Saṃgraha declares the connection to the wealth of only the self-restrained woman, and not of one appointed by the husband’s brother (*devara*) and so forth. Otherwise, [it would follow that...]
"The wife alone, being childless, guarding her husband’s bed and remaining steadfast in her vows,
shall offer that funeral cake (piṇḍa) and receive the entire share.
Likewise:
A childless widow, remaining faithful to her elders and protecting her husband’s bed, may live until death with self-restraint; after her passing, the heirs shall take possession of the estate.

Because this would result in a contradiction with the statements of Manu and Kātyāyana, therefore the following rule alone is superior: "The wife inherits the wealth of one who has died childless, divided [from his co-heirs], and not reunited [with them]. As for those statements establishing that women have no connection to property—such as: "Those who are not entitled to the wealth produced for the sake of sacrifice, none of them are sharers of the inheritance; they are merely entitled to food and clothing"—[these apply to a different context].
Wealth is ordained for the purpose of sacrifice; therefore, one should employ it in places approved by dharma, and not among women, fools, or those who act contrary to dharma.

Thus, that refers specifically to wealth acquired for the purpose of sacrifice. Furthermore, as stated by Kātyāyana: "The property of one who leaves no heir goes to the king, except for the wealth of a *śrotriya* and the funeral expenses for wives and servants; that [wealth of a *śrotriya*] he shall bestow upon other *śrotriyas*."

Thus—the meaning is this: setting aside what is required for the food and clothing of the women, as well as that which is required by the wealthy man for *śrāddha* rites and other such purposes, the estate of one who dies without heirs (*adāyika*) goes to the king. However, the property of a *śrotriya*, excluding what is needed for his wives, dependents, and funeral rites, belongs to the *śrotriya* and not to the king—this is the meaning. Furthermore, as stated by Nārada: "A king devoted to righteousness may take something from others, except from a *brāhmaṇa*; he should provide for the livelihood of [the *brāhmaṇa*'s] wives. This is declared to be the rule for inheritance" (NSm 13.52).

Thus, both of these [rules] refer to women who have been married, as indicated by the hearing of the word *patnī* (wife). Furthermore, that which was stated by Hārīta— “If a widow in the prime of youth becomes harsh [in disposition], then, for the sake of preserving her life, a livelihood must be provided”— [also applies to such a case].
Thus, even that refers to the case of a woman suspected of infidelity. As for the statement of Prajāpati:
"One should give an āḍhaka [of grain] to a woman deprived of her husband until the end of her life," and as for what is stated in another Smṛti:
“For the sake of food, [one should give] a *prastha* of rice along with fuel in the afternoon.

These two statements have the same meaning as the statement of Hārīta. As for the Vedic text: “Therefore women are powerless (*nirindriyāḥ*) and non-inheritors (*adāyādāḥ*),” that is intended to mean that there is no share for the wife in the *pātnīvata* cup. This is because the word *indriya* is seen to be used in reference to Soma in the passage: “The drinking of Soma is indeed the *indriya*. As for the statement of Bṛhaspati which prohibits the wife from taking immovable property—“Whatever has been ordained by law regarding acquisitions and so forth in respect of divided wealth,”... [the text continues].
Her husband's kinsmen, with the exception of her immovable property, shall receive it when she is left without a husband.

Thus, that [text] is intended to prohibit the sale of immovable property without the consent of other heirs; otherwise, [it would contradict]: "Having taken movable property, immovable property, gold, silver, grain, liquids, and clothing, one should cause the Śrāddha for the month, the year, and so forth, to be performed."

One should honor paternal uncles, preceptors, daughters' sons, the son of a husband's sister, maternal uncles, as well as elders, the protectorless, and guests, by means of offerings to the ancestors (kavya) and charitable works (pūrta).
Because this would lead to a contradiction, Manu states the method for the partition of those who have reunited after being divided:
"If those who were divided live together again and should divide once more, the division there shall be equal; in that case, the right of primogeniture does not exist. (MDh 9.210)

Since the exclusion of unequal partition is already established by the very rule prescribing equal division, the statement "seniority does not exist there" serves as a further exclusion of unequal partition for the purpose of obtaining an unequal division according to the wealth among those who have reunited with property. When it is asked with whom reunion occurs, Bṛhaspati states:
"He who, having been divided, again dwells together in one place with his father, brother, or paternal uncle out of affection—he is said to be reunited."

A son or other descendant who was previously separated from his father or others, but later reunites with him out of affection, is called *saṃsṛṣṭa* (one who has reunited). The meaning is that he has entered into a joint residence with anyone [of the family]. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati states a cause for unequal division among those who have reunited: "Among those who have reunited, whoever acquires more by means of learning, valor, or other such qualities, two shares shall be given to him; the remainder shall share equally. Thus it is said.

When wealth has been acquired through learning and other such means, two shares are to be given out of that surplus, not the whole; this is intended to establish that even property acquired without detriment to the joint estate is subject to partition. Yājñavalkya indicates the heir to the estate of a sonless reunited coparcener:

"But a reunited coparcener shall take the share of another reunited coparcener, and a uterine brother that of a uterine brother; he shall give and he shall take the share of one who is born or one who has died. (YDh 2.138)

This is the meaning: when one who was reunited in inheritance has died, another reunited kinsman shall give the share to the son born after the time of partition from a wife whose pregnancy was unknown; in the absence of such a son, the reunited kinsman alone shall take it, not the wife or others. For wives and unmarried daughters, there is only maintenance. As Nārada says: "They shall provide for his women until the end of their lives; if they preserve the bed of the husband, they shall receive it, but otherwise, that [inheritance] shall be forfeited."

"When her daughters are considered [the heirs] for the maintenance of their father's share, they shall take that portion until their marriage; thereafter, the husband shall maintain them. Regarding the rule "but a uterine brother [takes the share] of a uterine brother," this means that when a uterine brother who was a *saṃsṛṣṭin* (one reunited after partition) has died, his uterine brother shall give his share to the son born subsequently to that *saṃsṛṣṭin*. "But a uterine brother who is a *saṃsṛṣṭin* shall take the property, not a non-uterine brother even if he be a *saṃsṛṣṭin*. If among them the eldest or the youngest should be deprived of his share at the time of its distribution,

"His uterine brothers, having come together and assembled, shall divide it equally; as well as those brothers who are reunited and the uterine sisters. (MDh 9.211–12)

This is the meaning: among those reunited brothers who have different mothers, if any one—the youngest or the middlemost—should fall away from his share at the time of partition due to going to another country or other reasons, his share is not lost; it must be set aside separately. It is not the case that only the reunited brothers shall take it. Rather, having set aside that share, the uterine brothers who are not reunited, as well as the reunited brothers of different mothers, and the uterine sisters—even if they have gone to another country—must assemble together and divide it collectively, without regard for inequality of shares.
Others think that one may give even if not reunited, but one who is reunited shall not give to one born of a different mother. (YDh 2.139)

This is its meaning: where there are both reunited brothers born of different wombs and unreunited brothers born of the same womb, in that case the unreunited uterine brothers alone shall take the wealth, and not the brothers born of different wombs even if they are reunited. As for the statement of Manu beginning with "those among whom the eldest... and so forth, which establishes the right to inherit the property for all—both those born of different wombs who are reunited and those born of the same womb who are unreunited—that refers to a situation where both types of property, consisting of movable and immovable assets, exist. For this very reason, Prajāpati says:
"But whatever property is hidden shall belong to those who are reunited;
however, land and houses, those not reunited may take according to their respective shares. Thus [it is said].

The meaning is as follows: for uterine brothers who are not reunited (*asaṃsṛṣṭa*), the internal wealth, hidden wealth, or property consisting of movable assets shall be divided according to their respective shares; for those who are reunited (*saṃsṛṣṭa*), even if they are from different wombs, the immovable property such as houses and fields shall be divided according to their respective shares. As for the statement of Yājñavalkya, however, it refers to a situation where either movable or immovable property exists. In this regard, that which is logical should be accepted.

But when there is no longer a state of having separate bodies due to being reunited, then whichever father or paternal uncle was reunited shall alone take the inheritance. And so says Gautama: "When a reunited kinsman has died, the one who was reunited is the heir to the estate" (GDh 28.28).

"But when the husband has died, the wives who have no brothers, father, or mother—all the *sapiṇḍas*, such as the brothers' sons and others—shall divide the joint property according to their respective shares. This means that when the husband is deceased, all the *sapiṇḍas*—namely the brothers' sons and so forth—who are characterized by the absence of [other] brothers, fathers, or mothers [for those wives], shall divide the joint property; therein, the division of the joint wealth is such that the brothers' sons take their share from their own father, and the wives take their share from their husband. In the absence of wives, the brother's daughter takes the share belonging to the joint son. And so says Bṛhaspati:
His sister, however, deserves to receive a share from that [inheritance];
for one who is childless and lacks both a wife and a father, this is the law.

Having recited this, they say that in the absence of wives, the daughter shall take [the inheritance]. In the absence of daughters and sisters, the nearest *sapiṇḍa* or other relative shall possess the wealth of each respective person. Thus, all *sapiṇḍas* and others shall take the wealth according to the stated order of proximity, because there is no fault in such a position. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says:
"If one has died without offspring, without a wife, and without brothers, father, or mother,
all the *sapiṇḍas* shall divide that inheritance according to their respective shares.
When it is asked who takes the property of forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*), ascetics (*yati*), and lifelong celibates (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārin*), Yājñavalkya says:
"The heirs of forest-dwellers, renunciants, and students are, in order: the preceptor, the virtuous disciple, the spiritual brother, and the fellow student. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.137)

In this regard, according to the inverse order (*prātilomyakrama*), the teacher (*ācārya*) takes the wealth of lifelong celibates (*naiṣṭhikabrahmacārin*), not the father or others. The wealth of those who have returned home from studentship (*upakurvāṇaka*) is taken by the father and others alone. As for the wealth of an ascetic (*yati*), a virtuous disciple capable of hearing, retaining, and practicing the spiritual scriptures (*adhyātmaśāstra*) takes it, because one of evil conduct is unworthy of a share. The wealth of a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) is taken by a "dharma-brother" (*dharmabhrātṛ*) who shares the same sacred ford (*ekatīrthī*). A "dharma-brother" is one who has the same teacher; an "ekatīrthī" is one belonging to the same stage of life (*āśrama*). Thus, a dharma-brother who is also an ekatīrthī is called a "dharma-brother-ekatīrthī."

Alternatively: the property of forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*), ascetics (*yati*), and students (*brahmacārin*) is inherited by the teacher (*ācārya*), a virtuous disciple (*sacchiṣya*), a spiritual brother (*dharmabhrātṛ*), and a fellow student (*ekatīrthin*) respectively. The meaning is that in the absence of each preceding person, each subsequent one takes it. As for what was stated by Vasiṣṭha: “Those who have entered another stage of life (*āśrama*) are not entitled to a share” (VaDh 17.52), that is intended as a prohibition against members of one stage of life inheriting the wealth of those in a different stage of life; it is not intended as a prohibition against mutual inheritance among those in the same stage of life.

Now, one might object: these [mendicants] have no connection with wealth at all, so how could there be a partition of it? For means of acquiring wealth such as receiving gifts are forbidden for them, and because of the traditional teaching of Gautama: "A mendicant is one who has no accumulation of property" (GDh 3.11). In this regard: [there is a rule] for a day, a month, six months, or likewise for a year.
One should constantly accumulate wealth, but once it has been acquired, one should spend it in the month of Āśvayuja.
Thus, there is possession of wealth for the forest-dweller (vānaprastha).
However, the ascetic (yati) may wear even a garment for the sake of covering his private parts;
likewise, he may take up various requisites for yoga and sandals.

From such statements as these, it follows that even for an ascetic (*yati*), clothing, books, and so forth certainly exist. Since even for one who has reached the final stage of life (*naiṣṭhika*) there is indeed the acceptance of clothing and other items for the sake of bodily maintenance, the division [of inheritance] is entirely logical. Manu states those who are unworthy of inheritance:
"Those who are impotent, outcasts, those blind from birth, and likewise the deaf; those who are insane, idiotic, mute, and whoever are devoid of sense organs—these have no share. (MDh 9.201)

"Those who are without sense organs, those afflicted by disease, and those with impaired organs; Nārada also says: 'An enemy of the father, an outcast, a eunuch, and one who is born of adultery—even these do not receive a share, though they be legitimate sons (aurasa); how much less so those born of the wife (kṣetraja)?"* *N.B.: The asterisk indicates that the source text provided was incomplete.*
Vasiṣṭha also states: "But those who have entered another stage of life (āśrama) are not entitled to a share" (VaDh 17.52). Yājñavalkya says:

"The impotent, the outcaste, his offspring, the lame, the insane, the idiotic, the blind, and those afflicted with incurable diseases and the like, should be maintained but are not entitled to a share" (YDh 2.140).

"Born of that" means born of one who has fallen from caste (*patita*). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), those such as the mute and others are included. These, being without shares, do not become heirs to the estate; they are merely to be maintained—that is, nourished—by the provision of food and clothing. Regarding the sin incurred by failing to maintain them, Manu says: "But it is right for the wise man to give to all of them, according to his ability, food and clothing for life; for he who does not give becomes an outcast himself. (MDh 9.202)
"Extremely" means for as long as one lives. Devala states that even the obligation to support such a person no longer exists:
"To them, food and clothing are given, with the exception of those who have fallen [from their caste]."

By the word "outcast" (*patita*), those born of such [parents] are also implied, according to the Smṛti of Baudhāyana: "They should maintain [those who are] outcasts and those born of outcasts. Even those who have entered other stages of life (*āśrama*) must be maintained. For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha states: "Those who have entered other stages of life, as well as the impotent, the insane, and the outcast, are not entitled to a share; however, maintenance shall be provided for the impotent and the insane" (VaDh 17.52–54). The sons of those unworthy of a share, however, are entitled to a share. As Devala says:
"Their sons, being free from defects, shall receive a portion of their father's inheritance."

The legitimate (*aurasa*) and *kṣetraja* sons of those who are entitled to no share—provided they are free from defects such as impotence—are the inheritors; not the *dattaka* and other adopted sons. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya specifies:

"Among them, the *aurasa* and *kṣetraja* sons, being free from defects, are the inheritors. The daughters of those entitled to no share must be maintained and provided with the sacraments until their marriage. Their wives, if of virtuous conduct, must be maintained for as long as they live. And so says that same author:

And their daughters must be maintained until they are given away to husbands; likewise, the childless wives of these [deceased brothers] who have conducted themselves virtuously must be maintained. However, those who are unchaste or hostile shall be expelled. (YDh 2.141–42)
Kātyāyana also indicates other persons who are not entitled to a share:
"The son of a woman married out of order, one born of a woman of the same lineage (sagotra),
and one who has fallen from the religious life (pravrajyāvasita)— none of these is entitled to inherit property."
Manu also says:
"The son of a woman not authorized [to bear a child] and the son obtained from a brother-in-law by a woman who already has a son—
both of these are unworthy of a share, being born of an adulterer and born of lust" (MDh 9.143).

Yājñavalkya states the division of a woman's property: "That which is given by her father, mother, husband, or brother; that which is received near the sacred fire; and that which is given on account of supersession, and so forth—this is declared to be a woman's property."

“Likewise, Bandhudatta, Śulka, and Anvādheya—when the woman has died childless, her kinsmen shall obtain those. (YDh 2.143–44) *Adhyagnyupāgata* is that which was given by the maternal uncle or others at the time of marriage in the presence of the fire. And so says Kātyāyana:

"That which is given to women at the time of marriage in the presence of the fire is proclaimed by the virtuous as *adhyagnikṛta* (given near the fire), [and it is] *strīdhana* (woman’s property). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), that which is given on account of supersession (*ādhivedanika*)—meaning what is given to a woman who has been superseded—is included, as well as what is obtained through dowry (*adhyāvāhanika*), inheritance (*ṛktha*), purchase (*kraya*), and so on. And thus says Manu:

"Property given before the nuptial fire, that which is received at the wedding procession, that which is given as a token of affection, and that which is obtained from a brother, a mother, or a father—this is declared to be the sixfold property of a woman. (MDh 9.194).

The term "sixfold" is intended to exclude a smaller number, not to exclude a larger one. The specific nature of the property received at the wedding procession (*adhyāvāhanika*) and that which is given as a token of affection (*prītidatta*) has been described by Kātyāyana.
Furthermore, whatever a woman receives when being led away from her father’s house is declared to be the woman’s property known as *adhyāvāhanika*.

"Whatever is given out of affection by the mother-in-law or the father-in-law, as well as that which is given upon the salutation of their feet—that is called 'affectionately given' (*prītidatta*). Regarding "given by relatives," this refers to what is given by the girl's mother and father. "Dowry" (*śulka*) is that for which the girl is given after it has been received. "Subsequent gift" (*anvādheyaka*) is that which is given after the marriage ceremony. This was stated by Kātyāyana:
Whatever price is obtained for household utensils, vehicles, milch animals, ornaments, or articles for work— that is proclaimed as *śulka*.
"That property which is obtained by a woman from her husband's family after marriage,
as well as that which is obtained from her father's family, is called anvādheya.
Regarding the specific rules for the giving of gifts to women by fathers and others, Kātyāyana says:

"Women's property (strīdhana) must be given to a woman by her father, mother, husband, brother, or kinsmen according to their ability, up to two thousand [kārṣāpaṇas], with the exception of immovable property.

The meaning is that, according to one's ability, wealth other than immovable property should be given, limited to two thousand kārṣāpaṇas. And this rule is to be understood as applying to annual gifts; however, in the case of non-annual gifts given once for the purpose of maintenance, there is no such limit on the amount, nor is there an exclusion of immovable property. Thus says Bṛhaspati:
"And he should give sufficient wealth or a portion of land as she desires.
For this very reason, it was stated by that same author that even in the case of immovable property received as a dowry (*saudāyika*), there is the right to dispose of it as one wishes:
"Whether by a married woman or by a maiden, even in the husband's house or in her father's house..."
That which is obtained from a brother or from one's parents is known as saudāyika (gift of affection).
Upon receiving the wealth given as a dowry, independence is prescribed for women,
because that was granted by their [relatives] for the sake of compassion as a means of subsistence.
"And she may sell or give away even immovable property as she pleases.
Regarding immovable property given by a husband, Nārada states a specific rule:
"Whatever has been given to a woman by her husband out of affection, that remains hers even after he has died."

"She may eat or give it away as she pleases, with the exception of immovable property. Kātyāyana states that what has been given by the father and others under a condition (*upādhi*), or by reason of a connection (*yoga*), does not constitute *strīdhana* (woman's property). In that regard: "That which is given under a condition, or that which is given by way of a connection..."
"Neither by the father, nor by the brother, nor by the husband is that considered woman's property.

This refers to ornaments and the like given for the purpose of wearing during festivals and so forth; it means they are given under a specific condition (*sopādhika*). It further means that even what is obtained through craft (*śilpa*) and the like does not constitute woman's property. He (the same author) says:
"But that which is obtained through crafts, or that which is given out of affection from another," [550]
"The husband's ownership [extends] over that [portion], while the remainder is declared to be the woman's property (*strīdhana*).

"From another" means from a female friend and so forth. When this woman has passed away without a daughter, a daughter’s daughter, or a daughter’s daughter’s son, her kinsmen—the husband and others—take this *strīdhana*. Herein is the sequence: when the mother has died, the daughter takes it first. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya stated:
"The daughters [inherit] the remainder of the mother's [property] after her debts; in their absence, the lineage. (YDh 2.117)

Gautama also states: "The property of a woman belongs to her daughters who are unmarried and unsettled" (GDh 28.24). In the absence of daughters, the daughters of the daughter inherit, according to the traditional teaching of Yājñavalkya: "If [the daughter] has given birth, it belongs to her daughters. When there is a gathering of daughters of different mothers who have unequal shares, the distribution of portions is determined by the mother. Thus says Gautama: "In the case of the group of paternal and maternal aunts, there is a distinction in the shares" (GDh 28.17). Regarding the gathering of daughters and granddaughters, Manu [provides the rule].
"Whatever daughters they may have, to them also something should be given from the maternal grandmother's wealth, according to their merit and with affection. (MDh 9.193).
In the absence of the daughters' daughters as well, the daughters' sons are the heirs to the wealth. And so says Nārada:
"In the absence of the mother, [the inheritance goes to] the daughters; in the absence of the daughters, their offspring.

This means that in the absence of the daughters and their daughters, their offspring—the daughter's son (*dauhitra*)—takes [the estate]. However, in the absence of the daughter's sons, [it is stated]: "Upon the death of the parents, the sons shall divide the estate and the debt equally" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.117).
According to such statements by Yājñavalkya, sons take possession of the mother’s remaining property after she has been freed from her debts. As for that which was stated by Manu:
"But when the mother has passed away, all the uterine brothers and the uterine sisters shall divide the mother’s inheritance equally" (MDh 9.192).

Thus, this [text] does not intend to establish that sons and daughters together inherit the mother's estate; rather, it is for the purpose of securing an equal division when their connection to the wealth has been established, because of the hearing of the word "equal" (*sama*). Furthermore, as for what was stated by Śaṅkha and Likhita: "All uterine brothers and unmarried daughters (*kumāryaḥ*) are entitled to an equal share of the mother's estate," that too has the same meaning as the statement of Manu. Alternatively, these two statements refer to the property of a woman obtained from the family of her husband. Regarding this very subject, Bṛhaspati says:

"Women's property belongs to their offspring, and the daughter is entitled to a share thereof; provided she is unmarried, for if she is married, she does not receive her mother's property. Here, "offspring" refers to male offspring. As for that which was stated by Pāraskara:
The woman’s property (strīdhana) is declared to belong to an unmarried daughter;
however, a son does not receive it at all if she is married, for in that case he shares an equal portion [with her].
Thus, that [rule] refers to the case of a daughter who is not established [in marriage]. For this very reason, Manu says:
"But whatever may be the *yautaka* of the mother, that is indeed the share of the unmarried daughter" (MDh 9.131).

*Yautaka* is what has been obtained from the father's family. A daughter of a co-wife of superior caste takes the wealth of a childless woman of inferior caste; in her absence, her offspring [takes it]. This was stated by Manu:

"But whatever property may belong to a woman, having been given by her father in any way whatsoever, the Brāhmaṇī wife shall take that, or it shall belong to her daughter or her offspring" (MDh 9.198). Here, "Brāhmaṇī" is used as an indicative mark for the highest caste. In the absence of sons, grandsons take [the inheritance], because grandsons also have the authority to discharge their grandmother's debt, based on the scriptural injunction: "A debt is to be paid by a son or a grandson. Let it be granted that they have authority regarding the discharge of the debt.
If it is asked, "Why is there a right to inherit?"—
that is not so;
for when the appointed daughter has died, the husband does not deserve the property.

"And in the case of a daughter who has no son, that [property] should be taken by her brother. Thus it is said. In the case of an appointed daughter (*putrikā*), if a legitimate son (*aurasa*) is born after the father's death, that [son] alone shall take [the property], not the husband. As for the statement of Manu:
"But when an appointed daughter has died without a son, in any manner whatsoever..."

"And the husband of that daughter shall take that wealth without hesitation" (MDh 9.135); this is to be understood as applying when there is no brother born later. As for what was stated by Bṛhaspati—that in certain cases the woman's property belonging to one who has no offspring goes to the sister's son and others:
"The mother's sister, the maternal uncle's wife, the paternal uncle's wife, and the father's sister..."
A mother-in-law and the wife of one's elder brother are proclaimed to be equal to a mother.

"When these [women] have neither a biological son nor a daughter’s son, nor the son of such a daughter, their wealth shall be inherited by the sister’s sons and others. This is the meaning of this verse: in marriages such as the Brāhma and others, in the absence of the husband, and in marriages such as the Āsura and others, in the absence of both parents, the sister’s sons and others shall take the wealth of the mother’s sisters and so forth, respectively. Regarding the case where even a wife who is living and has offspring might inherit her husband's wealth, Yājñavalkya states: "Even while she lives, if she is childless, the husband may take the wife’s property; or, if she has offspring, he may take a share after providing for her maintenance. (YDh 2.145) The term "childless" (*aprajā*) here refers to one who has no son. The phrase "or, if she has offspring, he may take a share" means that he should provide for her maintenance according to his ability and then take the remainder. Alternatively, the word "share" (*bhāga*) may refer to a portion of the husband’s own property. The particle *vā* ("or") indicates an option based on the presence or absence of means. The word "even" (*api*) implies that this applies even when she is living with offspring. Thus, the meaning is that the husband may take the property of a wife who is living and has offspring, provided he maintains her according to his capacity. The use of the word "wife" (*patnī*) here is intended to exclude women other than those formally married. This is because the rule regarding the inheritance of a woman’s property by her mother and so forth applies specifically to those not married through the Brāhma and other [approved forms]. Therefore, the sense is that the husband inherits the property of a wife from a marriage such as the Āsura, provided she is living and has no son. However, if she has a son, the son inherits the property, not the husband. Furthermore, the husband inherits only after providing for her maintenance. This is because the rule concerning the husband’s right to take the property of a wife who has offspring is a general one, whereas the specific rule stating that the husband inherits the property of a wife who has no offspring is an exception. Since the general and the specific apply to different cases, there is no contradiction between them. Thus, the meaning is that the husband inherits the property of a wife who has no offspring, while the son inherits the property of a wife who has offspring. This is because the son is the primary heir to his mother’s property. As for the phrase "if she is living," it means that if she dies first, the husband inherits her property even if she has offspring. This is because the rule that the husband inherits the property of a wife who has offspring applies only while she is alive. Therefore, the meaning is that if she dies first, the husband inherits her property even if she has offspring. As for the phrase "according to his capacity," it means that the husband must maintain her according to his means. This is because the rule that the husband inherits the property of a wife who has offspring is contingent upon his providing for her maintenance. Therefore, the meaning is that the husband inherits the property of a wife who has offspring only after providing for her maintenance according to his ability. As for the phrase "the husband may take," it means that the husband alone takes the property, not the father-in-law or others. This is because the rule that the husband inherits the property of a wife who has offspring is a specific injunction. Therefore, the meaning is that the husband alone inherits the property of a wife who has offspring.
