"In times of famine, for the sake of religious duties, during illness, or when there is an obstruction, a husband is not required to return to his wife the woman's property he has taken" (YDh 2.147). This means that in cases such as being held captive by bandits, if he lacks his own wealth, he need not give back the woman's property after having taken it; however, if it was taken under other circumstances, he must certainly return it. And so says Kātyāyana:
Neither the husband, nor the son, nor the father, nor the brothers have authority over a woman’s property,
whether in its acquisition or its disposal.
And if even one among these should forcibly consume the woman’s property,
he shall be made to pay it back with interest and shall also incur a fine.

"If one should eat that very thing after having obtained permission and with a sense of pleasure, he should be made to pay the full amount [of the fine], provided that he is wealthy. Thus says Devala as well.
Maintenance, ornaments, the nuptial fee, and gains shall constitute a woman's property;
her husband is not entitled to enjoy this himself except in times of distress.
"In vain [is it] for liberation or enjoyment; one should give [the debt] to a woman along with interest.
Regarding the property to be divided, Kātyāyana says:
"That which belonged to the grandfather, that which belonged to the father, and whatever else was acquired by oneself..."

"But in the division among heirs, everything indeed is divided. This means that one should divide only that which has been acquired by oneself while subsisting on paternal property, because what is acquired without subsisting on it is not subject to division. One should divide even these three types of property after they have been cleared of debts. And so says the same author: "Having paid off debts and gifts made out of affection, one should divide the remainder."

For the purpose of discharging debts, even paternal debt should be divided in the absence of wealth, according to the statement: "The inheritance and the debt are equal. To clarify that the debt must be cleared rather than the inheritance being lost, that same author says:
"Such a debt must be cleared by the kinsmen together during the partition;
likewise [the division includes] houses, household utensils, draft animals, milch cattle, ornaments, and servants."
"Those who are being examined are divided; Bhṛgu declared that the ordeal by sacred libation (*kośa*) is secret.
In this context, the mention of the *kośa* is for the purpose of excluding other ordeals. And so says the same author:
"In cases of suspicion, establishing trust, making a compact, and the division of inheritance, [the *kośa*] is always [to be used]."
"In the case of being the performer of a collective action, one should cause the treasury itself to be delivered.
Thus [it is said]. Yājñavalkya states what property is indivisible:
"Whatever else has been acquired by oneself without detriment to the paternal estate..."
That which is given out of friendship or for the sake of marriage shall not belong to the heirs.

But he who recovers property that was seized and had come into his possession by succession need not give it to the co-heirs; the same applies to what has been acquired through learning. (YDh 2.118–19)

[558] Thus: that which is acquired by oneself through agriculture and the like without the destruction of the paternal estate, as well as that obtained through learning and the like, and that obtained from marriage, shall not belong to the brothers and others. However, regarding property inherited through the lineage of the father and so forth, which was seized by thieves and the like and not recovered by the father and others—if any one among the sons recovers it with the consent of the others, it belongs to him alone. But as for the field (immovable property), the recoverer takes only a fourth part; the remainder, however, is shared equally among all. And so says Śaṅkha:

"But whoever recovers, through exertion, land that was previously lost, others receive their respective shares after he has given them a fourth part. Likewise, what is obtained through learning—such as by teaching and so forth—belongs to him alone. The phrase "without contradicting the paternal property" is to be understood as a supplement in all cases. For this very reason, Manu says:
"What one acquires by one's own labor without depleting the paternal estate, as well as what is obtained through learning—one need not give that to the heirs;
for what is acquired by one's own effort, he is not obliged to give if he is unwilling. (MDh 9.208)
"By labor" means by agriculture and so forth. The mention of "father" is intended to include those who have not yet divided their inheritance. Vyāsa also states:

"What is acquired through learning, wealth gained by valor, and that which is a gift from a wife's family (saudāyika)—at the time of partition, these shall belong to him alone and need not be sought after by the other heirs."
Kātyāyana states the definition of wealth acquired through learning that is not subject to partition:
"But that learning which is acquired from another by means of subsisting on the food of another,
and whatever wealth is obtained through that [learning], is called 'wealth acquired through learning'."
Whatever is obtained through learning after it has been offered as a wager, one should know that to be "gained by knowledge" (vidyādhana); it is not subject to partition.

That which is obtained from a disciple, from officiating at a sacrifice, from answering questions, from resolving doubts raised by questions, from teaching one's own knowledge, from debate, and from lecturing; |||

That which is obtained from learning after setting aside what was previously acquired, being unprecedented, Bṛhaspati declares that to be "learning-wealth" (vidyādhanam) and that it is not to be divided.
For even among artisans, this dharma exists:
that which is standard, as well as what is additional, including that produced by the power of specialized knowledge, from a patron, or likewise from a pupil.
"This they call the common property of learning; that which is otherwise than this [is not].

By this, it is meant that wealth other than that acquired through learning—which was obtained by means of utilizing the undivided property of the father and others—is common or shared among those who have divided. In some cases, even wealth acquired through learning is subject to partition; thus says Nārada:
"He who maintains the family of a brother who is pursuing his studies..."
"Therefore, he shall receive a share from that wealth acquired through learning, even if he is unlearned. Thus says Kātyāyana:
"Among brothers who have been educated in learning within the family, or even those [so educated] by their father..."
"But that wealth which is acquired through valor is to be divided," so says Bṛhaspati.

Regarding wealth not acquired by paternal uncles or others in an undivided family—whether acquired from the father or even beyond him—which is obtained through learning or through valor and the like, that is "wealth of learning" (*vidyādhanam*) and is subject to division. Vasiṣṭha states that when wealth of learning is acquired using paternal property, the acquirer shall receive two shares: "Whatever among these [brothers] may have been acquired by someone, he shall receive two shares thereof" (VaDh 17.51). As for the rule: "But when there is a joint contribution toward an asset, the division is ordained to be equal."

Thus, that [rule] refers to wealth acquired through means other than learning, such as agriculture and the like. Regarding property acquired through learning (*vidyādhana*) which is otherwise indivisible, Gautama states that it may be divided according to the wish of the acquirer: "A learned man may, at his pleasure, give to those learned [co-heirs] what he has himself acquired. However, in the absence of such a wish, Nārada says: "A learned man shall not, against his will, give a share from his own wealth to one who is learned, unless that wealth was acquired by him while relying upon the paternal estate."
One should not give [the property] even with a desire [to benefit them] to one who is unlearned. Regarding this, Kātyāyana says:
"The wealth of learning must never be given by a learned man to those who are unlearned;
however, that wealth may be given by a learned man to those who are equally learned or superior."
He [Yājñavalkya] himself states that wealth acquired through valor and so forth, like wealth obtained through learning, is indivisible:
"That which is acquired through valor, that which is acquired through learning, and that which is designated as 'woman's property' (strīdhana)—
all this is not to be divided by the heirs during partition."
"But that which is acquired by means of a banner (dhvajāhṛta) is declared not to be divisible at all.
The definition of what is acquired by means of a banner was stated by that same [author]:
"That which is brought back from battle after putting to flight the enemy's forces..."
"Having sacrificed one's life for the sake of the master, that is called 'acquired under the banner' (*dhvajāhṛta*). Thus [says the law]. Bṛhaspati also says:
"That which may have been given by the grandfather, by the father, and by the mother..."
"His wealth acquired through valor, as well as that obtained from a wife, must not be taken away from him.
And the nature of wealth acquired through valor has been shown by Kātyāyana:
"When, having entered into danger, men perform a deed with force..."
The master, pleased with that deed, bestowed his favor upon him.
"In that regard, whatever wealth is acquired through valor shall belong [to the acquirer alone].

[562] Thus Vyāsa states that, just as one who has acquired wealth through learning while subsisting on the property of the father and others receives two shares, so too does the acquirer receive two shares of wealth acquired through valor:
"Whatever vehicle or weapon [is acquired] by relying upon common property..."
If one acquires wealth through valor or other such means, his brothers are entitled to share in it.
"Two shares should be given to him, while the remainder share equally.
Manu also states that other things are indivisible:
"Clothing, vehicles, ornaments, prepared food, water, and women [are indivisible]."
"Yogakṣema and the means of livelihood are declared not to be divisible. (MDh 9.219).
"Clothing worn by the father" refers to the garment. Clothing worn by the father must be given to the recipient of the *śrāddha* after the father's death during the partition. And so says Bṛhaspati:
"Clothing, ornaments, beds, and so forth, as well as whatever vehicles and such belonged to the father..."

"Having honored [the deceased] with perfumes and garlands, one should offer that [gift] to the recipient of the *śrāddha* feast. Other garments, however, are indeed to be divided. As for vehicles such as a leaf-seat, a horse, or a palanquin—that which was mounted by someone belongs to him alone; but that which was not mounted is to be divided among all. As for ornaments, too, whatever was worn by someone belongs to him alone; but what was not worn is common property and must be divided. Regarding ornaments worn by women while their husband is still living: [it is said: "If an ornament should have been worn by women while the husband is alive..."

"Heirs shall not divide that; those who do divide it fall. (MDh 9.200) Because this is stated as a specific rule by that very author, prepared food—such as rice, sweetmeats, and the like—must also be consumed according to availability and is not to be divided. Water refers to its source, such as a well; that too must be used in turn when needed and is not to be divided by means of a monetary valuation. Female slaves who are unequal in number should be made to perform work in turn. And so Bṛhaspati says:
"One should have a single woman perform work in each house according to her share."

"Many [shares] should be given in equal portions; this same rule applies even to slaves. However, those [properties] acquired by the father through marriage (*pitrāvaruddha*) are not to be divided, even if they are of equal value. Thus says Gautama: "There is no division among women who are united [in marriage]" (GDh 28.47). By the term *yoga*, the *iṣṭa* rites—those performed with the fires prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti—are indicated. By the term *kṣema*, the *pūrta* rites—such as giving gifts outside the sacrificial altar, constructing tanks, gardens, and so forth, which serve as the cause for the preservation of what has been acquired—are indicated. Both of these, even if acquired in opposition to the paternal estate, are indivisible. This was stated by Laugākṣi:
Those who perceive reality say that security, charitable works, sacrifices, and offerings are [meritorious];
they declare these, as well as beds and seats, to be indivisible.

[564] Thus it is said. Alternatively, by the term *yogakṣema*, the royal umbrella, chowries, weapons, vehicles, and so forth are meant. As for that which was stated by Uśanas regarding even the indivisibility of agricultural land:
"That which is to be cultivated by those of the same lineage (*sagotra*) is indivisible, even up to a thousand families;
likewise, the priestly office (*yājya*), a field, a document, prepared food, water, and women."

Thus, the statement that "land obtained as a gift is not to be divided between the son of a Kṣatriya wife and the son of a Brāhmaṇa wife" is intended to convey this very point, because of the traditional legal authority (smṛti) stating: "Land received as a gift must not be given to the son of a Kṣatriya wife or others.
Others, however, hold the view that even clothes and such items are indeed divisible; for Bṛhaspati says:
"Those who declared that clothes and other such things are indivisible have not reflected upon the matter."
The wealth of the prosperous consists of clothing and ornaments.
That which stands in the middle and cannot sustain life cannot be given to a single person;
it must be distributed through proper means, otherwise it would become useless.
Having sold clothing and ornaments, or having recovered a debt by means of a written document,
or having exchanged prepared food for unprepared food, the property is then divided.
Just as water from a well or a pond is drawn out and taken according to need,
so should one woman be made to perform labor in each household according to her share.
Many [shares] should be given in equal portions; this same rule applies even to slaves. The profit from [property] that provides for security and maintenance is divided equally.
"And the use [of these items] should be made by the heirs in proportion to their shares.
Therefore, the statement of Manu and the statement of Uśanas, which establish that clothing and other such items are indivisible, are to be disregarded.

That is untenable; for when there is a conflict between statements, it is proper to resort to a systematic allocation of their respective scopes (*viṣayavyavasthā*), not to treat them otherwise. It has already been stated previously that the statements of Bṛhaspati concern clothing and so forth that have not been worn, whereas the statements of Manu and others concern clothing and so forth that have been worn; thus, a systematic allocation of their scopes is consistent.
If, at the time of partition, something was concealed by someone and is subsequently brought to light, they should all divide that property equally. Thus says Yājñavalkya:
"Whatever property, previously taken from one another, is discovered after the partition, they shall divide that again into equal shares; such is the settled rule. (YDh 2.126)

The word *sama* (equal) is intended to exclude an unequal division. By using the plural form *vibhajeran* (they shall divide), it is shown that the property seen by one person alone must not be taken by him. Manu also says: "When all debts and assets have been divided according to rule, whatever may subsequently be discovered, all of that they shall bring to equality" (MDh 9.218).

Even property that has been divided unequally, provided it was done without transgressing the rules prescribed by the scriptures, should be brought to equality—just like property that was stolen. And so says Kātyāyana:
"Whatever property may have been mutually misappropriated or improperly divided, Bhr̥gu declares that when it is recovered later, it shall be divided into equal shares."

This being the case, since the rule for partition applies only to property that was concealed and subsequently discovered, it is understood that there is no further partition of what has already been divided. As for that which was stated by Manu:
"But when a partition has been made, if anything common is seen therein, this is not to be considered a valid partition; indeed, it must be performed all over again."

Thus, this should be understood as applying to cases where the liquid substances have been divided, prior to the accounting of income and expenditure; for otherwise, statements such as "mutually stolen" would become devoid of scope. Furthermore, there is a fault even in mutual deception. Thus says the Śruti: "He who deprives a sharer of his share—whether he destroys him or not—if he does not destroy him, then he destroys his son, or else his grandson. This is the meaning: he who "deprives" (nudate)—that is, excludes from the share or fails to give a share to—a "sharer" (bhāgin), one entitled to a share; then, having deprived him of his share, he "destroys" (cyavate)—that is, ruins or makes a sinner of—that "seizer" (apahāraka). If he does not ruin him, then he ruins his son or grandson. As for that which was stated by Manu:

"He who, out of greed, should defraud his younger brothers, though he be the eldest, shall lose his status as the eldest, shall receive no share, and must be restrained by the kings" (MDh 9.213). This [verse] is intended to demonstrate that even for an independent eldest brother there is fault in misappropriating the common property, let alone for the dependent younger brothers; it is not intended solely to establish the fault of the eldest. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of restricting the Vedic revelation (śruti) by means of the Smṛti. Nārada states what must be done regarding those who have been partitioned:
If many things born from a single source are distinct in nature, distinct in activity,
and endowed with distinct qualities and functions, they would not be considered as a unified whole in their effects.
"If they should give away their own shares, or even sell them,
they may do all that as they wish, for they are masters of their own property."

Brothers born of one father, though divided, may perform religious acts such as *iṣṭāpūrta*—which require wealth—for one another without mutual consent. Likewise, they may possess separate implements for work, such as mortars and pestles, along with the materials subordinate to those tasks. Thus, if brothers are not in agreement regarding their duties, they may perform them disregarding one another. Similarly, divided brothers may give away or sell their own shares, or even choose not to give them; they may do all this according to their own will. This is because, being divided, they are masters of their own property, meaning they are independent owners. As for the statement of Bṛhaspati:
Whether partitioned or unpartitioned, heirs have equal rights to immovable property;
for no single person has authority over it in matters of gift, mortgage, or sale.

Thus, it should be explained as follows: when properties are undivided, because they are common [to all], no single person has independent authority; therefore, permission must necessarily be obtained from all. However, in the case of divided properties, permission from all is required at a later time for the sake of easily dispelling doubts regarding whether they are divided or undivided, and not because of any lack of authority on the part of a single individual. Consequently, legal transactions are indeed established even in the absence of the consent of those who have already divided their shares. As for another Smṛti text:
"By the consent of one's own village, kinsmen, neighbors, and heirs, and by the gift of gold and water, one acquires ownership of land through these six means."
Thus, this is his intention: in that regard, the approval of the village [is required]; the acceptance [of a gift] should be public, especially in the case of immovable property.

According to this traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*), [the consent of the neighbors] is required solely for the purpose of clarifying the legal transaction; it is not the case, however, that a legal proceeding cannot be finalized without the consent of the village. The consent of the neighbors is likewise intended only for the purpose of removing disputes regarding boundaries. The consent of the heirs is also for the sake of facilitating the transaction by dispelling doubts as to whether they are divided or undivided. Furthermore, the giving of gold and water is for the purpose that when a sale is to be performed, one should effect the sale of immovable property in the form of a gift after having given gold and water along with it.
[569] "There is no sale of immovable property; one may, however, create a mortgage with permission.
Since the sale of immovable property is thus prohibited, it is said: "He who accepts land and he who bestows land..."
Both of them, being performers of meritorious deeds, will certainly go to heaven.
Thus, because both giving and receiving are praiseworthy, Yājñavalkya states the grounds for a decision when a partition is denied:

"In the case of a denial of partition, the determination of the partition should be known through cognates, kinsmen, witnesses, and documents, as well as by means of houses, fields, and separate property held individually. (YDh 2.149)

"Kinsmen" (*jñātayaḥ*) are paternal relatives; "relatives" (*bandhavaḥ*), however, are maternal uncles and others. A "document" (*lekhyam*) is a deed of partition. By these means, the determination of partition is to be known. [It is also known] by "separate property" (*yautakaiḥ*), meaning houses and fields that have been divided. Nārada states another mark of partition: "In a dispute regarding the law of partition among heirs, the decision is reached through kinsmen, a document of shares, and the commencement of separate activities."
For brothers who have not divided their inheritance, a single religious duty prevails;
once division has occurred, their religious duties also become separate for each.
Those brothers who are divided may act as witnesses, provide surety, give gifts, or receive them from one another; those who are undivided may not do so.
The giving and receiving of cattle, food, houses, and fields, as well as gifts,
religious duties, income, and expenditures, are to be understood as distinct for those who have divided their inheritance.
"Those among whom these [documents] circulate in the world regarding their own inheritances—
one should understand them to be divided even in the absence of a written record.
Thus says Bṛhaspati as well.
"Those who maintain separate income, expenditure, and assets, and engage with one another in lending at interest and trade, have undoubtedly divided their property.

Thus, in the absence of witnesses and other evidence, the determination of partition is to be understood from such signs as lending at interest, trade, and so forth. And likewise, that same [author] states:
"Forceful seizure, ownership of immovable property, prior partition,
and the inheritance of heirs are to be known by inference when there are no witnesses.
He [Yājñavalkya] has also stated the indicative marks that establish forceful seizure and the other such matters:
"Family connection, obstruction, seizure, and force are the means of proof;
separate wealth from one's own enjoyment of immovable property is the mark of partition.

Here, "family connection" (*kulānubandha*) refers to the continuity of enmity between ancestors. "Obstruction" (*vyāghāta*) refers to mutual [conflict]. "Seizure" (*hoḍha*) is property taken away by force; the sight of such [property] is the evidence. "One's own enjoyment" (*svasvabhoga*) of immovable property and the separate holding [of assets] by each other are to be understood as marks of partition, since they are prohibited among those who have not divided their inheritance. Thus says Yājñavalkya:

[571] "For it is recorded in the Smṛti that among brothers, between husband and wife, and between father and son, standing as surety, contracting debt, and giving testimony are declared to be common property when they are undivided. (YDh 2.52).
When a decision is impossible to reach through witnesses, documents, or logical reasoning, [the judge should act].
Vṛddha-Yājñavalkya prohibits the use of ordeals where he states: "If even logical arguments are insufficient, one should crush [the opponent] with oaths alone";
thus, he forbids the divine test (divya) in cases of doubt regarding the law of partition, which should instead be resolved by kinsmen, witnesses, and written documents.
"An investigation of the partition must be carried out; there shall be no divine ordeal. Thus [it is said].
To the inquiry, "How then is a decision reached in that case?", Manu says:
"Where there is a mutual dispute among heirs regarding a partition..."
"Furthermore, a division must be made even by those situated in separate places.
This means that where doubt persists even through logical arguments, a further division must be made. As for what was said by that same author:
"A share falls [to one] only once; a daughter is given away only once."
He says "I give" only once; these three things are each done but once.

Thus, this should be understood as being capable of determination through reasoning and other means. Bṛhaspati states that a king must punish one who, having himself made a doubtful partition, subsequently acts to subvert it:
"He who, having made a partition according to his own will, should again act in contradiction to it, may be restrained by the kings and punished according to the circumstances. [572]
By way of consequence and by way of persistence;
thus concludes the division of inheritance. Now, the two titles of legal dispute known as gambling (dyūta) and betting (samāhvaya) are being examined.

Manu states their essential natures: "In this world, that which is carried out by means of inanimate objects is called *dyūta* (gambling); that which is carried out by means of animate beings is to be known as *samāhvaya* (betting). (MDh 9.223)
[It is played] with inanimate objects such as dice, sticks, and small markers; and with animate beings such as cocks and the like. And so says Nārada:
"Gambling performed with crooked means using dice, sticks, small markers, and the like, as well as betting games with birds—this is termed *dyūta* (gambling) and *samāhvaya* (challenging)."

[573] Thus: *akṣāḥ* are dice; *vadhrāḥ* are leather straps; *śalākāḥ* are long, square pieces made of ivory and the like. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), cowries and other such items are included. Gambling (*dyūta*) is that play or sport performed with these [objects] preceded by a wager (*paṇa*). The meaning of *samāhvaya* is that sport preceded by a wager which is performed with living beings (*prāṇi*), such as cocks and the like, or with animals (*kāra*), such as wrestlers, rams, and the like. Bṛhaspati also says: "Cocks, rams, bulls, and so forth, mutually seized..."
"Those who have made a wager strike [at each other]; they call this *samāhvaya* (challenging).
He [Yājñavalkya] further states that the gambling place must be supervised by a *sabhika* (the master of the gaming house):
"The game must be conducted under the supervision of a *sabhika*, for the purpose of identifying thieves."
Regarding this, Nārada states another alternative:
"Alternatively, a gambler, having paid the king the share as prescribed, may conduct gambling openly; in this way, no fault is found."
Yājñavalkya states the livelihood of the superintendent of the gambling hall:
"The keeper of the hall shall take five percent from a gambler who stakes a hundred [coins] at the rate of ten percent interest;
from any other, he shall take ten percent. (YDh 2.199)

[574] Thus: A *glaha* is a stake devised by gamblers through mutual agreement. In that context, a *śatikā-vṛddhi* is interest—either amounting to one hundred or exceeding it—based upon that stake; such is called *śatikavṛddhi*. From that gambler, the *sabhika* (the master of the gaming house) shall take five percent (*pañcakaṃ śatam*) for his own livelihood. This means he shall take five *paṇas* out of every hundred won at the stake—that is, the twentieth part of the winnings. The *sabhā* is the hall for the residence of gamblers; the one stationed there is the *sabhika*. However, the *sabhāpati* (the master of the assembly) is one who provides all the gaming equipment, such as the dice, and subsists on the wealth accumulated therein. From another gambler who charges interest less than one hundred, he shall take ten percent (*daśakaṃ śatam*) of the won property—that is, the tenth part. He himself states the duty of the *sabhika* thus established:

"Having been properly protected, he should give the king the share as agreed; he should cause the winnings to be paid to the victor and, being patient, should utter truthful words. (YDh 2.200) The superintendent of gambling, whose livelihood has been fixed by the king and who is protected from rogue gamblers, shall give the king the share as stipulated. He should collect the won wealth from the defeated party through [official] agents and the like, and deliver it to the victor. Likewise, being patient, he should utter truthful words for the sake of inspiring confidence among the gamblers. Bṛhaspati also says:
"The keeper of the stakes (sabhika) shall pay there to the winner and to the king.

[575] This means that the keeper of the stakes should become the recipient of the wager from the defeated gamblers by means of imprisonment and so forth; the sense is that even before the taking of the wager, he should give his own stake to the king and to the winner according to their respective shares. And thus says Kātyāyana:
"The winner shall give his own property; the winnings are to be received after three fortnights."
"Or immediately by the keeper of the gambling house from the gambler himself; of this there is no doubt.
When the keeper of the gambling house is unable to cause the winner to pay the won wealth, then the king shall cause it to be paid; thus says Yājñavalkya:
"When the king's share has been obtained and the circle of gamblers is well-known..."
"One should cause the winner to pay [the stake] in a place where there is a keeper of the hall (*sabhika*); otherwise, however, not.

(YDh 2.201) "Otherwise" means that in a secret gambling match—one devoid of a *sabhika* and where no share has been paid to the king—the judge shall not cause the winner to receive the won stake; this is the meaning. Regarding this, he [Yājñavalkya] himself states the grounds for a decision when there is a dispute over victory or defeat: "For they alone are the observers of the legal proceedings, and they alone are the witnesses. (YDh 2.202)

For legal proceedings known as gambling, the gamblers themselves—those possessing the characteristics already described—are to be appointed by the king as judges, and not those endowed with learning and Vedic study; and they alone, the gamblers, shall be the witnesses. Viṣṇu also states: "Gamblers should remain among gamblers regarding doubtful points;
whoever are the observers there, they alone shall be the witnesses for them."
Bṛhaspati states that when there is mutual contradiction among witnesses, the king should deliberate:
"When both [parties] are in doubt, gamblers may serve as examiners;
but when they are hostile, then the king himself should deliberate."

Yājñavalkya states the punishment for those who practice fraudulent gambling: "Those who play with false dice or by means of fraudulent devices [such as] gems and mantras shall be banished from the kingdom by the king, marked with a brand. (YDh 2.202) The meaning is that those who gamble using false dice and the like, or through highly deceptive means such as gems and mantras, shall be branded on the foot with the mark of a dog and expelled from their own realm. Regarding the specifics of this banishment, Nārada says:

"The king should banish from the kingdom those wicked men who play with fraudulent dice; for it is traditionally taught that their punishment consists in placing a rosary around their necks. Regarding specific punishments, Viṣṇu states: "In gambling, the hands of those who play with fraudulent dice shall be cut off; the fingers of those who play by deceitful means shall be amputated at the joints. Nārada states the punishment for those who engage in gambling without authorization:
"But that man who should play at dice without being authorized by the king shall not receive the hundred [of the stake] as he pleases; rather, he deserves punishment.
Thus Yājñavalkya extends to gambling (samāhvaya) the entire set of rules prescribed for dice-play (dyūta).

"This same rule is to be understood as applying to gambling with living beings and to duels" (YDh 2.203). The meaning is that the dharma characterized by the appointment of the keeper of the gaming hall (*sabhika*) and so forth is to be recognized as applicable to duels as well. Regarding gambling with living beings, Bṛhaspati states:
"In a duel, whoever should suffer defeat, [the loss] belongs to his owner."
"The owner of that [property] must pay the wager which was stipulated therein.
Regarding this, Nārada states that even the stipulation of a wager may be either made or not made:
"That which is done in jest, and that which is unknown to the king..."

"Even in that case, he shall not obtain the desired object, or else that which is agreed upon by the two of them. Here, "kāmya" refers to the desired object, which is the stake. As for that which was stated by Manu:
"He who engages in gambling or betting, or causes another to do so..."
The king shall cause all of them to be executed, as well as Śūdras who assume the marks of the twice-born. (MDh 9.224) Gambling and betting are open forms of theft;
therefore, the king should always exert effort to suppress them. (MDh 9.222)
The king should prohibit gambling and betting within his realm;
these two vices bring about the destruction of kings who rule the earth.
[He should likewise banish] gamblers, actors, potters, and men belonging to heretical sects.

"Those engaged in improper occupations and liquor-sellers shall be quickly expelled from the city" (MDh 9.225), and so forth—all of this should be applied to the context of fraudulent gambling, or to cases involving kings who lack a superintendent or a gambling master. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says:
"Gambling, which destroys truth, purity, and wealth, was forbidden by Manu."
"But it may be permitted by others, provided it includes the king's share and is supervised by a master of the gaming house, for the purpose of identifying thieves. Thus,
the legal head of dispute known as gambling and betting has been defined.

Having defined the eighteen titles of legal procedure (*vyavahārapada*), beginning with non-payment of debt (*ṛṇādāna*) and ending with gambling (*samāhvaya*), in accordance with the sequence of their enumeration,
the title of dispute known as *prakīrṇaka* (miscellaneous matters), as defined by Bṛhaspati, is now set forth.
In that regard, Nārada has defined the distinctions between their characteristics;
it should be understood that among the miscellaneous matters (*prakīrṇaka*), there are legal disputes (*vyavahāra*) pertaining to the king,
such as the defiance of the king's commands and likewise the failure to perform his duties.
Furthermore, there is the confusion of authoritative means of knowledge, as well as that of the *prakṛtis*;
and the subversion of the dharma of heretics, guilds, corporations, and assemblies.

There is also dispute between father and son, as well as among those belonging to the various stages of life (āśramas) when [the tradition] is lost; furthermore, there is the fault of the intermixture of castes (varṇasaṃkara) and likewise the restriction of their respective duties.
"And that which has not been seen in the previous [titles] shall all be *prakīrṇaka* (miscellaneous).

Thus, those disputes which fall under the category of *prakīrṇaka*—namely, those concerning the violation of the king's commands, the execution of his orders, the protection of his person, and so forth—are exclusively dependent upon the sovereign. In such cases, the king himself must determine the legal decision after ascertaining the hostility of those who persist in a course of conduct deviating from the path of *smṛti* and established custom. By stating this, it is indicated that a lawsuit which relies upon the king is called *prakīrṇaka*. Regarding the specific punishment for the obstruction of the king's command in that context, Yājñavalkya says:
"He who writes a royal edict as either deficient or excessive, or he who releases an adulterer or a thief, shall be punished with the highest fine.

(YDh 2.295) He who writes a royal edict while declaring the measurement of land granted by a king or a fixed tenure (*nibandhana*) to be either less or more than it actually is, and he who, having apprehended an adulterer or a thief, releases them without reporting it to the king—both of these are to be punished with the highest fine. Vyāsa also says:
Having seized the matter in the court of justice, he renders a decision through unrighteousness and carries out subsequent actions, thereby destroying the king's wealth.
"Those who live by bribery, having been deprived of their wealth, shall be banished.
Regarding the punishment for performing such acts, Yājñavalkya says:
"The punishment for one who mounts the royal vehicle or seat is the highest amercement" (YDh 2.303).
Kātyāyana also says:
"Those who are addicted to the king's amusements, those who subsist on the king's service,
and whoever speaks what is unpleasant to him— for them he should ordain the death penalty."
Manu states the punishment for the embezzlement of the king’s treasury and similar offenses:

"Those who steal from the king’s treasury, and those who stand in opposition to him, he shall cause to be executed by various forms of punishment and shall confiscate their entire property" (MDh 9.275).
Nārada states that even in the event of the confiscation of all property, whatever constitutes a person’s means of livelihood must not be seized from them:
"The weapons of those who live by arms, the seeds of those who live by agriculture,
the ornaments of courtesans, and the musical instruments of those skilled in playing them."
"And whatever is the tool of anyone, by which artisans live—
that the king ought not to seize, even when all their possessions are being confiscated.
Thus Manu declares that for a Brāhmaṇa, shaving the head is the substitute for the death penalty.
"The killing of a Brāhmaṇa, shaving the head, banishment from the city,
branding on the forehead with the mark of the crime, and being paraded on a donkey.
Thus Yājñavalkya first states the punishment for mutual division arising from anger.

"For one who pierces two eyes, for one who issues commands hostile to the king, and likewise for a Śūdra bearing the marks of a Brahmin while living, the fine shall be eight hundred [paṇas]. (YDh 2.304).
As for that which has been stated in another Smṛti:

"One should have Śūdras who bear the marks of the twice-born executed with various forms of punishment"—this [rule] should be understood to apply to those who wear the marks of a Brāhmaṇa for the sake of their livelihood. Manu states the punishment for one who causes injury to a Brāhmaṇa:
"But a person of inferior caste who intentionally harasses Brāhmaṇas..."
"The king should slay him by various means of execution that cause him distress. (MDh 9.248).
Regarding the punishment for Śūdras who have renounced the world and so forth, Kātyāyana says:
"A Śūdra who has fallen from renunciation, as well as one devoted to recitation and burnt offerings..."
One should pacify the evil by execution, or else the offender should be fined double the amount.
"Wherever a matter has been decided and adjudicated, it should be known as legally settled; a wise man should not overturn it. (MDh 9.233)

If, due to the testimony of either the plaintiff or the defendant, there arises a suspicion that the legal proceeding was conducted unjustly, the king should initiate the case again, provided he first pledges to impose double the fine [if the second trial results in an injustice]. This is intended to mean that even when the justice of the proceeding has been ascertained, the king must not restart it out of greed or other such motives. Furthermore, even a decision rendered by another king that deviates from justice should be set right upon proper investigation and established on the path of righteousness; this applies to whatever has been done erroneously by another king through ignorance.
Even that which has been established unjustly, one should re-establish according to justice.
Thus it is from the Smṛti. Regarding the destiny of one who has seized fines through unjust means, [the text] says:
"The king shall offer to Varuṇa the fine that was unjustly taken;
he himself shall give to the Brahmins thirty times that amount. Thus it is said.

Whatever punishment has been unjustly imposed by a king out of greed or other such motives, he should himself give that multiplied thirtyfold to Brahmins, having resolved, "This is for Varuṇa. Furthermore, whatever was taken unjustly in the form of a fine must be returned to him, because otherwise the fault of theft would ensue; for otherwise, by taking an unjust fine, there would result the severance of the prior owner's possession. Yama states the fruit for a king who thus administers justice according to the path prescribed in the scriptures:
"For a king who thus proceeds according to Dharma and wields the rod of punishment..."
"His fame shall spread in this world, and his residence in heaven shall likewise be imperishable. Thus [says] Manu as well:
"In this manner, the king, concluding all these legal proceedings..."
"Having cast off all sin, he attains the supreme goal.

Thus [ends the section] in the work composed by Mādhava, the minister of the illustrious King Bukka— the sovereign lord of great kings, the supreme ruler, the promoter of the Vedic path, and the upholder of the imperial authority.
In the Mādhavīyā commentary on the Parāśara-smṛti, the third section, the Vyavahārakāṇḍa, is completed.
This Vyavahārakāṇḍa is finished,
and with it, this Parāśara-smṛti and its commentary are concluded.
